He defended his father's legal and philosophical legacy, answered questions from communities across the Mediterranean and led the Jewish court in Fustat. At the same time he developed an original pietist programme, seeking to restore practices of inward devotion, disciplined prayer, solitude and bodily humility that he regarded as authentically biblical and rabbinic, although some contemporaries opposed changes associated with his circle. His massive Arabic work כפאיה אלעאבדין, known in Hebrew as המספיק לעובדי השם, systematized halakhah, ethics and spiritual discipline; only portions survive. His פירוש התורה, responsa, ברכת אברהם and מלחמות השם preserve his biblical interpretation and his defense of ר׳ משה בן מימון. He remained nagid until his death in Fustat in 1237 and was succeeded by his son ר׳ דוד הנגיד.
title: הנגיד, בנו וממשיך דרכו של הרמב״ם
aliases: ר׳ אברהם בן משה בן מימון

name: ר׳ יחיאל בן יוסף מפריז
bio: ר׳ יחיאל בן יוסף מפריז was a leading French Tosafist, head of the Paris academy, and defender of the Talmud. Born near the end of the twelfth century, probably in Meaux, he studied under ר׳ יהודה שירליאון and succeeded him around 1225. His Paris yeshiva reportedly attracted hundreds of students; among those associated with it was ר׳ מאיר מרוטנבורג. In 1240, after the apostate Nicholas Donin accused the Talmud before Louis IX’s court, ר׳ יחיאל בן יוסף מפריז served as the principal Jewish disputant. The proceedings culminated in the public burning of wagonloads of Hebrew manuscripts in Paris in 1242, a catastrophe for northern French learning. He continued teaching and communal fundraising under mounting pressure. Around 1260 he emigrated with family and disciples to Acre, where he founded an academy that transmitted the French Tosafist tradition in the Land of Israel. His rulings and Tosafot survive through citations and collections rather than one securely authored comprehensive book. He is commonly said to have died in Acre in 1268, although alternate chronologies and competing burial traditions require caution. No authenticated portrait exists.
title: מבעלי התוספות וראש ישיבת פריז

name: ר׳ משה בן נחמן
bio: ר׳ משה בן נחמן (1194–c.1270), known as רמב״ן, Nachmanides, and in Catalan documents as Bonastruc ça Porta, was a Catalan Talmudist, halakhist, biblical commentator, kabbalist, communal leader, and physician. Born in Girona, he absorbed Spanish legal traditions together with the dialectical learning of the northern French Tosafists through teachers including ר׳ יהודה בן יקר and ר׳ נתן בן מאיר מטרינקטייל. His writings helped establish the dominant school of Talmudic interpretation in medieval Catalonia; major students included ר׳ שלמה בן אדרת and ר׳ אהרן הלוי. He sought a mediating position during the Maimonidean controversies while retaining substantive disagreements with ר׳ משה בן מימון. In 1263 King James I compelled him to represent Judaism against the convert Pablo Christiani at the Barcelona Disputation. His Hebrew account of the debate led to Dominican accusations and legal proceedings. After leaving the Crown of Aragon, he reached Acre and Jerusalem in 1267, helped renew organized Jewish worship in devastated Jerusalem, visited biblical sites, and later taught in Acre. His פירוש התורה integrates philology, midrash, halakhah, theology, geography, and guarded kabbalistic interpretation; he revised it after seeing the Land of Israel. His final years created a durable intellectual bridge between Catalonia and the eastern Mediterranean.
title: רמב״ן

name: ר׳ משה מקוצי
bio: ר׳ משה בן יעקב מקוצי (approximately 1200–1260), known as the סמ״ג after ספר מצוות גדול, was a French Tosafist, preacher and halakhic codifier. Associated with Coucy and educated in Paris under ר׳ יהודה בן יצחק שירליאון, he drew on the pietistic teaching of ר׳ יהודה החסיד and the Franco-German Tosafist tradition. In 1235–1236 he traveled through France, Provence and Spain, preaching practical observance and ethical conduct to Jewish communities. In 1240 he was one of four rabbis summoned to defend the Talmud at the Paris disputation initiated by Nicholas Donin; the subsequent confiscation and burning of Talmud manuscripts sharpened the need for a portable halakhic code. Completed around 1247–1250, ספר מצוות גדול organizes Jewish law through the 365 prohibitions and 248 positive commandments, combines Talmudic discussion with Ashkenazic rulings and makes extensive, though sometimes critical, use of ר׳ משה בן מימון. The work became one of medieval Ashkenaz’s most influential codes and directly inspired ר׳ יצחק מקורביל’s ספר מצוות קטן.
title: בעל ספר מצוות גדול; הסמ״ג

name: ר׳ יעקב בן ששת גירונדי
bio: ר׳ יעקב בן ששת גירונדי was a thirteenth-century Catalan kabbalist and writer associated with the celebrated mystical circle of Girona. Almost nothing securely personal survives: his parents, teachers, birth and death dates, family, offices and travels are unknown. Sources call him Gerondi and place his activity in Girona, probably also his birthplace. His writings show close knowledge of the teachings of ר׳ יצחק סגי נהור and the Girona kabbalists, including ר׳ עזריאל מגירונה, but he does not call ר׳ יצחק his teacher; a direct discipleship therefore should not be asserted. His major work, משיב דברים נכוחים, is a thirty-chapter response to מאמר יקוו המים by ר׳ שמואל אבן תיבון. It attacks conclusions he considered religiously dangerous while engaging seriously with philosophy and natural science rather than rejecting all rational inquiry. He defended creation, providence, prayer and divine recompense through a kabbalistic account of continuous emanation from the sefirotic realm into the physical world. שער השמים presents kabbalistic teaching in elaborate rhymed prose. Modern scholarship also assigns ספר האמונה והבטחון to him; medieval manuscripts and printings frequently attributed it to ר׳ משה בן נחמן, and alternative authorship proposals were once influential. His writings were later used extensively by ר׳ בחיי בן אשר and ר׳ מנחם רקנאטי, making his thought more influential than the scarcity of explicit medieval citations to his name suggests.
title: מקובל ופולמוסן מחוג גירונה

name: ר׳ יונה בן אברהם גירונדי
bio: ר׳ יונה בן אברהם גירונדי (c.1200–1263), known as רבנו יונה and רבנו יונה החסיד, was a Catalan Talmudist and one of medieval Judaism’s most influential moral teachers. Originating in Girona and related to ר׳ משה בן נחמן, he studied in the Franco-Provençal scholarly world, most notably with ר׳ שלמה בן אברהם מן ההר at Montpellier. He joined the 1232 ban against philosophical writings of ר׳ משה בן מימון. Later accounts connect the Christian burning of Talmud manuscripts in Paris in 1242 with his public remorse over the dangers of recruiting ecclesiastical power into Jewish controversy; the precise details and chronology are debated. He subsequently taught in Barcelona, where ר׳ שלמה בן אברהם אבן אדרת became his foremost disciple, and then moved to Toledo. His שערי תשובה, ספר היראה and אגרת התשובה shaped Jewish ethical and penitential literature. His Talmudic teaching survives partly through students: תלמידי רבנו יונה on Alfasi’s Berakhot is not a verbatim autograph, while עליות דרבנו יונה preserves his analysis of Bava Batra. He died in Toledo in November 1263 before completing a planned journey to the Land of Israel.
title: רבנו יונה; מחבר שערי תשובה

name: ר׳ צדקיה בן אברהם הרופא
bio: ר׳ צדקיה בן אברהם הרופא, a member of Rome’s distinguished Anaw family, was a thirteenth-century Italian halakhist and the compiler of שבולי הלקט. He was the younger brother of ר׳ בנימין בן אברהם הרופא and studied both in Italy and in the Ashkenazic world. Sources associate his training with ר׳ ישעיה בן מאלי דטראני and with ר׳ יעקב מווירצבורג; his responsorial network included ר׳ אביגדור כהן מווינה and ר׳ מאיר בן ברוך מרוטנבורג. שבולי הלקט arranges the laws of prayer, Sabbaths, festivals, mourning and other recurring practice into 372 sections, preserving a particularly rich collection of Italian, French and German customs and rulings. Its value is therefore both legal and historical: it records traditions that might otherwise have disappeared. A supplementary collection treats dietary and other prohibitions. The work circulated in manuscript for centuries before modern printing, and later abridgements and expansions reflect its continuing authority. Rome is his secure home and principal centre; the Würzburg study point is included because the biographical tradition names that teacher, while the exact travel year and his lifespan endpoints remain approximate.
title: בעל שבולי הלקט; מחכמי רומא
aliases: רבי צדקיה בן אברהם מן הענוים

name: ר׳ יצחק מקורביל
bio: ר׳ יצחק בן יוסף מקורביל (approximately 1210–1280), known as the סמ״ק, was a French Tosafist and halakhist. He studied in the Paris academy of his father-in-law ר׳ יחיאל מפריז and under the scholars of Évreux, especially ר׳ שמואל מאיוורא. Settled at Corbeil, he became renowned for piety and teaching; his students included ר׳ פרץ בן אליהו מקורביל, ר׳ ברוך חיים בן מנחם מניאור and ר׳ יוסף בן אברהם. At their urging he completed עמודי הגולה, usually called ספר מצוות קטן, in 1277. Drawing heavily on ר׳ משה מקוצי’s ספר מצוות גדול, he recast the commandments into a concise practical handbook arranged for regular study, combining law, ethics and religious exhortation. Communities in France and Germany quickly adopted the work, and successive scholars surrounded it with glosses, notably הגהות רבנו פרץ. He also composed collections of ritual decisions and Talmudic material, only fragments of which survive. The סמ״ק’s portability and daily-study structure gave it lasting influence in Ashkenazic legal culture.
title: בעל ספר מצוות קטן; הסמ״ק

name: ר׳ מאיר בן ברוך מרוטנבורג
bio: ר׳ מאיר בן ברוך מרוטנבורג (c.1215–1293), the Maharam of Rothenburg, was the leading German Tosafist, halakhic respondent and communal authority of the later thirteenth century. Born in Worms to the scholar ר׳ ברוך, he studied in German academies and in France under figures including ר׳ יחיאל מפריז, and witnessed the public burning of the Talmud in Paris in 1242, which inspired his elegy שאלי שרופה באש. He established a major academy at Rothenburg ob der Tauber and answered questions from communities across Europe. His pupils, including ר׳ אשר בן יחיאל and ר׳ מרדכי בן הלל, transmitted his rulings into the central codes of Ashkenaz. Attempting to leave the empire with his family amid intensified royal exploitation in 1286, he was arrested in Lombardy and handed to Emperor Rudolf I. He continued teaching and answering questions while imprisoned, first at Wasserburg and then Ensisheim, where he died. His body was released only in 1307, when Alexander ben Salomon Wimpfen paid for its burial in Worms.
title: מהר״ם מרוטנבורג; מגדולי בעלי התוספות

name: ר׳ אליעזר מטוך
bio: ר׳ אליעזר מטוך (fl. second half of the thirteenth century; d. before 1291) was one of the final French Tosafists and a decisive editor of Tosafist literature. Very little is securely known of his biography. He was a nephew of ר׳ חזקיה ממגדבורג and may be identical with ר׳ אליעזר בן שלמה who signed a responsum concerning residence rights at Goslar; modern scholarship has also debated his precise patronymic. He studied with ר׳ יצחק בן משה מווינה, the אור זרוע, and taught ר׳ חיים פלטיאל. Contemporaries ranked him with ר׳ מאיר בן ברוך מרוטנבורג, and a later authority called him head of the French yeshiva. At Touques in Normandy he adapted, abridged, and reorganised earlier Tosafot, especially those of ר׳ שמשון בן אברהם משאנץ, while incorporating later interpretations and his own marginal גליון תוספות. After further revision by subsequent scholars, תוספות טוך became the principal foundation for the Tosafot printed beside many tractates of the Babylonian Talmud. His redaction is especially associated with Shabbat, Pesachim, Ketubot, Gittin, Bava Kamma, Bava Metzia, Bava Batra, Shevuot, and Hullin. A Torah commentary attributed to him is known only from a manuscript book-list. He died before 1291. No portrait exists.
title: מבעלי התוספות ועורך תוספות טוך

name: ר׳ חזקיה בן מנוח
bio: ר׳ חזקיה בן מנוח (fl. mid-thirteenth century), known as the Chizkuni, was a French biblical commentator whose surviving biography is almost entirely contained in his commentary and its rhymed introduction. His precise birthplace, teachers, movements and lifespan are unknown. Around 1240 he compiled a commentary on the Pentateuch drawing selectively on approximately twenty earlier works, especially the northern French exegetical tradition of ר׳ שלמה יצחקי, ר׳ שמואל בן מאיר and ר׳ יוסף בכור שור, as well as ר׳ אברהם אבן עזרא, midrash and halakhic sources. Rather than merely reproducing them, he condensed, compared and often reformulated interpretations, preserving otherwise lost material and numerous Old French glosses. A passage in the introduction associates the work with his father Manoah and has been interpreted—uncertainly—as referring to persecution and injury. The commentary was first printed in Venice in 1524 and remains a standard medieval Torah commentary.
title: החזקוני; פרשן התורה

name: ר׳ יצחק בן מאיר הלוי מדורא
bio: ר׳ יצחק בן מאיר הלוי מדורא was a thirteenth-century Ashkenazic halakhist whose name is attached to the Rhineland town of Düren. He studied in the Franco-German scholarly world and is traditionally associated with ר׳ טוביה בן אליה מווינה and ר׳ מאיר בן ברוך מרוטנבורג. His principal work, שערי דורא, organizes the practical laws of prohibited foods, mixtures, slaughter and related domestic observance. Its concise utility made it a standard medieval Ashkenazic manual. Successive generations surrounded the text with glosses, including traditions associated with ר׳ ישראל איסרלין, ר׳ שלמה לוריא, ר׳ נתן שפירא and ר׳ משה איסרליש, showing how the book remained a living legal text rather than a static treatise. A documentary manual, תיקון שטרות, has also been attributed to an author of the same name, but the identification is not certain and it is therefore omitted from the canonical works list. The surviving evidence supports Düren as his mature centre; other movements and exact lifespan dates remain approximate.
base_name: Isaac ben Meir HaLevi of Duren
title: בעל שערי דורא; פוסק אשכנזי
aliases: רבי יצחק בן מאיר הלוי מדורא

name: ר׳ יצחק בן ישראל
bio: ר׳ יצחק בן ישראל was a thirteenth-century Castilian Jewish scribe and Masoretic specialist associated with the celebrated Ben Israel family workshop. He must be distinguished from his older relative ר׳ ישראל הסופר בן יצחק בן ישראל, whose signed biblical codices date from 1222 and 1241, and from the modern Israeli professor who bears the same name. ר׳ יצחק’s securely identifiable achievement is the production of the lavish three-volume Hebrew Bible now Marseille, Bibliothèque municipale, MS 1626. Modern codicological cataloguing dates it about 1245–1255 and locates its manufacture in central Castile, probably Toledo. Its carefully written biblical text, vocalization, cantillation, Masorah, micrography, and richly ornamented carpet pages place it within the distinctive Toledo school of Sephardi Bible production. Scholars connect the manuscript’s vegetal and geometric decoration with the continuing Islamic artistic vocabulary of Christian Castile. Documentary reconstruction places ר׳ יצחק within a multigenerational family of scribes active in Toledo and Burgos; the surviving evidence illuminates his professional work far more clearly than his private life. No reliable information currently establishes his parents beyond the patronymic, education, rabbinic office, marriage, or exact birthplace.
title: הסופר
aliases: Isaac the Scribe son of Israel

name: ר׳ אהרן בן יוסף הלוי מברצלונה (הרא״ה)
bio: ר׳ אהרן בן יוסף הלוי מברצלונה (c.1235–before 1303), known as הרא״ה, was a major Catalan Rishon, Talmudist and halakhic critic. Probably born in Girona, he descended through his father ר׳ יוסף הלוי from ר׳ זרחיה הלוי, בעל המאור. His formative teachers included his elder brother ר׳ פנחס הלוי and ר׳ משה בן נחמן; he belonged to the same Catalan scholarly world as ר׳ שלמה בן אדרת, at times colleague and at times formidable opponent. After becoming identified with Barcelona, he served by royal appointment in Zaragoza in 1284/1285 to help settle communal disputes, spent a short period in Toledo, and returned to Barcelona. His most famous work, בדק הבית, respectfully but sharply criticized תורת הבית of ר׳ שלמה בן אדרת, who answered in משמרת הבית. הרא״ה also wrote extensive Talmudic novellae, a commentary on the הלכות of ר׳ יצחק אלפסי and practical halakhic treatises. His best-known student was ר׳ יום טוב בן אברהם אשבילי, whose writings preserve many teachings otherwise lost. ספר החינוך was traditionally attributed to הרא״ה, but contradictions with his authenticated writings led modern scholarship to reject or seriously doubt that identification. Claims that he ended his life in Montpellier rest on a likely misreading and are not used as a map movement.
title: הרא״ה

name: ר׳ שלמה בן אברהם אבן אדרת
bio: ר׳ שלמה בן אברהם אבן אדרת (1235–1310), universally known as הרשב״א, was the dominant Catalan halakhist of his generation. Born into a prosperous Barcelona family, he studied Talmud with ר׳ יונה גירונדי and also received the teaching of ר׳ משה בן נחמן and ר׳ יצחק בן אברהם. He combined commercial activity with scholarship before serving for decades as rabbi and communal leader of Barcelona. Questions reached him from Iberia, Provence, France, Germany, Italy, North Africa and the eastern Mediterranean; the thousands of surviving responsa are an exceptional source for medieval Jewish law and social history. His חידושים interpret numerous Talmudic tractates, while תורת הבית systematizes dietary, purity and household law and עבודת הקודש treats Sabbath and festival observance. He defended Judaism against Christian and Muslim polemicists and intervened in communal disputes. In 1305, responding to renewed conflict over philosophy, he and the Barcelona leadership restricted the study of Greek natural science and metaphysics by the young while explicitly exempting medicine. His synthesis of Sephardic Talmudic analysis and practical halakhah profoundly influenced later codifiers, including ר׳ יוסף קארו.
title: הרשב״א; רבה של ברצלונה ופוסק

name: ר׳ משה בן שם טוב די ליאון
bio: ר׳ משה בן שם טוב די ליאון (c.1240–1305) was a Castilian kabbalist whose writings transformed Jewish mystical literature. His birthplace is uncertain: León and Guadalajara are both proposed, and the family name may have been inherited. A 1264 manuscript copied for him provides an early documentary trace. He lived and wrote in Guadalajara from at least 1286 to 1293, later moving among Castilian towns including Valladolid and Ávila. In Hebrew works such as ספר הרימון, הנפש החכמה, שקל הקודש, and משכן העדות, he developed a symbolic theosophy closely related to the Aramaic material he circulated as the זוהר. Traditional attribution presents the Zohar as teachings of ר׳ שמעון בר יוחאי transmitted from an ancient manuscript; modern scholarship generally understands its central strata as a late-thirteenth-century Castilian composition associated especially with ר׳ משה די ליאון, while continuing to debate sources, layers, and collaborators. He died unexpectedly in Arévalo in 1305 while returning toward his home in Ávila. The subsequent testimony attributed to his widow became central to the authorship controversy. The record distinguishes documented residence from later printing places and replaces an invalid portrait link; only a modern commemorative statue is known, not an authentic likeness.
title: מקובל קסטיליאני ומפיץ ספר הזוהר
aliases: Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon
משה בן שם טוב די ליאון
known_as: ר׳ משה בן שם טוב די ליאון

name: ר׳ פרץ בן אליהו מקורביל
bio: ר׳ פרץ בן אליהו מקורביל (fl. later thirteenth century; d. c.1295), usually called רבנו פרץ, was one of the last and most influential French Tosafists. The son of ר׳ אליהו of Tours, he studied with ר׳ יחיאל מפריז, ר׳ שמואל מאיוורא, and ר׳ יצחק בן יוסף מקורביל, the סמ״ק. He travelled through Brabant and spent time in the German lands, where he became acquainted with ר׳ מאיר בן ברוך מרוטנבורג and helped transmit that scholar’s customs and rulings into France and Provence. Returning to Corbeil, he led a major academy and was remembered as “head of the French yeshivot.” His own explanations and the redactions made by his pupils became known as תוספות רבנו פרץ or תוספות תלמידי רבנו פרץ; material from this school entered the standard printed Tosafot. His הגהות on ספר מצוות קטן became inseparable from the later reception of his teacher’s code, while glosses on the ritual collection תשב״ץ preserved further Ashkenazi practice. He also wrote on tractates, prayer, and halakhic custom, though authorship and recension are sometimes complex because students edited oral lectures. He died before the 1298 persecutions, probably in 1295. No authenticated portrait is known.
title: רבנו פרץ; מבעלי התוספות וראש ישיבות צרפת

name: ר׳ מנחם בן שלמה המאירי
bio: ר׳ מנחם בן שלמה המאירי (1249–1315) was a major Catalan-Provençal Talmudist and legal synthesiser who spent his documented life in Perpignan. His teachers included ר׳ ראובן בן חיים of Narbonne, whose method combined close Talmudic study with attention to the codification of ר׳ משה בן מימון. The Meiri’s monumental בית הבחירה, composed principally from 1287 to 1300, presents the conclusions and reasoning of approximately thirty-five Talmudic tractates in exceptionally clear Mishnaic Hebrew. It incorporates traditions of Provence, Spain, and northern France while arranging disputes and practical outcomes more systematically than ordinary line-by-line commentary. His מגן אבות defended local Provençal customs during controversies with exiles arriving from Spain after 1306, while introductions and historical writings preserved valuable accounts of rabbinic transmission. Modern readers often emphasise his category of law-governed religious societies when discussing relations with non-Jews, though the scope and novelty of that doctrine remain subjects of scholarly debate. Despite his later stature, surviving evidence does not show that he held a formal communal rabbinate or yeshiva appointment. Much of בית הבחירה remained in manuscript until modern publication, contributing to the delayed but now extensive influence of his work. He died at Perpignan in 1315. No authenticated portrait survives.
title: המאירי; פרשן התלמוד מחכמי פרפיניאן

name: ר׳ אבא מארי בן משה הירחי
bio: ר׳ אבא מארי בן משה הירחי (נולד בקירוב בשנת 1250; נפטר לאחר 1306), שנודע גם כדון אסטרוק מלוניל, היה מחכמי פרובנס ומנהיג ההתנגדות לפרשנות פילוסופית־אלגורית קיצונית במחלוקת מונפלייה. הוא נולד בלוניל למשפחת תלמידי חכמים מצאצאי ר׳ משולם בן יעקב, הכיר היטב את הספרות התלמודית ואת הפילוסופיה היהודית, ועבר למונפלייה. אף שהעריך את ר׳ משה בן מימון, חשש כי צעירים מקומיים משתמשים ברציונליזם האריסטוטלי כדי לערער ניסים, התגלות ומצוות. בשנים 1303–1306 פנה במכתבים אל ר׳ שלמה בן אדרת בברצלונה וביקש הגבלות על לימוד פיזיקה ומטפיזיקה בגיל צעיר. החרם שפרסם ר׳ שלמה בן אדרת בשנת 1305 והחרם הנגדי של המחנה הפילוסופי העמיקו את הקרע. גירוש יהודי צרפת ב־1306 קטע את המחלוקת; ר׳ אבא מארי עבר דרך ארל לפרפיניאן, ושם ערך את מכתביה בספר מנחת קנאות. הספר הוא מקור מרכזי לתולדות המחלוקת המיימונית המאוחרת. ידיעות מוצקות על שנותיו האחרונות ועל תאריך מותו אינן קיימות, ולכן סוף חייו במפה מסומן בקירוב בלבד.
title: בעל מנחת קנאות; מחכמי פרובנס
aliases: Abba Mari ben Moses ben Joseph
known_as: ר׳ אבא מארי בן משה הירחי

name: ר׳ אשר בן יחיאל
bio: ר׳ אשר בן יחיאל (c.1250–1327), the Rosh, was a decisive bridge between the Tosafist tradition of Ashkenaz and the rabbinic culture of Christian Spain. Probably born in the Cologne region, he learned first from his scholarly family and became a leading disciple and dayan of ר׳ מאיר בן ברוך מרוטנבורג at Worms. After his teacher’s imprisonment in 1286, he helped lead German Jewry and dealt with the communal dislocation caused by the Rintfleisch massacres. Fearing arrest and confiscation, he left Germany in 1303 with his family, travelled through Provence, and stayed in Barcelona with ר׳ שלמה בן אברהם אדרת. On the latter’s recommendation he became rabbi and head of the Toledo academy in 1304–1305. There he transmitted Franco-German Talmudic analysis and communal custom while engaging Spanish legal realities and resisting what he regarded as excessive philosophical rationalism. פסקי הרא״ש, arranged along the Talmud and the digest of ר׳ יצחק אלפסי, became a central pillar of later halakhah. His responsa, Tosafot, and ethical צוואה likewise circulated widely. His son ר׳ יעקב בן אשר made his rulings foundational to ארבעה טורים, and they later entered שולחן ערוך. He died in Toledo in 1327.
title: הרא״ש; פוסק, ראש ישיבה ורבה של טולדו

name: ר׳ אברהם בן יצחק מן ההר
bio: ר׳ אברהם בן יצחק מן ההר (d. c.1315) was a Provençal Talmudist associated principally with Montpellier. His early life and teachers are poorly documented, and the map’s 1250 birth year is only a conventional estimate. A contemporary and scholarly friend of ר׳ מנחם בן שלמה המאירי, he wrote extensive commentaries on much of the Talmud. Like the Meiri, he repeatedly used the legal conclusions and terminology of ר׳ משה בן מימון to clarify difficult sugyot, an approach distinctive within Provençal learning. Surviving commentaries include treatments of Yevamot, Nedarim, Nazir, Kiddushin, and other tractates. His commentary on Kiddushin entered Vilna editions under the erroneous title תוספות ר״י הזקן; textual analysis and explicit evidence show that it is the work of ר׳ אברהם מן ההר rather than ר׳ יצחק בן שמואל הזקן. Near the end of his life he moved from Montpellier to Carpentras and joined the rabbinical court of ר׳ מרדכי בן יוסף, author of שערי נדרים. He died around 1315. His work is valuable both for independent interpretation and for preserving Provençal readings and Maimonidean legal analysis. No authenticated image is known.
title: מחכמי מונפלייה ופרשן התלמוד
known_as: ר׳ אברהם בן יצחק מן ההר

name: ר׳ מאיר הכהן מרוטנבורג
bio: ר׳ מאיר הכהן מרוטנבורג was a late-thirteenth-century German Tosafist and one of the distinguished pupils of ר׳ מאיר בן ברוך מרוטנבורג. Almost no independent biographical detail survives, and neither his birth nor death place is securely known. His enduring importance rests on הגהות מיימוניות, annotations to ר׳ משה בן מימון’s משנה תורה that integrate the Ashkenazic halakhic traditions of Germany and northern France with the Maimonidean code. The work preserves rulings, responsa and customs associated especially with ר׳ מאיר בן ברוך מרוטנבורג and earlier בעלי התוספות. It circulated in two related components: running glosses and collections commonly called תשובות מיימוניות. Through later manuscript and print traditions it became an essential conduit by which Franco-German material entered subsequent halakhic literature. Because the evidence securely associates him with the Rothenburg scholarly circle but does not document a fuller itinerary, this map record deliberately avoids invented journeys and treats its dates as approximate.
title: בעל הגהות מיימוניות; מתלמידי מהר״ם מרוטנבורג

name: ר׳ מרדכי בן הלל הכהן
bio: ר׳ מרדכי בן הלל הכהן (c.1250–1298), conventionally called “the Mordechai,” was a leading late Tosafist and Ashkenazi halakhic compiler. He descended from the scholarly family of ר׳ אליעזר בן יואל הלוי and was related to ר׳ אשר בן יחיאל. His principal teacher was ר׳ מאיר בן ברוך מרוטנבורג; he also learned from ר׳ פרץ בן אליהו מקורביל and other German and French authorities. Rather than writing a concise independent code, he gathered rulings, responsa, communal customs, and Tosafist discussions around the order of the Talmud, frequently preserving material otherwise lost. Around 1291 he lived at Goslar, where a bitter legal challenge to his right of residence was decided in his favour. He then settled in Nuremberg. On 1 August 1298, during the Rintfleisch persecutions, he, his wife Selda, and their five children were murdered with the city’s Jewish community. His ספר המרדכי survived in significantly different Rhenish and Austrian recensions and became one of the most authoritative Ashkenazi sources used by later decisors. It was printed alongside the Talmud and profoundly influenced ר׳ משה איסרליש and the European reception of שולחן ערוך. No authenticated portrait survives.
title: בעל המרדכי; פוסק אשכנזי

name: ר׳ יום טוב בן אברהם אשבילי
bio: ר׳ יום טוב בן אברהם אשבילי (approximately 1250–1330), known by the acronym Ritva, was one of medieval Spain’s foremost Talmud commentators. His family name indicates origins in Seville, but the best documentary evidence associates his mature career with Zaragoza, where an Aragonese record identifies him as a hakham and dayan by 1280. He studied in Barcelona under ר׳ שלמה בן אברהם אבן אדרת and ר׳ אהרן הלוי, absorbing the Catalan school descending from ר׳ משה בן נחמן. His novellae combine close explanation of the Talmud with comparison of Spanish and northern European traditions and became standard works of advanced study. He answered halakhic questions from across Spain and, after his teachers’ deaths, was regarded as a major communal authority. Additional works include Sefer HaZikaron, defending formulations of ר׳ משה בן מימון against criticisms by ר׳ משה בן נחמן, Hilkhot Berakhot and a Passover Haggadah commentary. Because many texts circulated under his name and manuscript attribution is complex, this record lists only well-established works.
title: The Ritva; Spanish Rishon, dayan and Talmud commentator
aliases: Yom Tov ben Abraham of Seville

name: ר׳ יעקב בן הרא״ש
bio: ר׳ יעקב בן הרא״ש (c.1269–c.1343), known as בעל הטורים or simply הטור, was one of medieval Judaism’s most influential halakhic codifiers. Born in Cologne, he learned principally from his father, ר׳ אשר בן יחיאל. When the family fled the Rhineland in 1303, he passed through Barcelona and ultimately settled in Toledo, where his father headed the community and court. Living with unusual personal austerity, he declined salaried rabbinic office but served as a scholar, court participant and editor of his father’s teachings. His ארבעה טורים reorganized practical Jewish law into four subject divisions—אורח חיים, יורה דעה, אבן העזר and חושן משפט. Its structure mediated Ashkenazi and Sephardi traditions and became the framework for בית יוסף and שולחן ערוך by ר׳ יוסף קארו. His concise Torah commentary, popularly called בעל הטורים, became famous for textual allusion and gematria. Because medieval sources disagree, his exact birth and death dates remain approximate.
title: בעל הטורים; מחבר ארבעה טורים

name: ר׳ יעקב בן מאיר מנורדהאוזן
bio: ר׳ יעקב בן מאיר מנורדהאוזן was an early-fourteenth-century Ashkenazic scholar and head of the yeshiva at Nordhausen in Thuringia. Later rabbinic scholarship probably identifies him as the compiler of the brief פסקי תוספות printed alongside many tractates of the Babylonian Talmud, although the attribution is not certain and another scholar of the same name has sometimes been proposed. He is traditionally counted among the younger students of ר׳ מאיר בן ברוך מרוטנבורג and is named as a teacher of ר׳ שלום מנוישטאדט. His biography is inseparable from the Black Death persecutions. In 1349 Jews across German lands were falsely accused of poisoning wells. Nordhausen’s community was destroyed after territorial authorities encouraged its burning. Jewish martyrological tradition describes ר׳ יעקב, his son ר׳ מאיר, his students and community preparing themselves in prayer and entering the fire together. German civic histories and Jewish memorial sources agree that the community was annihilated and identify its rabbi among the victims, while details of the final scene come from a later Jewish narrative. Because his earlier itinerary is poorly documented, the map keeps him at Nordhausen apart from an approximate study association.
title: ראש ישיבת נורדהאוזן; מיוחס לו חיבור פסקי תוספות

name: ר׳ אהרן בן יעקב הכהן
bio: ר׳ אהרן בן יעקב הכהן (fl. late thirteenth–early fourteenth century) was a Provençal halakhic compiler best known for ארחות חיים. Older literature calls him “of Lunel,” but internal references to Narbonne customs and scholars make Narbonne the stronger association. He came from a learned family: his grandfather ר׳ דוד wrote on the laws of forbidden animals, and an ancestor studied with ר׳ אברהם בן דוד מפושקיירא. When Philip IV expelled the Jews from royal France in 1306, ר׳ אהרן הכהן left Provence, apparently passing through Spain before settling on Majorca. There, before 1327, he assembled ארחות חיים, a broad compendium of daily prayer, blessings, Sabbath, festivals, dietary and family law, mourning, ethics, and doctrine. Unlike a terse code, it preserves long extracts from earlier Provençal and Spanish works, local customs, explanations, and variant opinions, making it an important repository for texts otherwise lost. Its first section was printed in Florence in 1752; the complete work appeared much later. The closely related כל בו may be an earlier abridgment or draft by the same author, but its authorship and textual relationship remain debated. Because neither birth nor death is securely dated, the numeric lifespan is explicitly conventional. No authenticated portrait survives.
title: בעל ארחות חיים מחכמי פרובאנס

name: ר׳ אשתורי הפרחי
bio: ר׳ אשתורי הפרחי (c.1280–c.1355) was a physician, halakhist, traveller and the pioneering Hebrew geographer of the Land of Israel. Born into a scholarly Provençal family, he studied with relatives, ר׳ אליעזר בן יוסף of Chinon and ר׳ יעקב בן מכיר אבן תיבון at Montpellier, acquiring Torah alongside Arabic, Latin, medicine and science. Expelled from France in 1306, he travelled through Spain and Egypt before reaching the Land of Israel. After about a year in Jerusalem he settled at Beit She’an, where he practised medicine and systematically explored the country. Over seven years he compared biblical and rabbinic place names with living Arabic names, routes, ruins, agricultural conditions and local traditions. He completed כפתור ופרח in 1322 and submitted it for rabbinic review. The work combines geography with the commandments dependent on the land, Temple measurements, calendar questions and practical halakhah. Rediscovered and printed in Venice in 1549, it became an indispensable source for historical topography and the study of medieval Jewish settlement. He remained in Beit She’an until his death around 1355.
title: חוקר ארץ ישראל ופוסק; בעל כפתור ופרח

name: ר׳ לוי בן גרשון
bio: ר׳ לוי בן גרשון (1288–1344), known as Gersonides or the רלב״ג, was a Provençal biblical exegete, philosopher, mathematician, astronomer, and halakhic scholar. Probably born at Bagnols-sur-Cèze, he spent most of his career in Orange and made several documented visits to papal Avignon. He apparently held no communal rabbinic office, supporting an unusually independent programme of Hebrew scholarship. מעשה חושב advanced arithmetic, combinatorics, and proof by induction. His philosophical masterpiece מלחמות ה׳, written from 1317 to 1329, examined immortality, prophecy, providence, divine knowledge, astronomy, creation, and miracles, sometimes departing sharply from ר׳ משה בן מימון. His astronomical observations and models criticised Ptolemy; his cross-staff and trigonometric work circulated beyond Jewish learned circles, and part of his astronomy was translated into Latin for Pope Clement VI. Between 1329 and 1338 he produced major biblical commentaries distinguished by close language, philosophical argument, scientific explanation, and practical moral lessons. Later authorities admired his learning while debating his positions on providence and divine foreknowledge. He died in 1344; the exact location is not securely established. No authentic likeness survives, and the former purported portrait has been removed.
title: הרלב״ג; פרשן המקרא, פילוסוף, מתמטיקאי ואסטרונום

name: ר׳ ירוחם בן משולם
bio: ר׳ ירוחם בן משולם (c.1290–c.1350), universally known as רבנו ירוחם, was a major codifier among the later Rishonim. Born in Provence, he was displaced by the French expulsion of 1306 and wandered before reaching Toledo. There, despite severe poverty, he studied under the רא״ש and ר׳ אברהם בן משה איסמעיל, a student of the רשב״א. His first major compilation, ספר מישרים, reorganised the laws of civil jurisprudence by subject, identified their talmudic sources and compared the rulings of earlier authorities. Encouraged by colleagues, he then composed תולדות אדם וחוה, a practical code covering the Jewish life cycle: “Adam” treats obligations before marriage, while “Havah” addresses marriage and the duties that follow it. His clear thematic arrangement made difficult material readily accessible to scholars and students. ר׳ יוסף קארו quoted him extensively in בית יוסף and incorporated numerous rulings into the שולחן ערוך. Very little is securely known about his later personal life, but his books made this impoverished refugee one of the most consequential transmitters of Provençal and Spanish halakhah.
title: רבנו ירוחם; פוסק ומחבר ספר מישרים

name: ר׳ דוד בן יוסף אבודרהם
bio: ר׳ דוד בן יוסף אבודרהם was a fourteenth-century Sephardi liturgist whose surviving biography is much less certain than the influence of his book. He lived in Seville and completed his great commentary on blessings and prayers there in 1340. The work explains the order, wording, sources, laws, customs, calendar, and meanings of Jewish worship, bringing together Talmudic and geonic material, halakhic authorities, grammar, astronomy, and local Sephardi practice. Older accounts call him a student of ר׳ יעקב בן אשר; the evidence securely shows familiarity and personal association with that scholarly circle, but a formal teacher-student relationship is disputed. Commonly called simply ספר אבודרהם, the commentary became an enduring guide to the siddur and synagogue year, especially in Sephardi communities, and was repeatedly printed from the fifteenth century onward. Because no reliable evidence fixes his birth or death, the numeric lifespan used by the map is explicitly approximate; 1340 is the firm chronological anchor. No authenticated contemporary portrait is known.
title: בעל ספר אבודרהם; פרשן התפילה

name: ר׳ משה בן יהושע נרבוני
bio: ר׳ משה בן יהושע נרבוני (c.1300–1362), also called Mestre Vidal Bellshom, was a Catalan Jewish physician and one of the fourteenth century’s most important Averroist philosophers. Born at Perpignan, he began philosophy with his father at thirteen, studied medicine and learned from members of the Caslari family. He travelled widely through Catalonia and Castile, practising medicine while commenting on Arabic and Jewish philosophical classics. During the Black Death persecutions of 1348–49, a mob attacked the Jews of Cervera; he escaped but lost his property and books. He later worked in Barcelona, Toledo and Soria. Narboni wrote commentaries on al-Ghazali, Ibn Tufayl, Avicenna and Averroes, alongside medical, ethical and polemical treatises. His crowning work was an extensive commentary on the Rambam’s מורה נבוכים, composed over roughly seven years and completed at Soria. Its uncompromising rationalism made him a central figure in medieval Jewish Averroism and influenced later interpreters of Maimonides. He died around 1362, apparently while attempting to return north from Soria toward his native region; the exact place remains uncertain.
title: פילוסוף ורופא; מפרש מורה נבוכים

name: ר׳ וידאל די טולושא
bio: ר׳ וידאל די טולושא (approximately 1300–1378), universally known as the Maggid Mishneh, was a Catalan rabbi and one of the foundational commentators on ר׳ משה בן מימון’s Mishneh Torah. His precise origins and dates remain uncertain: older writers placed “Tolosa” in Spain, while modern scholarship has argued for Toulouse in southern France. Evidence associates him with Villefranche-de-Conflent and later Barcelona, where he was a colleague or personal friend of ר׳ ניסים בן ראובן. Maggid Mishneh identifies the Talmudic and Geonic sources behind Mishneh Torah, reconstructs its legal reasoning and frequently defends it against the strictures of ר׳ אברהם בן דוד מפושקירה, while openly acknowledging unresolved sources or disagreement. Surviving commentary covers six of Mishneh Torah’s fourteen books, though early testimony suggests a wider original scope. From its first printing alongside Mishneh Torah in Constantinople in 1509, it became a standard page commentary and a major source for later decisors, including ר׳ יוסף קארו. A philosophical commentary in Arabic on a work of al-Ghazali is also attributed to him.
title: The Maggid Mishneh; fourteenth-century commentator on Mishneh Torah

name: ר׳ מנחם בן אהרן אבן זרח
bio: ר׳ מנחם בן אהרן אבן זרח (c.1310–1385) was a Navarrese and Castilian rabbi whose life was repeatedly reshaped by persecution and civil war. His father, a refugee from the French expulsion of 1306, settled at Estella in Navarre. During the anti-Jewish massacre there in March 1328, ר׳ מנחם’s parents and four younger brothers were killed; he survived severe wounds through the intervention of a Christian knight. He studied for two years under ר׳ יהושע אבן שועיב, continued at Alcalá with ר׳ יוסף אבן אל־עיש, and received his most extensive talmudic formation from ר׳ יהודה בן הרא״ש. In 1361 he succeeded his teacher as rabbi of Alcalá and taught there for eight years. Civil war destroyed his property in 1368, forcing him to Toledo, where ר׳ שמואל אברבנאל supported his scholarship. For that patron he wrote צדה לדרך, a distinctive practical code aimed especially at wealthy Jews active at royal courts, presenting essential law in a concise and accessible form. He died in Toledo in July 1385.
title: פוסק ומחבר צדה לדרך
aliases: ר׳ מנחם בן אהרן אבן זרח

name: ר׳ ניסים בן ראובן גירונדי
bio: ר׳ ניסים בן ראובן גירונדי, universally known as the Ran, was among fourteenth-century Catalonia’s leading Talmudists, halakhic decisors, preachers, and communal authorities. Although his epithet associates him with Girona and both birthplace and birth year remain disputed, the documentary centre of his adult life was Barcelona. A Torah scroll that he copied and donated there in 1336 survives as evidence of his scribal and scholarly activity. He later served as judge and headed an influential academy, training scholars including ר׳ יצחק בר ששת and ר׳ חסדאי קרשקש. His lucid commentary accompanying the digest of ר׳ יצחק אלפסי became a standard aid to practical Talmud study; his novellae, responsa, and philosophical-theological sermons likewise shaped later Sephardi learning. Communal leadership exposed him to political danger, including imprisonment with other Barcelona notables following a false accusation. He died in Barcelona during the winter of 1375–1376, possibly amid an epidemic. The record maps Barcelona rather than incorrectly treating Girona as his documented mature residence. No authenticated portrait survives.
title: הר״ן; ראש ישיבה ודיין בברצלונה

name: ר׳ יצחק בר ששת ברפת
bio: ר׳ יצחק בר ששת ברפת, known by the acronym Rivash, was a major late-medieval Sephardi halakhist and communal rabbi. Born in Valencia in 1326, he spent his formative and early professional years in Barcelona, where he studied with ר׳ פרץ הכהן and especially ר׳ ניסים בן ראובן גירונדי. For many years he supported himself in commerce rather than accepting rabbinic office. His prominence also exposed him to communal danger: he and other Barcelona leaders were jailed after a false accusation. He subsequently held rabbinic posts in Zaragoza, Calatayud, and Valencia. The persecutions of 1391 transformed his life. After coercion and flight, he crossed to North Africa and settled in Algiers, where he became the community’s leading rabbinic authority despite local controversy. His hundreds of responsa address civil and ritual law, communal governance, persecution, conversion, and the practical conditions of Jewish life across Spain and North Africa. They preserve invaluable historical testimony as well as precise halakhic analysis and deeply influenced later decisors, including ר׳ יוסף קארו. He died in Algiers in 1408. No authenticated lifetime portrait is known.
title: הריב״ש; פוסק ורבה של אלג׳יר

name: ר׳ חסדאי בן אברהם קרשקש
bio: ר׳ חסדאי בן אברהם קרשקש was a Catalan-Aragonese halakhist, communal statesman, and original Jewish philosopher. Born in Barcelona around 1340, he studied in the academy of ר׳ ניסים בן ראובן גירונדי and was recognised by 1370 as a scholar and judge. Royal confidence and communal standing made him a central spokesman for the Jews of the Crown of Aragon. In 1389 he moved to Zaragoza as rabbi and communal leader. The anti-Jewish violence of 1391 killed his only son and devastated communities across Iberia; thereafter he organised relief, sought to rebuild Jewish life, and helped endangered Jews and coerced converts. His philosophical masterpiece אור ה׳ attacked the necessity of Aristotelian physics and metaphysics and reconstructed Jewish belief around divine unity, love, providence, and creation. His critique later influenced major Jewish thinkers and is often discussed in relation to Spinoza. He also wrote a Catalan refutation of Christian dogma and a historically important letter describing the persecutions. He died in Zaragoza in late 1410 or early 1411. The supposed portrait formerly attached to this record could not be authenticated and has been removed.
title: פילוסוף, פוסק ומנהיג יהודי אראגון

name: ר׳ יוסף בן דוד חביבא
bio: ר׳ יוסף בן דוד חביבא (approximately 1340–1420), known as the Nimukei Yosef, was one of the last major Spanish Rishonim. Very little secure biographical information survives. He studied in the intellectual world of Barcelona associated with ר׳ ניסים בן ראובן and ר׳ חסדאי קרשקש, and later evidence associates him with Zaragoza. His principal work, Nimukei Yosef, is a sustained commentary on the halakhot of ר׳ יצחק אלפסי. It carefully edits and transmits earlier Spanish talmudic traditions, especially those of ר׳ יום טוב בן אברהם אשבילי and ר׳ ניסים בן ראובן, while marking the author’s own interventions with the phrase “אמר המחבר.” The commentary probably once covered substantially more of the Rif than survives or was printed. Portions on Moed Katan and Makkot were long printed under the name of ר׳ ניסים בן ראובן, while manuscripts have enabled modern recovery of additional sections. Because documentation of his life is sparse, this record maps only the broad, defensible Barcelona-to-Zaragoza scholarly trajectory and does not invent rabbinic offices or travels.
title: The Nimukei Yosef; late Spanish Rishon and commentator on the Rif

name: ר׳ יצחק בן משה הלוי דוראן
bio: ר׳ יצחק בן משה הלוי דוראן (c.1350–c.1415), known as Profiat Duran or האפודי, was a Catalan physician, grammarian, philosopher and one of medieval Judaism’s sharpest anti-Christian polemicists. Probably born near Perpignan, he studied Talmud as well as philosophy and science and later served as tutor in the Crescas household. During the violence of 1391 he was forcibly baptised and appears in Christian records as Honoratus de Bonafide. After escaping and openly returning to Judaism, he transformed personal catastrophe into scholarship. His satirical letter אל תהי כאבותיך was written so subtly that some Christian readers initially mistook it for praise. כלימת הגוים offered a systematic historical critique of Christian texts and doctrine. מעשה אפוד, completed in 1403, is an important Hebrew grammar embedded in a broader programme for renewing Jewish learning; חשב האפוד treats calendar and astronomical calculation. He also wrote an influential commentary on the Rambam’s מורה נבוכים. His attempted journey east and his death place remain uncertain, so this map does not claim that he reached the Land of Israel.
title: האפודי; מדקדק, פילוסוף ופולמוסן
aliases: ר׳ יצחק בן משה הלוי דוראן

name: ר׳ יעקב בן משה הלוי מולין
bio: ר׳ יעקב בן משה הלוי מולין (c.1360–1427), the מהרי״ל or מהר״י סג״ל, was the foremost late-medieval authority on the customs of Ashkenaz. Born in Mainz to its rabbi ר׳ משה הלוי מולין, he studied with his father and later in Austria under scholars including ר׳ שלום מנוישטאדט. Returning to Mainz after his father's death, he led the community and founded a major yeshiva whose students included ר׳ יעקב וייל. Communities across Germany, Austria and Bohemia addressed halakhic questions to him. During the crises surrounding the Hussite wars and persecution of Jewish communities, he organised prayer, fasting and communal relief. He was also a renowned prayer leader who insisted on preserving inherited liturgical melodies. His practices, rulings, sermons and melodies were recorded by disciples, especially ר׳ זלמן משט־גואר, in מנהגי מהרי״ל, first printed posthumously in 1556. That work became a foundation of Western Ashkenazi practice and was repeatedly cited by later authorities. Late in life he moved to Worms, where he died and was buried in 1427.
title: המהרי״ל; רבה של מגנצא ואבי מנהגי אשכנז
aliases: רבי יעקב בן משה הלוי מולין

name: ר׳ שמעון בן צמח דוראן
bio: ר׳ שמעון בן צמח דוראן (1361–1444), the רשב״ץ, was a Majorcan-born rabbi, physician, philosopher and communal leader whose career bridged Christian Iberia and North Africa. Educated in Palma in Torah, medicine, mathematics, astronomy and philosophy, he lost his property during the anti-Jewish violence of 1391 and fled with his family to Algiers. There he worked beside ר׳ יצחק בר ששת ברפת and helped frame communal ordinances in 1394. He later became the leading rabbinic authority of Algiers. His hundreds of responsa illuminate the law, economy and communal life of western Mediterranean Jewry; מגן אבות ranges across theology, philosophy, polemic and a commentary on Pirkei Avot. His descendants formed an influential Algerian rabbinic dynasty.
title: הרשב״ץ; בעל שו״ת תשב״ץ

name: ר׳ יוסף אלבו
bio: ר׳ יוסף אלבו (c.1380–1444) was an Aragonese-Castilian rabbi, preacher and philosopher, best known for ספר העיקרים. He was probably born at Monreal in Aragon and studied with ר׳ חסדאי קרשקש, likely in Zaragoza. By 1413 he represented the Jewish community of Daroca at the Disputation of Tortosa, the prolonged, coercive Christian-Jewish debate convened by Antipope Benedict XIII. The collapse of Daroca’s Jewish community in 1415 was followed by his relocation to Soria in Castile. There he served as rabbi and preacher and completed ספר העיקרים around 1425; he is still documented preaching in Soria in 1433. The work responds both to Christian polemic and to earlier Jewish debates over dogma. In place of the thirteen principles formulated by ר׳ משה בן מימון or the six roots of ר׳ חסדאי קרשקש, ר׳ יוסף identifies three fundamental principles of divine religion: the existence of God, revelation and reward and punishment. His method is deliberately synthetic, drawing upon earlier Jewish philosophy and occasionally scholastic terminology while allowing substantial interpretive latitude within Judaism. The book became one of the most widely read medieval Hebrew works on Jewish belief and was first printed at Soncino in 1485. He probably died in Soria around 1444.
title: בעל ספר העיקרים; פילוסוף ודרשן

name: ר׳ יעקב בן יהודה וייל
bio: ר׳ יעקב בן יהודה וייל, known as מהרי״ו or מהר״י וייל, was one of the principal halakhic authorities of fifteenth-century Germany. Born around 1385 at Weil, he studied in Mainz under ר׳ יעקב בן משה הלוי מולין, the מהרי״ל, who ordained him. By 1422 he was active at Nuremberg. Although authorized to establish a yeshiva there, he initially declined to displace the older local scholar ר׳ זלמן כ״ץ, reflecting the conciliatory temperament evident in his responsa. He later became rabbi of Erfurt, from where communities across Ashkenaz addressed legal questions to him. His decisions emphasize clear Talmudic reasoning and practical adjudication while criticizing scholars who claimed special social privilege merely from rabbinic status. שו״ת מהרי״ו, first printed posthumously in Venice in 1549, became a major source for ר׳ משה איסרליש. Its appended הלכות שחיטה ובדיקה circulated especially widely, passing through dozens of editions and attracting commentaries. The exact year and place of his death are unknown, but he was no longer alive by the mid-1450s. He should not be confused with his teacher, the מהרי״ל.
title: מהרי״ו; פוסק ורבה של ארפורט

name: ר׳ ישראל איסרלין
bio: ר׳ ישראל איסרלין בן פתחיה (בערך 1390–1460), הידוע כמהרא״י וכבעל תרומת הדשן, was the pre-eminent late-medieval Ashkenazic halakhist of Austria. Born in Regensburg, he was orphaned young and educated in Wiener Neustadt in the household of his maternal uncle ר׳ אהרן בלומל. The Vienna persecutions of 1421 killed his mother and uncle. After further study and a period connected with Italy, he led communities in Marburg (Maribor) and, from about 1445, Wiener Neustadt, where his court and yeshiva drew students from Central Europe. His 354 responsa in תרומת הדשן combine learned legal analysis with evidence about actual Ashkenazic practice; פסקים וכתבים, assembled by a disciple, preserves further rulings. Both collections deeply shaped later Ashkenazic law, especially through their use by ר׳ משה איסרליש.
title: בעל תרומת הדשן; מהרא״י

name: ר׳ יהודה הלוי מינץ
bio: ר׳ יהודה בן אליעזר הלוי מינץ (c.1405–1508), known as מהר״י מינץ, was the leading Ashkenazi rabbinic authority of Renaissance Italy. Born at Mainz, from which the family name derives, he received an Ashkenazi Talmudic education before moving to northern Italy around 1462. At Padua he founded or reorganized a yeshiva on the German model and served as rabbi for roughly forty-seven years. The academy attracted students from across Europe and helped make Padua a major centre of rabbinic learning. Among the scholars connected to his school were his son ר׳ אברהם מינץ and his descendant by marriage ר׳ מאיר קצנלבוגן, who later preserved his responsa. ר׳ יהודה issued communal ordinances, adjudicated marriage and divorce questions and defended established rabbinic authority in disputes such as his controversy with Elijah Delmedigo. A later claim that he lectured in philosophy at the University of Padua is disputed and may confuse him with Delmedigo, so it is not treated here as fact. Much of his writing was reportedly destroyed during warfare and upheaval. Sixteen responsa and several rulings survived and were printed with the responsa of ר׳ מאיר קצנלבוגן. He died at Padua on 27 September 1508, at an exceptionally advanced age according to contemporary tradition.
title: מהר״י מינץ — רבה וראש ישיבתה של פאדובה

name: ר׳ משה בן אליהו קפשאלי
bio: ר׳ משה בן אליהו קפשאלי (c.1420–c.1495) was the principal rabbinic and communal leader of Constantinople during the transition from Byzantine to Ottoman rule. Born into a prominent family at Candia on Venetian Crete, he travelled as a young scholar through the German lands and studied in Ashkenazi yeshivot. By about 1450 he was serving the Jewish community of Constantinople. After Mehmed II conquered the city in 1453, the sultan recognized ר׳ משה as the community’s senior representative. His authority included adjudication, supervision of communal taxation and influence over rabbinic appointments, although modern scholarship cautions against treating this early arrangement as identical to the later centralized office of Hakham Bashi. He was renowned for personal integrity and for enforcing marriage and family law, but accusations sent to ר׳ יוסף קולון produced a major controversy; after receiving fuller testimony, ר׳ יוסף withdrew his condemnation. Under Bayezid II, ר׳ משה helped organize assistance and settlement for refugees from Spain and Portugal and mediated the tax burden between wealthy and poor households. His surviving learning is dispersed mainly through responsa, rulings and citations rather than a single securely transmitted major book. He died in Constantinople around 1495 and was succeeded in communal prominence by ר׳ אליהו מזרחי.
title: מנהיג יהודי קושטא ופוסק בראשית התקופה העות׳מאנית

name: ר׳ יצחק עראמה
bio: ר׳ יצחק בן משה עראמה (c.1420–1494), best known as the עקדת יצחק, was a Spanish rabbi, preacher and philosophical biblical commentator. His earliest recorded office was as head of an academy at Zamora. He subsequently became rabbi and communal preacher at Tarragona, where he answered Christian conversionist sermons by presenting Judaism’s intellectual claims publicly. He next served at Fraga and finally at Calatayud, leading its academy and rabbinical court. His weekly discourses joined close biblical reading, midrash, philosophy and moral instruction; revised and expanded, they became the 105 thematic “gates” of עקדת יצחק. The work places revealed Torah above autonomous philosophy while treating reason as an important instrument of interpretation, and it became a major bridge between medieval Jewish philosophy and later homiletical commentary. He also wrote חזות קשה, a critique of philosophical overreach, and commentaries connected with the Five Scrolls and Proverbs. The expulsion of 1492 ended his long Aragonese career. He left Spain and settled in Naples, where he died about two years later. His son ר׳ מאיר עראמה preserved biographical information and continued the family’s exegetical activity.
title: בעל עקדת יצחק — דרשן, פרשן ופילוסוף יהודי

name: ר׳ יוסף בן שלמה קולון טרבוט
bio: ר׳ יוסף בן שלמה קולון טרבוט, universally known as מהרי״ק, was the foremost Italian halakhic authority of his generation. Born around 1420 at Chambéry in Savoy into a learned family, he studied with his father ר׳ שלמה and with ר׳ מרדכי נתן before moving through northern Italy. By 1469 he served at Piove di Sacco, and his later rabbinic career included Mestre, Bologna and Mantua. His responsa address communal taxation, marriage, commerce, rabbinic jurisdiction and the authority of custom, and were sought across Italy and beyond. In Mantua a major conflict with ר׳ יהודה מסר ליאון led the authorities to expel both scholarly camps in the mid-1470s. מהרי״ק subsequently settled in Pavia, where he headed a yeshiva and died in 1480. His responsa were gathered posthumously and first printed at Venice in 1519; their numbered ‘roots’ became foundational sources for later decisors, especially ר׳ משה איסרליש. This record distinguishes the dates of composition from the later printing and maps only places supported by the biographical tradition.
title: מהרי״ק; מגדולי פוסקי איטליה

name: ר׳ יצחק אבוהב
bio: ר׳ יצחק אבוהב (1433–January 1493), often called the last Gaon of Castile, was a leading Spanish rosh yeshiva, halakhist and biblical commentator. Born in Toledo, he studied under ר׳ יצחק קנפנטון and succeeded him in leadership of the Castilian academy. He taught for periods in Toledo, Buitrago and Guadalajara, transmitting the disciplined Talmudic method of late medieval Castile. His pupils included ר׳ אברהם זכות, while ר׳ יצחק אברבנאל studied with or consulted him shortly before the expulsion. Later authorities, including ר׳ יוסף קארו, treated his rulings with exceptional respect. His Torah scholarship survives in a supercommentary on the Pentateuch commentary of ר׳ משה בן נחמן, homiletical material titled נהר פישון, notes on the Tur and manuscript rulings. When the 1492 expulsion decree was issued, ר׳ יצחק joined a delegation of roughly thirty prominent Jews that negotiated with John II in Lisbon for the admission of Spanish refugees to Portugal. He and close associates received permission to settle at Porto. He died there only about seven months after leaving Spain, in January 1493; his disciple ר׳ אברהם זכות delivered the funeral address. His final journey made him both a scholar of Castile’s closing generation and an early leader of its displaced community.
title: אחרון גאוני קסטיליה; ראש ישיבה ופרשן

name: ר׳ יצחק בן יהודה אברבנאל
bio: ר׳ יצחק בן יהודה אברבנאל (1437–1508), commonly called Don Isaac Abarbanel, was a Portuguese Jewish statesman, financier, theologian, and biblical commentator whose life followed the upheavals of Iberian Jewry. Born in Lisbon to a distinguished Sephardi family, he received extensive Torah and philosophical education and succeeded his father as a financier and royal servant under Afonso V. In 1471 he helped ransom Jewish captives taken at Arzila. Accused after João II attacked the Braganza faction, he fled Portugal in 1483 and entered Castilian royal finance. In 1492 he tried unsuccessfully to avert the expulsion and left Spain with the exiles rather than accept conversion. At Naples he again served a royal court and resumed his commentaries, but the French invasion drove him through Messina and Corfu. From 1496 to 1503 he lived at Monopoli, devoting himself to exegetical, philosophical, and messianic writing, before settling in Venice, where he assisted negotiations with Portugal. His commentaries treat each biblical book as a literary and historical whole, posing structured questions and drawing on political experience, Jewish tradition, philosophy, and Christian exegesis. His works on redemption gave voice to the post-1492 exile. He died in Venice and was buried at Padua; the original grave location was later lost.
title: דון יצחק אברבנאל — פרשן המקרא ומדינאי

name: ר׳ יוסף יעבץ
bio: ר׳ יוסף בן חיים יעבץ (c.1440–1508), known as החסיד יעב״ץ, was a preacher, exegete and theologian shaped by the catastrophe of the Iberian expulsions. Born in Lisbon, he became associated with the learned Jewish world of Spain and Portugal and witnessed the displacement of 1492. His subsequent route took him through Portugal, Sicily and Naples before he settled at Mantua. During these migrations he preached faith, divine providence and consolation to refugees. The expulsion also became the central problem of his writings: he argued that simple religious loyalty had sustained many ordinary Jews, while excessive devotion to philosophy had weakened parts of the intellectual elite. His critique was directed not against reason itself but against philosophical systems that, in his view, displaced revelation and observance. אור החיים presents this argument most forcefully; חסדי ה׳ interprets suffering and messianic expectation, while מאמר האחדות and יסוד האמונה discuss the principles of Judaism. He also wrote a widely studied commentary on Pirkei Avot. Most of these works were printed only decades after his death, and their publication dates must not be mistaken for travel to the printing cities. Later kabbalistic and Hasidic authors repeatedly cited his defence of faith and his interpretation of the Spanish exile.
title: החסיד יעב״ץ — דרשן והוגה ממגורשי ספרד

name: ר׳ עובדיה מברטנורא
bio: ר׳ עובדיה ירא מברטנורא (בערך 1445–1515), commonly called the Bartenura or רע״ב, was an Italian rabbi, traveler and the author of the standard commentary on the Mishnah. A student of ר׳ יוסף קולון, he served communities in Bertinoro and Città di Castello before leaving Italy in 1486. His surviving letters describe a journey through Rome, Naples, Salerno, Palermo, Rhodes, Alexandria, Cairo, Gaza, Hebron and Bethlehem, ending in Jerusalem shortly before Passover 1488. Finding a small and impoverished community, he became its rabbinic and communal leader, strengthened charitable provision and Torah study, and established a yeshiva. His concise Mishnah commentary, drawing especially on ר׳ שלמה יצחקי and ר׳ משה בן מימון, became the most widely printed traditional guide to the text.
title: הברטנורא; פרשן המשנה

name: ר׳ אברהם זכות
bio: ר׳ אברהם בן שמואל זכות (1452–c.1515) was a Sephardi astronomer, mathematician, historian and rabbinic scholar whose tables helped transform practical navigation. Born in Salamanca, he studied Jewish learning within his family and under ר׳ יצחק אבוהב while mastering mathematical astronomy. In the 1470s he composed החיבור הגדול, a Hebrew astronomical handbook with tables calculated for Salamanca. ר׳ יוסף ויזיניו translated and adapted these into Latin and Castilian as the Almanach Perpetuum, printed at Leiria in 1496 and used by Portuguese navigators. After the 1492 Spanish expulsion, ר׳ אברהם entered Portugal, where King John II and then Manuel I employed his astronomical expertise. Portugal’s forced-conversion policy drove him into a second exile in 1496–97. He eventually reached Tunis, where in 1504 he completed ספר יוחסין, a chronology of Jewish tradition and rabbinic transmission that also preserves valuable historical notices. His final itinerary is imperfectly documented; leading modern authority records place his death probably in Damascus around 1515, while traditions also connect his last years with Jerusalem. His career links the final flowering of Iberian Jewish science, the age of Atlantic navigation and the post-expulsion reconstruction of Sephardi intellectual life.
title: אסטרונום, היסטוריון ובעל ספר יוחסין

name: ר׳ אליהו מזרחי
bio: ר׳ אליהו בן אברהם מזרחי (c.1455–1526), the הרא״ם, was a Constantinopolitan halakhist, biblical commentator, communal leader and mathematician. A member of the longstanding Romaniote community, he studied under ר׳ אליהו הלוי and was connected with the learning of ר׳ יהודה מינץ. He established a school in Constantinople that taught Talmud alongside mathematics and other sciences, reflecting his conviction that disciplined secular knowledge could serve Torah scholarship. After the death of ר׳ משה קפשאלי, he became the city’s foremost Jewish authority, conventionally dated to 1498. His tenure coincided with the arrival of large numbers of Jews expelled from Iberia; he raised funds for refugees, defended their communal needs and negotiated a Jewish society increasingly divided among Romaniote and Sephardi congregations. His best-known work, ספר המזרחי, is a supercommentary on the Torah commentary of ר׳ שלמה יצחקי, clarifying its rabbinic sources and defending it against objections, especially those of ר׳ משה בן נחמן. He also wrote responsa and mathematical works, including מלאכת המספר. These were printed mainly after his death in Constantinople, but established the הרא״ם as a central authority in biblical interpretation and early Ottoman halakhah.
title: הרא״ם — פוסק, מפרש רש״י ומתמטיקאי

name: ר׳ יעקב בן שלמה אבן חביב
bio: ר׳ יעקב בן שלמה אבן חביב (c. 1460–1516), author of עין יעקב, was a Spanish Talmudist and a principal leader of the Sephardi exiles in Ottoman Salonica. Born at Zamora, he studied under ר׳ שמואל ואלנסי and became associated with a major yeshiva at Salamanca. Expelled from Spain in 1492, he passed through Portugal and eventually settled in Salonica, where the Benveniste family’s extensive libraries enabled his literary work. He helped organize the large and internally diverse exile community, sought to preserve Castilian traditions and participated in communal ordinances and halakhic decisions. עין יעקב gathers the aggadic passages of the Babylonian Talmud, selected Jerusalem Talmud material and major medieval commentaries, adding his own explanations. Its accessible focus on ethics, theology and narrative made Talmudic teaching available far beyond advanced yeshiva circles. He personally supervised the first Salonica printing in 1516 but died after the orders Zeraim and Moed appeared; his son ר׳ לוי בן חביב completed the remaining sections. The work became one of the most frequently printed rabbinic anthologies.
title: בעל עין יעקב; מנהיג מגורשי ספרד בסלוניקי
aliases: ר׳ יעקב בן שלמה אבן חביב

name: ר׳ יעקב בן יוסף פולק
bio: ר׳ יעקב בן יוסף פולק (c.1460–1541?) was the first great rosh yeshiva of early modern Polish Jewry and the figure most associated with the analytical method called חילוקים, later labelled pilpul. His birthplace is uncertain. He studied with ר׳ יעקב מרגליות of Nuremberg and around 1490 served as rabbi and rosh yeshiva in Prague alongside ר׳ יצחק מרגליות. A bitter 1492 dispute over a minor’s annulment of marriage brought opposition from ר׳ יהודה מינץ and others and eventually pushed him from Prague. In Kraków he established what YIVO describes as Poland’s first major Talmudic academy, transferring the German-Bohemian hillukim method into Polish learning. King Alexander appointed him in 1503 as rabbi of Poland or Lesser Poland, an unusually senior communal office. Internal disputes later led him to leave Kraków. Evidence for his final decades is fragmentary: a 1532 approbation may place him in Constantinople en route to Jerusalem, and traditions place him in the Land of Israel before a return to Poland. His outstanding student ר׳ שלום שכנא transmitted his method to the generation of ר׳ משה איסרליש. He deliberately left no systematic book, reportedly resisting the idea that later generations should be bound by written rulings. His conventional death date is 1541, though the attribution of a Lublin grave is doubtful.
title: ראש הישיבה הראשון בפולין; מייסד שיטת החילוקים

name: ר׳ יוסף בן שלמה טאיטאצק
bio: ר׳ יוסף בן שלמה טאיטאצק (c.1465–1546), sometimes called מהריט״ץ, was one of the foremost Talmudic authorities and kabbalists of Ottoman Salonica. Born in Castile, he grew up in the same broad scholarly world as ר׳ לוי בן חביב. The 1492 expulsion took his family first to Portugal, and the Portuguese crisis of 1497 brought them to Salonica. There he led the Portuguese congregation, headed a council representing the city’s multiple congregations and directed a celebrated yeshiva for approximately forty years. His pupils included ר׳ שמואל די מדינה, ר׳ יצחק אדרבי and ר׳ שלמה אלקבץ, giving his academy lasting influence in Ottoman halakhah and Safed kabbalah. Contemporary rabbis praised him as a pre-eminent authority, and his responsa circulated widely even though no complete collection survives. He practised a markedly ascetic devotional life and studied kabbalah, astronomy and mathematics alongside Talmud and halakhah. In 1529 he supported the messianic preacher Solomon Molcho during his appearance in Salonica, an episode that must be understood within the intense post-expulsion atmosphere. His writings include בן פורת on Ecclesiastes, לחם סתרים on Daniel and the Five Scrolls, commentaries on rabbinic and biblical texts and a treatise on the astrolabe. Most appeared only long after his death at Salonica in 1546.
title: ראש ישיבת שאלוניקי; פוסק ומקובל

name: ר׳ משה אלשקר
bio: ר׳ משה בן יצחק אלשקר (1466–1542), known as מהר״ם אלשקר, was a Spanish-born halakhist whose career connected the Sephardi communities of Iberia, North Africa, Greece, Egypt and the Land of Israel. Born in Zamora, he studied under ר׳ שמואל ולנסי and belonged to the same learned circle as ר׳ יעקב בן חביב. The expulsion of 1492 sent him across the Mediterranean; his voyage was threatened by shipwreck and piracy before he reached Tunis. There he spent about eighteen years and helped lead the community alongside ר׳ אברהם זכות. Spanish military pressure in North Africa forced another departure in 1510. After stages including Tripoli and Patras, where he founded a yeshiva, he moved to Egypt and by 1522 served as a dayan in Cairo, associated with the court of ר׳ דוד בן זמרא. His extensive responsa circulated across the Ottoman and Italian Jewish worlds and preserve valuable evidence about communal practice and legal geography. Around 1539 he moved to the Land of Israel, lived for a time in Safed and then Jerusalem, where he died. His writings combine practical halakhah, fidelity to the intellectual tradition of ר׳ משה בן מימון and a forceful rebuttal of the theological claims of ר׳ שם טוב אבן שם טוב.
title: מהר״ם אלשקר — פוסק וממנהיגי מגורשי ספרד

name: ר׳ יעקב בירב
bio: ר׳ יעקב בירב (c.1474–1546), known as מהר״י בירב, was a Spanish-born Sephardi halakhist and the leading advocate of restoring classical semikhah in sixteenth-century Safed. Born at Maqueda near Toledo, he studied with ר׳ יצחק אבוהב. Expelled from Spain in 1492, he reached Fez, where tradition says the large refugee community chose the exceptionally young scholar as rabbi, and later served or taught in Tlemcen. His subsequent career took him through Jerusalem, Cairo, and Damascus before he settled principally in Safed, then the largest Jewish centre in Ottoman Palestine. Seeking a central court capable of resolving post-expulsion legal problems, he relied on a ruling of ר׳ משה בן מימון that consensus among the sages of the Land of Israel could renew ordination. In 1538 twenty-five Safed rabbis ordained him, after which he ordained ר׳ יוסף קארו, ר׳ משה מטראני, and others. ר׳ לוי בן חביב of Jerusalem rejected the procedure, generating an enduring halakhic controversy and a temporary retreat by ר׳ יעקב to Damascus. The chain nevertheless continued through several generations. He returned to Safed, where he died on 3 April 1546. His responsa were printed posthumously in 1663; exegetical notes survive in later rabbinic Bibles.
title: מהר״י בירב — מחדש הסמיכה בצפת

name: ר׳ עובדיה ספורנו
bio: ר׳ עובדיה בן יעקב ספורנו (c.1475–1550), known simply as the Sforno, was an Italian rabbi, biblical commentator, philosopher and physician. Born at Cesena into a Jewish banking family, he pursued medicine and philosophy in Rome and taught Hebrew to the Christian humanist Johannes Reuchlin in 1498–1500. He obtained a medical degree at Ferrara in 1501, returned to Rome and became a prominent member of its Jewish community with access to papal circles. After the Sack of Rome in 1527, he settled in Bologna, where he practised medicine, served as a rabbi, taught a select circle and probably helped revive Hebrew printing. His philosophical אור עמים, printed in Bologna in 1537, challenged propositions of scholastic and Aristotelian philosophy that he considered incompatible with revelation; a revised Latin version, Lumen gentium, appeared in 1548. His concise commentary on the Torah combines close reading, ethical interpretation, rational inquiry and occasional medical knowledge. Most of his biblical commentaries, including the Torah commentary edited by his brother ר׳ חננאל ספורנו, appeared only after his death. He died in Bologna in 1550; subsequent expulsions and destruction of the Jewish cemetery left his burial place unidentified.
title: הספורנו

name: ר׳ דוד בן שלמה אבן זמרא
bio: ר׳ דוד בן שלמה אבן זמרא (1479–1573), universally known by the acronym רדב״ז, was a leading Sephardi halakhist, communal head and kabbalist. Born in Spain shortly before the 1492 expulsion, he reached Safed as a youth and studied in the developing Sephardi scholarly community. In early adulthood he travelled to Fez and then Egypt. Following the Ottoman conquest in 1517, he succeeded ר׳ יצחק שולאל as head of Egyptian Jewry and led Cairo’s rabbinical court and yeshiva for roughly four decades. Financial independence and wide communal standing enabled him to answer questions from across the Ottoman and Mediterranean worlds; more than three thousand responsa are attributed to him. Among his prominent students were ר׳ בצלאל אשכנזי and ר׳ יצחק לוריא. In 1553 he relinquished his Egyptian office and returned to the Land of Israel, residing first in Jerusalem and ultimately in Safed. His writings span responsa, commentary on ר׳ משה בן מימון’s משנה תורה, legal methodology and kabbalah. Important works were printed only decades or centuries after his death, so publication places are not mapped as travels. He died in Safed in 1573. The record deliberately distinguishes him from the twentieth-century Ridvaz, ר׳ יעקב דוד וילובסקי.
title: הרדב״ז; רבה של מצרים ופוסק
aliases: David ben Solomon ibn Abi Zimra
ר׳ דוד בן שלמה אבן זמרא

name: ר׳ מאיר קצנלנבוגן
bio: ר׳ מאיר קצנלנבוגן (1482–1565), known as מהר״ם מפדובה, was a German-born Italian rabbi, rosh yeshiva and halakhic authority. Born at Katzenelnbogen, he studied in Prague under ר׳ יעקב פולק and then at the Padua academy of ר׳ יהודה מינץ. He married Hannah, daughter of ר׳ אברהם מינץ, and eventually succeeded that family as rabbi and head of the Padua yeshiva. Although also recognized by Venice’s Ashkenazi community, Padua remained his home and institutional base. His responsa preserve a wide Mediterranean and European network; correspondents included ר׳ משה אלשקר and ר׳ עובדיה ספורנו, and rulings were cited by his relative ר׳ משה איסרליש. His attempted Padua printing of ר׳ משה בן מימון’s משנה תורה became entangled in the Bragadin–Giustiniani publishing dispute. The controversy helped precipitate censorship and the burning of Hebrew books in Italy, although he did not cause the burnings. Ninety of his responsa appeared with those of ר׳ יהודה מינץ at Venice in 1553. He presided at the Ferrara rabbinic synod in 1554 and led Padua until his death in 1565.
title: מהר״ם מפדובה; רב וראש ישיבה בפדובה

name: ר׳ לוי בן חביב
bio: ר׳ לוי בן יעקב אבן חביב (c.1483–1545), the הרלב״ח, was a leading Sephardi halakhist and head of Jerusalem’s rabbis. Born in Zamora to ר׳ יעקב בן חביב, he was a child of the Spanish expulsion. In Portugal, under King Manuel’s forced-conversion campaign, the young ר׳ לוי was baptized against his will. He escaped as soon as possible and returned openly to Judaism in Ottoman Salonica, where he studied and later taught. After his father’s death, he completed and published the unfinished sections of עין יעקב in 1516, an important act of literary preservation. He first visited Jerusalem in 1523, returned briefly to Salonica and settled permanently in Jerusalem in 1525, becoming its chief rabbinic authority. He worked to sustain the impoverished community and maintained correspondence across the Ottoman Jewish world. His defining public controversy began in 1538, when ר׳ יעקב בירב and the Safed scholars attempted to renew classical semikhah. Although offered ordination, הרלב״ח rejected the procedure as legally defective and defended Jerusalem’s right to be consulted in קונטרס הסמיכה. His responsa, calendar studies and semikhah materials were printed posthumously at Venice in 1565 and remained important precedents in later halakhic debate.
title: הרלב״ח — ראש חכמי ירושלים ומתנגד חידוש הסמיכה
aliases: ר׳ לוי בן יעקב אבן חביב

name: ר׳ יוסף קארו
bio: ר׳ יוסף קארו (1488–1575), known as מרן, הבית יוסף and המחבר, was the pre-eminent Sephardi halakhic codifier of the sixteenth century. Traditionally born in Toledo, he was carried into exile after the Iberian expulsions and spent roughly four decades in the Ottoman Balkans, principally Constantinople, Adrianople, Nikopol and Salonica. He first learned from his father ר׳ אפרים קארו and, after his father’s death, from his uncle ר׳ יצחק קארו. He began בית יוסף, his vast source-based commentary on ארבעה טורים, during his Ottoman years. Settling in Safed about 1536, he joined its rabbinical court and received renewed semikhah from ר׳ יעקב בירב. He later headed the court and academy, alongside leading scholars including ר׳ משה מטראני. בית יוסף established his method by weighing the major earlier authorities; שולחן ערוך distilled its conclusions into a practical code. With the glosses of ר׳ משה איסרליש, it became the central framework of later Jewish law. His mystical diary מגיד מישרים also reveals the ascetic and kabbalistic dimensions of his religious life. He died in Safed in 1575.
title: הבית יוסף; מחבר השולחן ערוך ואב בית דין צפת

name: ר׳ משה בן יוסף מטראני
bio: ר׳ משה בן יוסף מטראני (1500–1580), the המבי״ט, was a central halakhic authority and communal leader of sixteenth-century Safed. Born in Salonika into a family originating in Trani, Italy, he studied as a boy in Adrianople under his uncle ר׳ אהרן מטראני. At about sixteen he moved to Safed and completed his studies under ר׳ יעקב בירב. From 1525 he served the city for more than five decades as rabbi, dayan and head of an academy, working alongside—and sometimes disagreeing sharply with—ר׳ יוסף קארו. After Karo’s death he became the senior spiritual authority of the Safed community.
