Illness brought him back to Galicia in 1855, and he died in Lwów. His הגהות מהר״ץ חיות became a standard feature of the Vilna Talmud.
title: מהר״ץ חיות

name: ר׳ יצחק אייזיק אייכנשטיין מזידיטשוב
bio: ר׳ יצחק אייזיק אייכנשטיין מזידיטשוב (1805–1873), known as מהרי״א מזידיטשוב, was an important Galician Hasidic rebbe and kabbalist. A son of ר׳ ישכר בעריש אייכנשטיין of Safrin, he became the close disciple of his uncle ר׳ צבי הירש מזידיטשוב, author of עטרת צבי, and absorbed the dynasty’s distinctive emphasis on systematic study of the Zohar and Lurianic Kabbalah. He also learned from ר׳ שלום רוקח of Belz. Although he functioned as a spiritual leader earlier, tradition records that he declined the formal title of Rebbe until the death of the שר שלום in 1855. His court at Zhydachiv drew thousands and became a principal centre for the transmission of Zidichov Kabbalah. His foremost disciple, ר׳ יוסף מאיר וייס, later founded the Spinka dynasty. His teachings were published after his death in ליקוטי תורה והש״ס, ליקוטי מהרי״א and commentaries on Midrash, combining Hasidic homily with extensive Zoharic and Lurianic interpretation. He died on 9 Sivan 5633, 4 June 1873, and was buried at Zhydachiv.
title: אדמו״ר מזידיטשוב; בעל ליקוטי תורה והש״ס

name: ר׳ שמשון רפאל הירש
bio: ר׳ שמשון רפאל הירש (1808–1888) was a German rabbi, biblical commentator and principal architect of modern Neo-Orthodoxy. Born in Hamburg, he studied with חכם ר׳ יצחק ברנייס and in Mannheim under ר׳ יעקב יוקב עטלינגר before attending the University of Bonn. He served as Landesrabbiner of Oldenburg, district rabbi in Emden, and chief rabbi of Moravia and Austrian Silesia in Nikolsburg. In 1851 he accepted leadership of Frankfurt’s newly formed Israelitische Religionsgesellschaft, building schools, welfare institutions and an independent Orthodox communal structure. His formula Torah im Derech Eretz argued for uncompromising halakhic life together with disciplined engagement in general culture and civic society. Through The Nineteen Letters, Horeb, his German Pentateuch commentary and the journal Jeschurun, he articulated Judaism as an integrated system of law, symbolism and ethical vocation. He opposed Reform and fought for legal permission for Orthodox Jews to secede from religious communities they regarded as incompatible with their commitments.
title: Rabbi of the Frankfurt Israelitische Religionsgesellschaft and architect of Neo-Orthodoxy

name: ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר (המלבי״ם)
bio: ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר (1809–1879), universally known by the acronym המלבי״ם, was a rabbi, halakhist, Hebrew grammarian, preacher and one of the nineteenth century’s most systematic Jewish biblical commentators. Born in Volochysk, Volhynia, he was orphaned young and educated by his father, his stepfather ר׳ לייב מוולוצ'יסק and ר׳ משה הלוי הורוויץ; he later studied in Warsaw and with ר׳ צבי הירש אייכנשטיין מזידיטשוב. After promoting his first halakhic work across Europe, he served communities in Wreschen and Kempen and became known as the Kempener Maggid. As chief rabbi of Bucharest he strengthened kashrut, education, Hebrew printing and the eruv, but his opposition to religious reform and conflicts with communal elites led to arrest and expulsion in 1864. Thereafter he moved through Ruse, Istanbul, Paris, Łęczyca, Kherson, Mogilev and Königsberg, repeatedly encountering political or communal opposition. His התורה והמצוה argued through detailed linguistic rules that rabbinic halakhic interpretation is rooted precisely in the biblical text; מקראי קודש applied his distinction between verbal explanation and contextual interpretation across most of the Prophets and Writings. While traveling to accept the Kremenchuk rabbinate, he became ill and died in Kyiv on Rosh Hashanah 5640.
title: המלבי״ם
aliases: Meir Leibush ben Yechiel Michel Wisser
ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל

name: ר׳ ישראל ליפקין מסלנט
bio: ר׳ ישראל ליפקין מסלנט (1809–1883), known as ר׳ ישראל סלנטר, founded the Musar movement. Born in Žagarė to ר׳ זאב וולף ליפקין, he settled after marriage in Salant and studied especially with ר׳ יוסף זונדל מסלנט. He taught in Vilna, where his emotionally intense ethical instruction developed into an organised programme of character formation. During the 1848 cholera epidemic he publicly stressed preservation of life; after refusing a post in the state rabbinical seminary he moved to Kovno and established a Musar-oriented yeshiva. From 1857 he worked in Prussia and Germany, living or teaching in Halberstadt, Memel, Königsberg and Berlin. He published the journal תבונה and encouraged institutions that shaped the Lithuanian Musar movement through disciples including ר׳ יצחק בלאזר, ר׳ נפתלי אמסטרדם and ר׳ שמחה זיסל זיו. Late in life he organised Russian Jewish immigrants in Paris, then returned to Königsberg, where he died. His surviving letters and teachings emphasise disciplined self-examination and the equal gravity of interpersonal and ritual duties.
title: מייסד תנועת המוסר

name: ר׳ אברהם צבי הירש אייזנשטט
bio: ר׳ אברהם צבי הירש אייזנשטט (probably 1812–21 August 1868), commonly identified by his work פתחי תשובה, was a rabbi and halakhic compiler in the western Russian Empire. Born in Białystok to ר׳ יעקב אשר אייזנשטט and Rachel, he descended from ר׳ מאיר אייזנשטט, author of פנים מאירות. After marrying Yenta Reizel, he continued studying while she operated a stationery business. The family later followed government offices to Grodno; when the business failed there, he became a dayan. He served as rabbi of Bristovitz from 1836 and of Utena from 1856. His פתחי תשובה arranged concise conclusions and references from a vast responsa literature according to the sections of שולחן ערוך. The Yoreh De'ah volume appeared in Vilna in 1836, Even HaEzer during his lifetime, and Choshen Mishpat posthumously. His accompanying נחלת צבי supplied original discussions rather than bibliographic abstracts. Seriously ill in his final year, he travelled from Utena to Königsberg for treatment, died there on 3 Elul 5628 and was buried in the local Jewish cemetery. פתחי תשובה subsequently became a standard commentary printed alongside שולחן ערוך.
base_name: Avraham Tzvi Hirsch Eisenstadt, author of Pitchei Teshuvah
title: בעל פתחי תשובה

name: ר׳ עבדאללה סומך
bio: ר׳ עבדאללה סומך (1813–13 September 1889), whose fuller Hebrew name was ר׳ עובדיה אברהם יוסף סומך, was the leading educator and a major halakhic authority of nineteenth-century Baghdad. Born there to ר׳ אברהם יוסף יחזקאל and Khatun, he traced his family to ר׳ נסים גאון. He studied under ר׳ יעקב בר יוסף הרופא, who called him his outstanding and discerning pupil, and also learned from ר׳ משה חיים. After marriage to Sarah he initially worked successfully in commerce. Concerned by declining advanced Torah study, he left business and taught a small group without payment. With patron Ezekiel Reuben Manasseh, this circle became Midrash Abu Menashi in 1840 and later the renowned Midrash Beit Zilkha, which he headed until his death. His students included ר׳ יוסף חיים, ר׳ אליהו מני, ר׳ אברהם הלל, ר׳ יצחק מג׳לד, ר׳ ששון שמוחה and many later leaders of Iraqi Jewry. Communities across Iraq, Persia, India and Central Asia sent him legal questions; surviving responsa show engagement with technological and social change as well as ritual law. His best-known work, זבחי צדק, systematized practical rulings and Baghdadi custom on Yoreh De'ah, especially shechita and treifot. It appeared posthumously, so its printing place must not be mistaken for a movement in his lifetime. During Baghdad's 1889 cholera epidemic he became ill near the city and died after being brought home. Conflict over his first burial caused arrests and anti-Jewish violence; about three months later Ottoman authorities permitted reburial in Baghdad's Jewish cemetery. His school and rulings helped connect Baghdad's rabbinic centre with the expanding Baghdadi diaspora throughout Asia.
title: בעל זבחי צדק, ראש מדרש בית זלכה ופוסק יהדות בבל

name: ר׳ נפתלי צבי יהודה ברלין
bio: ר׳ נפתלי צבי יהודה ברלין (1816–1893), known by the acronym Netziv, was a leading Lithuanian scholar and head of the Volozhin Yeshiva. Born in Mir, he married Rayna Batya, granddaughter of ר׳ חיים מוולוז׳ין, at fourteen and became permanently associated with Volozhin. He eventually joined the yeshiva faculty and, after a contested succession, became its principal rosh yeshiva. During roughly four decades of leadership Volozhin grew into the central advanced yeshiva of Eastern European Jewry. His scholarship combined close Talmudic analysis with unusual attention to tannaitic midrash, Geonic literature, textual variants and biblical peshat. Major works include Ha'amek She'elah on the She'iltot, Ha'amek Davar on the Torah and the responsa Meishiv Davar. He opposed communal separatism and supported Hovevei Zion while insisting on religious unity. Russian demands for curricular and administrative control culminated in the yeshiva’s closure in 1892. Ill and hoping ultimately to reach the Land of Israel, he went to Warsaw, where he died the following year.
title: The Netziv; rosh yeshiva of Volozhin

name: ר׳ יצחק אלחנן ספקטור
bio: ר׳ יצחק אלחנן ספקטור (1817–1896) was the pre-eminent halakhic authority and a central public leader of late imperial Russian Jewry. Born in Ros in the Grodno region, he studied first with his father and later under ר׳ בנימין דיסקין in Vawkavysk. After early rabbinates in Izabelin and Biaroza, he served successively in Nyasvizh and Novogrudok. In 1864 he became rabbi of Kovno, where his responsa, communal judgment and extensive correspondence gave him influence far beyond Lithuania. He worked with both traditional and secular communal leaders to oppose harmful state policies, secure kosher provisions for Jewish soldiers, defend Jewish education and organize famine and pogrom relief. He supported Hovevei Zion while maintaining a pragmatic approach to wider communal cooperation. His responsa Be'er Yitzchak and Ein Yitzchak and his Choshen Mishpat commentary Nachal Yitzchak became authoritative works. The Rabbi Isaac Elchanan Theological Seminary in New York, later central to Yeshiva University, was named in his memory.
title: Rabbi of Kovno and leading halakhic authority of Russian Jewry

name: ר׳ עזריאל הילדסהיימר
bio: ר׳ עזריאל הילדסהיימר (1820–1899) was a German Orthodox rabbi, educator and communal organizer who created a model joining traditional Torah scholarship with university learning. Born in Halberstadt, he studied under ר׳ יעקב עטלינגר in Altona and pursued Semitic languages and philosophy in Berlin and Halle, receiving a doctorate in 1844. In 1851 he became rabbi of Eisenstadt, where he founded a yeshiva and school whose curriculum combined intensive Talmud with languages and general studies. Opposition from both Reform advocates and traditionalists accompanied his Hungarian work. Called to Berlin’s independent Orthodox congregation in 1869, he founded the Rabbiner-Seminar für das orthodoxe Judenthum in 1873 and led it until his death. The seminary trained rabbis for German and Eastern European communities; its faculty included ר׳ דוד צבי הופמן and ר׳ אברהם ברלינר. Hildesheimer also organized relief for Russian Jewry, supported the Jewish settlement of Ottoman Palestine and defended Orthodox communal autonomy. His responsa and articles were collected posthumously.
title: רב עדת ישראל ומייסד בית המדרש לרבנים בברלין

name: ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק
bio: ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק (c.1820–1 May 1892), known as the בית הלוי, was a Lithuanian Talmudist, communal rabbi and the first major rabbinic leader of the Brisk branch of the Soloveitchik family. Born in Nesvizh to ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק and Rivka, a descendant of ר׳ חיים מוולוז׳ין, he studied at Volozhin and taught in Minsk while still young. In 1854 he joined ר׳ נפתלי צבי יהודה ברלין in leading the Volozhin Yeshiva, where his dialectical, conceptual approach helped prepare the ground for the later Brisker method developed by his son ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק. He became rabbi of Slutsk in 1865, established advanced study there and was remembered for organized assistance to poor children. Conflict with communal modernizers led him to resign and live in Warsaw under difficult financial circumstances. After ר׳ יהושע לייב דיסקין left Brisk, ר׳ יוסף דוב accepted that city’s rabbinate around 1878–1879 and served until his death. His responsa בית הלוי address all four sections of Shulchan Aruch and combine close textual analysis with practical communal judgment. בית הלוי על התורה preserves discourses on Genesis, part of Exodus and festival themes. His students included ר׳ יוסף רוזין and ר׳ זלמן סנדר שפירא; his son ר׳ חיים succeeded him in Brisk.
title: בעל בית הלוי; רבה של בריסק

name: ר׳ צדוק הכהן מלובלין
bio: ר׳ צדוק בן ר׳ יעקב הכהן רבינוביץ (1823–1900), known as ר׳ צדוק הכהן מלובלין, was a Hasidic master, Talmudist, halakhist, kabbalist and unusually wide-ranging religious thinker. Born in Kreuzburg in Courland to a Lithuanian rabbinic family, he was orphaned young and raised by his uncle ר׳ יוסף בן אשר, a student of ר׳ חיים מוולוז׳ין. His early formation was learned and non-Hasidic. A marital crisis led him to travel through Poland seeking the exceptional authorization of one hundred rabbis for divorce; the precise route is imperfectly preserved. During those journeys he encountered Hasidism and became a disciple of ר׳ מרדכי יוסף ליינר מאיזביצה. After his teacher's death in 1854, he supported his friend ר׳ יהודה לייב איגר as leader of the Lublin circle and spent more than three decades in study, prayer, writing and relative seclusion. Only after ר׳ יהודה לייב איגר died in 1888 did he accept leadership. His thought extends the Izbica concern with divine providence, human will, sin and repentance while developing original accounts of Oral Torah, historical change, imagination, language, psychology, sacred time and the spiritual potential latent in every Jew. He combined extraordinary command of rabbinic and kabbalistic sources with interests extending to astronomy, mathematics and general knowledge. He refused to publish most writings during his lifetime but authorized posthumous publication; many remaining manuscripts were later destroyed in the Lublin ghetto. His surviving books—especially צדקת הצדיק, פרי צדיק, רסיסי לילה and תקנת השבין—became foundational works of modern Hasidic thought and influenced figures including ר׳ אליהו אליעזר דסלר, ר׳ יצחק הוטנר and ר׳ גדליה שור.
title: הכהן מלובלין

name: ר׳ שמחה זיסל זיו
bio: ר׳ שמחה זיסל זיו (1824–1898), known as the Alter or Saba of Kelm, was among the principal architects of the Musar movement. Born in Kelmė as Simcha Mordechai Ziskind Broida, he travelled to Kovno to study with ר׳ ישראל סלנטר and became one of his foremost disciples. He absorbed Musar’s disciplined programme of ethical self-formation. Around 1865 he established the Kelm Talmud Torah, combining intensive Torah study, moral reflection, order, and exacting personal conduct. Government pressure led him to transfer the institution to Grobiņa in Courland in 1880; ill health brought him back to Kelm the following year, though the Grobiņa branch continued until 1886. His Kelm school trained an influential circle that carried Musar into Lithuanian yeshivot and, from 1892, into Ottoman Palestine. He avoided a formal rabbinic office and taught through personal example, carefully structured study, letters, and discourses. His teachings were assembled posthumously in חכמה ומוסר and כתבי הסבא מקלם. He died in Kelm on 26 July 1898, the eve of Tisha B’Av.
title: הסבא מקלם; מייסד תלמוד תורה דקלם

name: ר׳ יחיאל מיכל הלוי אפשטיין
bio: ר׳ יחיאל מיכל הלוי אפשטיין (1829–1908), known as the Aruch HaShulchan, was one of the leading halakhic authorities of nineteenth-century Eastern Europe. Born in Bobruisk, he studied briefly at Volozhin and was guided and ordained by ר׳ אליהו גולדברג. He married Michlah Berlin, sister of ר׳ נפתלי צבי יהודה ברלין. After work in commerce and on the Bobruisk rabbinical court, he accepted his first communal rabbinate in Novozybkov, whose mixed Hasidic and non-Hasidic population broadened his practical experience. In 1874 he became rabbi of Novogrudok and remained there until his death. His Aruch HaShulchan systematically explains and rules on the four divisions of the Shulchan Aruch, giving unusual weight to the Jerusalem Talmud, Maimonides, established custom and the conditions of lived communal law. He also wrote Aruch HaShulchan HeAtid on laws not then practiced, Or LaYesharim and Leil Shimurim.
title: The Aruch HaShulchan; rabbi of Novogrudok and halakhic authority

name: ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני
bio: ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני (7 Cheshvan 5593–24 Kislev 5665; 1832–1904), commonly called the Sdei Chemed after his encyclopedic halakhic work, was a Jerusalem-born Sephardi rabbi, communal leader and prolific legal scholar. The son of ר׳ רפאל אשר אליהו מדיני and Kalu Vida, he studied in Jerusalem under ר׳ יצחק קובו and ר׳ יוסף נסים בורלא, married Rivka at eighteen and received semikhah while still young. His father's death in 1853 left him responsible for an extended household and prompted relocation to Constantinople, where he taught, lectured and wrote while declining opportunities that would interrupt his study. In 1867 he accepted the rabbinate of Karasubazar—now Bilohirsk—in Crimea. During thirty-two years there he founded schools and yeshivot, issued communal regulations, addressed the distinctive traditions of Krymchak Jewry and maintained an international halakhic correspondence. Most of שדי חמד was assembled there. The work alphabetically synthesizes Talmudic and later legal rules, responsa, bibliographical information and scholarly biographies; its scale made it an important bridge between dispersed rabbinic literature and later Torah encyclopedias. He returned to Jerusalem in 1899. Wishing to avoid nomination as Rishon LeZion, he moved to Hebron in 1901, but after the deaths of ר׳ אליהו מני and ר׳ חיים רחמים יוסף פרנקו he accepted leadership of the community. He taught and completed parts of his work at Beit Romano, died in Hebron in 1904 and was buried in its ancient Jewish cemetery.
base_name: Chaim Hezekiah Medini, the Sdei Chemed
title: בעל שדי חמד — רבה של קראסובאזר וחברון
aliases: חיים חזקיה בן רפאל אליהו מדיני

name: ר׳ יוסף חיים מבגדאד
bio: ר׳ יוסף חיים מבגדאד (1835–1909), universally known as the Ben Ish Chai, was the pre-eminent Baghdadi halakhist, preacher, kabbalist and communal teacher of his generation. Born into Baghdad’s rabbinic elite, he studied first in his family and then under his uncle ר׳ דוד חי בן מאיר and the great academy head ר׳ עבדאללה סומך. After his father’s death in 1859 he assumed the central weekly preaching role at Baghdad’s Great Synagogue, though he did not hold a salaried chief-rabbinic office. His sermons joined practical halakhah, aggadah, ethics and Lurianic Kabbalah and reached Baghdadi communities across Iraq, India and Southeast Asia. In 1869 he made a formative pilgrimage to Jerusalem, Hebron and holy sites before returning to Baghdad. He wrote dozens of works, including בן איש חי, the responsa רב פעלים, בן יהוידע and works in accessible Judeo-Arabic. His rulings remain foundational in many Iraqi and Sephardi communities.
title: הבן איש חי; מנהיגה הרוחני של יהדות בגדאד

name: ר׳ ישראל מאיר הכהן קגן
bio: ר׳ ישראל מאיר הכהן קגן (1838–1933), universally known as the Chofetz Chaim, was a Lithuanian rabbi, halakhic authority and ethicist. Born in Zhetel, he moved to Vilna after his father’s death and studied in its batei midrash. After marriage he settled in Radin, where he lived modestly, taught and helped establish the yeshiva later identified with his name. His first major book, Chofetz Chaim, systematized the laws of harmful speech; Shemirat HaLashon developed their ethical and spiritual dimensions. His six-part Mishnah Berurah became the most influential modern Ashkenazi commentary on Orach Chaim. He also promoted kindness, study of neglected priestly laws and practical preparation for Jewish communal life. During the First World War the yeshiva and its community were displaced eastward, returning to Radin after the war. Although he held no grand rabbinic office, his scholarship, personal reputation and involvement in Agudath Israel made him one of the most authoritative Orthodox figures of his generation.
title: The Chofetz Chaim; author of Mishnah Berurah and rosh yeshiva in Radin

name: ר׳ אברהם בורנשטיין
bio: ר׳ אברהם בורנשטיין (1839–1910), the Avnei Nezer, was a major Polish posek and founder of the Sochatchov Hasidic dynasty. Born in Będzin to ר׳ זאב נחום בורנשטיין, he displayed exceptional Talmudic ability and became a disciple and son-in-law of ר׳ מנחם מנדל מורגנשטרן of Kotsk. The Kotsker’s insistence on truth and intellectual precision deeply shaped his synthesis of Hasidic devotion and exacting halakhic analysis. After his father-in-law’s death he served successively as rabbi of Parczew (1862), Krośniewice (1866), Nasielsk (1876), and Sochaczew (1883–1910). In Sochaczew he founded a yeshiva and emerged as a rebbe, creating the Sochatchov court. His אגלי טל, published in 1905, offers a systematic treatment of the Sabbath labours and a famous introduction defending the joy of Torah study. His vast responsa, אבני נזר, cover all four sections of Shulchan Aruch and were published mainly after his death. He also explored a religious agricultural settlement in Ottoman Palestine, sending family representatives, though Ottoman restrictions frustrated the plan. He died in Sochaczew in 1910 and was succeeded by his son ר׳ שמואל בורנשטיין, already represented separately in this project.
title: האדמו״ר הראשון מסוכטשוב; בעל אבני נזר

name: ר׳ נפתלי צבי הירש הכהן אדלר
bio: ר׳ נפתלי צבי הירש הכהן אדלר (1839–1911), generally known as Hermann Adler, was Chief Rabbi of the United Hebrew Congregations of the British Empire. Born in Hanover to ר׳ נתן מרקוס אדלר, he moved to London after his father became chief rabbi. He combined university and rabbinical study in London, Prague and Leipzig, receiving a doctorate in 1862 and rabbinical authorisation from ר׳ שלמה יהודה ליב רפפורט. In 1863 he became principal of Jews' College and in 1864 minister of Bayswater Synagogue. From 1879 he carried much of his ageing father's workload, succeeding him formally in 1891. Adler defended Judaism publicly, supervised an expanding imperial congregational network, wrote on Anglo-Jewish history and published sermons. He consecrated synagogues across Britain and Ireland and received the CVO in 1909. His polished public role strengthened the status of the British chief rabbinate, although his centralised authority also operated amid substantial religious and social diversity. He died in London in 1911 and was buried at Willesden Jewish Cemetery.
title: הרב הראשי של בריטניה והאימפריה הבריטית
known_as: ר׳ נפתלי צבי הירש הכהן אדלר

name: ר׳ מאיר שמחה הכהן מדווינסק
bio: ר׳ מאיר שמחה הכהן מדווינסק (1843–1926) was a major Lithuanian halakhist, biblical commentator and communal rabbi. Born in Butrimonys, he married young and settled in Białystok, where he devoted himself to study while his wife supported the household. In 1888 he was appointed rabbi of Dvinsk’s non-Hasidic community, serving alongside the Hasidic community’s rabbi, ר׳ יוסף רוזין. His first great work, Ohr Somayach, analyzes ר׳ משה בן מימון’s Mishneh Torah with exceptional command of rabbinic literature. Meshech Chochma, published immediately after his death, combines close biblical interpretation, halakhah, philosophy and historical reflection. He was also an influential communal authority whose practical rulings and relief work earned respect across party lines. The frequently quoted passage warning Jews who imagined “Berlin is Jerusalem” belongs to his cyclical philosophy of exile and assimilation; it should not be misrepresented as a dated prophecy of the Holocaust. He died while receiving medical treatment in Riga and was buried in Dvinsk.
title: The Ohr Somayach and Meshech Chochma; rabbi of Dvinsk

name: ר׳ יהודה אריה ליב אלתר
bio: ר׳ יהודה אריה ליב אלתר (1847–1905), known from his writings as the שפת אמת, was the second rebbe of the Ger Hasidic dynasty and an influential Polish Jewish leader. Born in Warsaw to ר׳ אברהם מרדכי אלתר and Esther, he lost both parents in childhood and was raised in Góra Kalwaria by his grandparents, ר׳ יצחק מאיר אלתר, the חידושי הרי״ם, and Feige. His grandfather supervised an exceptionally demanding programme of Talmud and Hasidic study and took him to ר׳ מנחם מנדל מקוצק. After marrying Yocheved Rivka Kaminer in 1862, his name was expanded to Yehudah Aryeh Leib. When his grandfather died in 1866 he declined immediate leadership and followed ר׳ חנוך העניך הכהן לוין of Aleksander. After that rebbe’s death in 1870, the twenty-three-year-old reluctantly accepted leadership of Ger. He combined a restrained public style with intense pastoral responsibility, regular Talmud teaching and discourses connecting biblical language, Midrash, Kabbalah and the inner work of mitzvot. Ger grew into a major Polish Hasidic movement under him. During the Russo-Japanese War he addressed conscripted followers and reportedly died after illness aggravated by concern for them. His Torah and festival teachings were edited posthumously as שפת אמת beginning in 1905, while his Talmudic novellae were printed separately. His son ר׳ אברהם מרדכי אלתר succeeded him.
title: האדמו״ר השני מגור ובעל שפת אמת

name: ר׳ יוסף יוזל הורביץ
bio: ר׳ יוסף יוזל הורביץ (1847–1919), known as הסבא מנובהרדוק, was one of the most radical institution-builders of the Lithuanian mussar movement. Born in Plungė and educated in the Lithuanian rabbinic world, he married young and entered business in Švėkšna. An encounter in Memel with ר׳ ישראל סלנטר redirected his life toward disciplined ethical self-formation. He studied in Kovno with figures including ר׳ יצחק בלאזר, ר׳ נפתלי אמסטרדם and ר׳ אברהם שנקר, then pursued prolonged periods of solitude and introspection. Encouraged by ר׳ שמחה זיסל זיו to serve the public, he created kollelim and yeshivot across the Russian Empire. The central yeshiva opened at Navahrudak in the 1890s and generated the decentralized Novardok network. Its demanding pedagogy sought freedom from status, fear and social approval through bitachon, rigorous self-examination, communal study and deliberately discomfiting exercises. During the First World War he refused to abandon his students: the displaced movement regrouped in Homel and later expanded around Kyiv. He died there during the 1919 typhus epidemic after attending the sick. His teachings, recorded and edited by disciples as מדרגת האדם, made radical trust in God and the struggle against self-interest the enduring intellectual signature of Novardok. His remains were reinterred at Har HaMenuchot in Jerusalem in 1963; that posthumous event is not represented as a map movement, so the figure correctly disappears in 1919.
title: הסבא מנובהרדוק

name: ר׳ נתן צבי פינקל (הסבא מסלבודקה)
bio: ר׳ נתן צבי פינקל (1849–1927), universally known as the Alter or Saba of Slabodka, was a formative architect of the Lithuanian Musar yeshiva. Born in Raseiniai and orphaned young, he grew up among relatives and entered the circle of ר׳ שמחה זיסל זיו, the Alter of Kelm, who shaped his educational outlook. In Kovno and its Slabodka suburb he organized kollelim and, during the early 1880s, established Knesses Yisrael. Its distinctive ideal of גדלות האדם—cultivating the dignity and latent greatness of the human personality—joined rigorous Talmud study to disciplined ethical formation. He recruited and mentored scholars rather than normally delivering the principal Talmud lecture himself; among the institution’s leaders and alumni were ר׳ משה מרדכי אפשטיין, ר׳ איסר זלמן מלצר, ר׳ אהרן קוטלר and ר׳ יחזקאל סרנא. He also helped create or strengthen branches and associated institutions at Slutsk and elsewhere. During the First World War the yeshiva was displaced into the Russian interior before returning to Lithuania. When Lithuanian educational regulations threatened its traditional curriculum, he supported transferring a major branch to Mandatory Palestine. He joined the students in Hebron in 1925 and guided the new Knesses Yisrael there until his death in Jerusalem. His talks and letters were assembled posthumously as אור הצפון and related collections, transmitting the Slabodka approach internationally.
title: מייסד ישיבת כנסת ישראל סלבודקה ומראשי תנועת המוסר

name: ר׳ ישעיה שטיינר מקרסטיר
bio: ר׳ ישעיה בן ר׳ משה שטיינר (1851–1925), universally known as ר׳ ישעיה׳לה מקרסטיר, was a Hungarian Hasidic rebbe celebrated for hospitality, charity and practical care for the poor. Born at Zboró, now Zborov in Slovakia, he lost his father when young and entered the circle of ר׳ צבי הירש פרידמן מליסקא, whom he served as a devoted attendant and regarded as his principal teacher. He also visited ר׳ חיים הלברשטאם מצאנז and ר׳ מרדכי לייפר מנדבורנה. After his teacher’s death and tension surrounding the Liska succession, he established himself at Bodrogkeresztúr, where his open house, food distribution and personal counsel drew Jews from across Hungary and Galicia. His reputation rests chiefly on oral teaching, acts of חסד and the Kerestir court rather than on an authored book. He died at Bodrogkeresztúr on 3 Iyar 5685 and was succeeded by his son ר׳ אברהם שטיינר.
title: האדמו״ר הראשון מקרסטיר

name: ר׳ שמעון אהרן אגסי
bio: ר׳ שמעון אהרן אגסי (1852–1914), commonly called ר׳ שמעון אגסי and known by the acronym רשב״א, was a leading Baghdadi rabbi, kabbalist, preacher and communal educator. Born into a prosperous merchant family of Persian origin, he chose intensive Torah study over the family business and learned at Midrash Bet Zilkha under ר׳ שמואל מג׳לד and ר׳ נסים הלוי. He became especially close to ר׳ יוסף חיים, the בן איש חי, with whom he exchanged Torah correspondence and whose public teachings deeply shaped Baghdadi religious life. In 1879 he married Rachel, daughter of ר׳ עבדאללה בן אליה בחר. The death of his eldest son Aharon before marriage inspired בני אהרן, his commentary on שער הגלגולים of ר׳ חיים ויטאל. Agassi established a yeshiva to train rabbis and dayanim, combined Torah with Turkish-language instruction, and founded the support society תומכי תורה. His pupils included ר׳ יצחק נסים, ר׳ יעקב מוצפי, ר׳ סלמן חוגי עבודי and ר׳ אפרים כהן. His writings span Kabbalah, homiletics, poetry and Jewish belief. He died in Baghdad during a plague outbreak on 31 July 1914, shortly after the outbreak of the First World War.
title: רשב״א; מחכמי ומקובלי בגדאד

name: ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק
bio: ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק (1853–1918), commonly called ר׳ חיים מבריסק, transformed modern Talmudic study through the conceptual method known as the Brisker derekh. Born in Volozhin to ר׳ יוסף דוב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק, author of בית הלוי, he spent part of his youth in Slutsk and returned to Volozhin after marrying Lifsha, daughter of ר׳ רפאל שפירא. In 1880 he joined the Volozhin faculty alongside ר׳ נפתלי צבי יהודה ברלין. His lectures replaced accumulations of local textual solutions with exact definitions of legal categories, frequently explaining apparent contradictions in the Mishneh Torah of ר׳ משה בן מימון through two distinct conceptual frameworks. When the Russian authorities closed Volozhin in 1892, he moved to Brest-Litovsk and succeeded his father as communal rabbi. There his household became renowned not only for learning but for material assistance to the poor and a broad approach to saving life. His influence spread through students and family, especially his sons ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק and ר׳ משה סולובייצ׳יק. He died while seeking medical treatment in Otwock on 30 July 1918 and was buried in Warsaw. His carefully revised חידושי רבנו חיים הלוי, published posthumously, became the foundational printed expression of Brisker analysis.
title: רבה של בריסק; מייסד דרך בריסק

name: ר׳ שמואל בורנשטיין
bio: ר׳ שמואל בורנשטיין (4 Cheshvan 5616–24 Tevet 5686; 1855–1926), known from his teachings as the שם משמואל, was the second Sochatchover Rebbe and a major interpreter of the Kotsk–Sochatchov tradition. He was born in Kock in the household of his maternal grandfather ר׳ מנחם מנדל מורגנשטרן. His parents were ר׳ אברהם בורנשטיין, later author of אבני נזר and founder of the Sochatchov dynasty, and Sarah Tzina Morgenstern. He accompanied his father through successive rabbinates in Parczew, Krośniewice, Nasielsk, and finally Sochaczew, remaining his closest student. In 1891 his father sent him to Ottoman Palestine to investigate purchasing land for an observant agricultural settlement, but Ottoman restrictions frustrated the project. After his father’s death in 1910, he succeeded him as rebbe and head of the Sochaczew yeshiva. The First World War destroyed Sochaczew as a functioning Hasidic centre; after wartime detention in Germany he re-established his court in Łódź and then, in 1919, in quieter Zgierz. His discourses combine close biblical and rabbinic interpretation, Kabbalistic structures, Kotsk moral intensity, and teachings received from ר׳ אברהם בורנשטיין and ר׳ מנחם מנדל מורגנשטרן. Collected from manuscripts and students’ copies, they were published posthumously as שם משמואל. He died in the resort town of Otwock and was buried beside his father in Sochaczew.
title: האדמו״ר השני מסוכטשוב; בעל שם משמואל

name: ר׳ משה גסטר
bio: ר׳ משה גסטר (1856–1939) was a Romanian-born rabbi, linguist, folklorist, manuscript collector and Zionist leader who served as Haham of London's Spanish and Portuguese Jews. Born in Bucharest, he studied at Leipzig and the Jewish Theological Seminary of Breslau, receiving rabbinic ordination in 1881. He then taught Romanian literature at the University of Bucharest and pioneered the scholarly study of Romanian folklore. His public advocacy against discrimination toward Romanian Jews led the government to expel him in 1885. Settling in England, he lectured on Slavonic literature at Oxford and in 1887 became Haham at Bevis Marks. He also directed the Judith Lady Montefiore College at Ramsgate from 1890 until institutional disputes prompted his resignation in 1896. Gaster was active in חובבי ציון and became a founder and president of the English Zionist Federation; discussions connected with the future Balfour Declaration took place at his London home. His scholarship ranged across Romanian literature, Jewish and comparative folklore, Samaritan texts, liturgy, Bible, Anglo-Jewish history and Hebrew manuscripts. Retiring from the Hahamship in 1918/19 as his eyesight weakened, he remained an influential scholar and collector until his death near Abingdon in 1939.
title: חכם קהילת הספרדים בלונדון; חוקר ופולקלוריסט

name: ר׳ יוסף רוזין
bio: ר׳ יוסף רוזין (1858–1936), universally known as the Rogatchover Gaon, was an exceptionally original Talmudist and the Hasidic rabbi of Dvinsk. Born in Rogachev to a Kapust-Chabad family, he was sent at thirteen to Slutsk to study under ר׳ יוסף דוב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק alongside ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק, and later studied in Shklov under ר׳ יהושע לייב דיסקין. In 1889 he became rabbi of Dvinsk’s Hasidic community, serving alongside the non-Hasidic communal rabbi ר׳ מאיר שמחה הכהן. His method ranged freely across the Babylonian and Jerusalem Talmuds, midrash, legal codes, and philosophical terminology, often reducing distant passages to a single abstract principle. His extraordinarily compressed responsa typically direct the reader through chains of citations rather than conventional exposition. The multivolume צפנת פענח includes commentaries on the Mishneh Torah of ר׳ משה בן מימון, Talmud, Torah, responsa, and correspondence. During the First World War he was evacuated to Petrograd and returned to Dvinsk in 1924. Illness brought him to Vienna for surgery in 1936; he died there on 5 March and was returned to Dvinsk for burial. His daughter Rachel Citron and ר׳ ישראל אלתר ספרן־פוקס later risked their lives to preserve his manuscripts on microfilm, enabling extensive posthumous publication.
title: הגאון הרוגצ׳ובר; בעל צפנת פענח

name: ר׳ ברוך הלוי אפשטיין
bio: ר׳ ברוך הלוי אפשטיין (1860–1941) was a Lithuanian Talmudic scholar, writer, and author of תורה תמימה. Born in Bobruisk to ר׳ יחיאל מיכל הלוי אפשטיין, later author of ערוך השולחן, he grew up in Novogrudok and studied at Volozhin under his uncle ר׳ נפתלי צבי יהודה ברלין. After marrying the daughter of ר׳ אלעזר משה הורוויץ, he settled in Pinsk. Although ordained, he declined communal rabbinates and worked professionally as an accountant and banker, devoting his remaining hours to scholarship. תורה תמימה, composed in Pinsk and published in 1902, arranges rabbinic interpretations alongside biblical verses and explains their relationship; it became one of the era’s most widely used Torah commentaries. His other writings include the expansive autobiographical-historical מקור ברוך, תוספת ברכה, and ברוך שאמר. From 1923 to 1926 he lived in New York, seeking publishing and rabbinic opportunities and serving for a time as director of Ezras Torah, before returning to Pinsk. After German forces occupied Pinsk in July 1941, the elderly and ill scholar died in the Jewish hospital. Some reference works date his death to 1942, but the early-occupation account supports 1941.
title: בעל תורה תמימה

name: ר׳ שמעון יהודה שקופ
bio: ר׳ שמעון יהודה שקופ (1860–1939) was one of the most influential Lithuanian Talmudists of the modern yeshiva world. Born in Turets, in present-day Belarus, he studied at Mir and Volozhin, where ר׳ חיים סולובייצ׳יק became his principal intellectual influence. In 1884 ר׳ אליעזר גורדון appointed him to teach at Telz. Over seventeen years there he developed a conceptual method centred on precise legal categories and underlying principles. He left during the Musar controversy, served as rabbi and teacher in Maltsh from 1903 and Bransk from 1907, and in 1920 assumed leadership of Shaar HaTorah in Grodno. He also became rabbi of Grodno’s Vorstadt district in 1926. A fundraising visit brought him to the United States in 1928; he briefly taught at RIETS before returning to Grodno. His שערי יושר, first published in 1928, systematized his approach and remains a cornerstone of lomdut. He died in Grodno shortly after the Soviet occupation in 1939. His introduction to שערי יושר articulated a lasting ethical vision: intellectual achievement should enlarge responsibility to the community rather than serve private brilliance.
title: ראש ישיבת שער התורה; בעל שערי יושר

name: ר׳ שלום דובער שניאורסון
bio: ר׳ שלום דובער שניאורסון (20 Cheshvan 5621/1860–2 Nisan 5680/1920), known as the Rebbe Rashab, was the fifth rebbe of Chabad-Lubavitch. Born in Lyubavichi to ר׳ שמואל שניאורסון and Rivkah, he began transcribing his father’s discourses as a youth and married Shterna Sarah, granddaughter of ר׳ מנחם מנדל שניאורסון, in 1875. After his father’s death in 1882 he delivered original maamarim and guided Hasidim, though he accepted the full public mantle only in 1893. His long, analytically structured series of discourses gave Chabad thought an unprecedented systematic form; continuations beginning in 5666 and 5672 are particularly influential. In 1897 he founded Tomchei Temimim in Lyubavichi, combining advanced Talmud and halakhah with sustained Chabad study and contemplative prayer. He organized economic aid, religious provision for Jewish soldiers, and educational emissaries to distant Russian communities. Ideologically he resisted secularizing movements and political Zionism while advocating practical support for Jews in Ottoman Palestine, including purchasing land in Hebron. The First World War forced the Chabad court and yeshivah from Lyubavichi to Rostov-on-Don in 1915. There, amid revolution and civil war, he began organizing resistance to Soviet suppression of Jewish religious life. He died in Rostov in 1920 and was succeeded by his son ר׳ יוסף יצחק שניאורסון. His thousands of manuscripts were published posthumously.
title: האדמו״ר הרש״ב; האדמו״ר החמישי מחב״ד

name: ר׳ ברוך בער ליבוביץ
bio: ר׳ ברוך בער ליבוביץ (c. 1862–1939), renowned as Reb Baruch Ber and בעל ברכת שמואל, was a central transmitter of the Brisk analytical method. Born near Slutsk, he studied at Volozhin Yeshiva and became deeply attached to ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק, whose conceptual approach shaped his lifelong teaching. After marriage to the daughter of ר׳ אברהם יצחק צימרמן, he served in Halusk. In 1904 he succeeded ר׳ חיים רבינוביץ as head of Yeshivat Knesset Beit Yitzchak in Slabodka. The First World War drove the institution through Minsk and Kremenchug; after the Bolshevik revolution he re-established it in Vilna. In 1926 Polish pressure over competing yeshivot led him to move the academy to Kamianets, where it became a leading prewar Lithuanian yeshiva. He travelled to the United States in 1928 with his son-in-law ר׳ ראובן גרוזובסקי to raise funds. His lectures, edited as ברכת שמואל, develop precise conceptual distinctions while repeatedly crediting his teacher. When war began in 1939, the yeshiva fled east into independent Lithuania. He became gravely ill and died in November 1939, shortly after reaching Vilna, where he was buried. His students carried his method into major postwar yeshivot.
title: ראש ישיבת כנסת בית יצחק; בעל ברכת שמואל

name: ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי
bio: ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי (24 August 1863–9 August 1940) was a Lithuanian posek, av beit din and communal leader whose Vilna office became a clearing-house for halakhic questions, institutional policy and relief across Eastern European Orthodox Jewry. Born in Iwye to ר׳ דוד שלמה גרודזינסקי, the town’s rabbi, he studied among the perushim of Eishyshok and at Volozhin, where ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק influenced his analytical learning. After marrying Leah, daughter of Vilna dayan ר׳ אליהו אליעזר גרודזינסקי, he joined the Vilna beit din in 1887. He never held an uncontested title of ‘chief rabbi of Vilna’; rather, his authority grew through the rabbinical court, scholarship and communal trust. He supported the Ramailes yeshiva, taught an elite scholars’ group and answered correspondents internationally. At Agudath Israel’s 1912 founding conference he entered its leading rabbinic council, while retaining an independent Lithuanian leadership role. After the First World War he and ר׳ ישראל מאיר הכהן organized support for devastated yeshivot; the Vaad Hayeshivot, founded in 1924, coordinated fundraising and material aid for a large regional network. His three-volume שו״ת אחיעזר, published in Vilna between 1922 and 1939, addresses all sections of the Shulchan Aruch and modern communal problems with conceptual precision and practical responsibility. He also advocated for persecuted German Jews after 1933. When war divided Poland in 1939, he urged displaced yeshivot toward temporarily Lithuanian Vilna and organized assistance for thousands of refugees. He died before Soviet repression and Nazi mass murder destroyed the institutional world he had laboured to sustain.
title: בעל שו״ת אחיעזר, אב בית הדין וממנהיגי יהדות וילנה

name: ר׳ אברהם מרדכי אלתר
bio: ר׳ אברהם מרדכי אלתר (1865–1948), known by the title אמרי אמת, was the third Gerrer Rebbe and one of the most influential Orthodox leaders of interwar Poland. Born in Góra Kalwaria to ר׳ יהודה אריה ליב אלתר, the שפת אמת, and Yocheved Rivka Kaminer, he succeeded his father in 1905. Ger expanded into a vast Hasidic movement under his leadership, with a network of batei midrash, yeshivot and communal organizations. He helped establish Agudath Israel and promoted Orthodox political organization and education while making several visits to Mandatory Palestine. During the First World War he left Ger for Warsaw, which became his principal Polish base. After the German invasion he was hunted and concealed in Warsaw; an international rescue effort enabled him and part of his family to leave occupied Europe in 1940. His eldest son ר׳ מאיר אלתר and much of the family were murdered in the Holocaust. In Jerusalem he rebuilt the Gerrer court and its institutions among survivors. His teachings, letters and halakhic material were published as אמרי אמת, largely posthumously. Trapped in Jerusalem during the 1948 war, he died on Shavuot and was buried in the courtyard of Yeshivat Sefat Emet because access to the Mount of Olives was impossible. His son ר׳ ישראל אלתר succeeded him.
title: האדמו״ר מגור; בעל אמרי אמת

name: ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק
bio: ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק (7 September 1865–1 September 1935), known as Rav Kook or הראי״ה קוק, was a halakhist, mystic, Hebrew thinker and formative religious-Zionist leader. Born in Grīva beside Dvinsk to ר׳ שלמה זלמן קוק and Perel Zlata Felman, he combined Lithuanian yeshivah learning with Hasidic and kabbalistic traditions. He studied at Volozhin under ר׳ נפתלי צבי יהודה ברלין and served the communities of Žeimelis and Bauska. In 1904 he became rabbi of Jaffa and the surrounding agricultural settlements, addressing the practical religious questions of renewed Jewish life in the Land of Israel. Stranded in Europe during the First World War, he lived in St Gallen and then led London’s Machzike Hadath congregation. Returning in 1919, he became Ashkenazi chief rabbi of Jerusalem; in 1921 he helped establish the Chief Rabbinate and became the first Ashkenazi chief rabbi of Mandatory Palestine. He founded Mercaz HaRav in 1924. His writings—including אורות, אורות התשובה, עין איה, שבת הארץ and responsa—joined halakhah, spirituality, national rebirth and universal ethics. Many works were edited posthumously by his son ר׳ צבי יהודה הכהן קוק and students including ר׳ דוד כהן and ר׳ יעקב משה חרל״פ.
title: הראי״ה קוק; הרב הראשי האשכנזי הראשון לארץ ישראל

name: ר׳ יחיא יצחק הלוי
bio: ר׳ יחיא יצחק הלוי (c. 1867–1932) was chief jurist, chief rabbi and communal leader of Yemenite Jewry during a period of famine, political change and internal controversy. Born in Sana’a to Musa Yitzhak Halevi, a tanner, he studied first with his maternal grandfather ר׳ שלום מנצורה and later in the Maharitz synagogue and the beit midrash of ר׳ חיים קורח. Trained in Talmud, halakhah, ritual slaughter and communal administration, he became head of the Sana’a rabbinical court in 1902 and hakham bashi by 1905. After the devastating siege and famine of 1904–06, he rebuilt communal structures, supervised judges and slaughterers across Yemen and represented Jewish communities before Imam Yahya, including collection of the jizya. He corresponded with leaders abroad, among them ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק, and dealt with emigration, education and the rescue of Jewish orphans threatened with forced conversion. Although he opposed the Dor De’ah reforms associated with ר׳ יחיא קאפח and defended established Kabbalistic custom, the two continued serving together on the court. Thousands of his rulings, letters and legal documents survive in manuscript and were later gathered in the איש ימיני memorial series. He died in Sana’a in 1932.
title: הרב הראשי וראב״ד צנעא ותימן

name: ר׳ יוסף צבי דושינסקי
bio: ר׳ יוסף צבי דושינסקי (1867–1948), known as מהרי״ץ דושינסקי, was a Hungarian rabbi who became chief rabbinic leader of Jerusalem’s Edah HaChareidis and founder of the Dushinsky community. Born at Paks, Hungary, he studied with leading Hungarian scholars and received semikhah before serving as rabbi of Galanta from 1895 and of Khust from 1921. Following the death of ר׳ יוסף חיים זוננפלד, he was invited to Jerusalem and arrived in 1933 with students and his library. He established Yeshivat Beit Yosef Tzvi at 54 Shmuel HaNavi Street and served as גאב״ד of the Edah HaChareidis, while also holding senior positions in Agudath Israel. He defended the institutional autonomy and anti-Zionist outlook of the Old Yishuv, yet dealt pragmatically with wartime relief, refugees and public authorities. In 1947 he testified before the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine. Ill health took him briefly to Bat Yam in 1948; he died on 17 October in Jerusalem and was buried in the temporary Shaare Zedek cemetery. His responsa, sermons and Torah commentary were published in the שו״ת מהרי״ץ and תורת מהרי״ץ series.
title: גאב״ד העדה החרדית ומייסד קהילת דושינסקי

name: ר׳ חיים אלעזר שפירא
bio: ר׳ חיים אלעזר שפירא (1868–1937), known as the מנחת אלעזר, was the third Munkács Rebbe, chief rabbi of Munkács and a prolific halakhic authority. Born in Strzyżów into the Spira dynasty, he was educated principally by his father ר׳ צבי הירש שפירא, author of דרכי תשובה. The family settled in Munkács, where he became head of the rabbinical court in 1903 and succeeded his father as chief rabbi and rebbe in 1913. He developed Darchei Teshuva Yeshiva and a broad network of traditional schools, charities and communal services. His six-volume responsa מנחת אלעזר addressed ritual, communal and contemporary questions; his many other books treated prayer, custom, Kabbalah and Hasidic teaching. He fiercely opposed Zionism, religious Zionism, Agudath Israel and modernizing trends, positions central to his public leadership and controversies. In 1930 he travelled to Mandatory Palestine, especially Jerusalem and Safed, and met the aged kabbalist ר׳ שלמה אליעזר אלפנדרי; the journey was recorded in מסעות ירושלים. The 1933 wedding of his only daughter Chaya Fruma Rivka to ר׳ ברוך יהושע ירחמיאל רבינוביץ drew an enormous crowd and survives on film. He died in Munkács in 1937 and was succeeded by his son-in-law. His grave became a pilgrimage site after its restoration.
title: האדמו״ר ממונקאטש; בעל מנחת אלעזר

name: ר׳ איסר זלמן מלצר
bio: ר׳ איסר זלמן מלצר (1870–1953) was a leading Lithuanian rosh yeshiva and halakhic scholar. Born in Mir, he studied in Mir, Volozhin—where ר׳ חיים סולובייצ׳יק profoundly shaped his analytical method—and Radin under ר׳ ישראל מאיר הכהן. After marrying Beila Hinda, daughter of ר׳ שרגא פייבל פרנק, he helped lead the Slabodka yeshiva and in 1897 founded a major yeshiva in Slutsk. He became Slutsk’s rabbi in 1903. Soviet repression forced the institution across the Polish border to Kletsk; after arrest and mounting danger he joined it there in 1923. In 1925 he immigrated to Jerusalem and became rosh yeshiva of Etz Chaim, while serving prominently in the Moetzes Gedolei HaTorah. His monumental אבן האזל analyzes the Mishneh Torah of ר׳ משה בן מימון and became a foundational work of twentieth-century Brisker-style lomdus. His Jerusalem home and lectures influenced generations of scholars, notably his son-in-law ר׳ אהרן קוטלר. He died in Jerusalem and was buried on Har HaMenuchot.
title: ראש ישיבת עץ חיים; בעל אבן האזל

name: ר׳ משה רוזן
bio: ר׳ משה בן יהודה אריה רוזן (1870–12 October 1957), known as בעל נזר הקודש, was a Polish-Lithuanian and American Talmudist specializing in Seder Kodashim. Born in Brańsk, he studied locally, in Bielsk with ר׳ אריה ליב ילין, in Ruzhin with ר׳ מרדכי גימפל יפה and independently. At the Kovno kollel he received ordination from ר׳ יצחק אלחנן ספקטור and ר׳ משה דנישבסקי. In 1897 he became rabbi of Kvėdarna, Lithuania, serving there for roughly three decades and forming a close scholarly friendship with ר׳ אברהם ישעיהו קרליץ, who reviewed part of his work on Zevahim. His נזר הקודש provided sustained commentary on the difficult sacrificial tractates and eventually appeared in numerous volumes. He immigrated to the United States in 1928, taught during the early development of Mesivta Torah Vodaath, and then served a Brownsville congregation in Brooklyn while continuing to publish. His writings also include שאלות משה and דברי סופרים. Contemporary and later testimony remembers both his learning and his place among the Lithuanian scholars who helped establish advanced Torah study in New York. He died during Sukkot 1957 and was buried at Mount Judah Cemetery in Queens. This canonical record deliberately excludes the Romanian chief-rabbi biography previously attached to his name.
title: בעל נזר הקודש; רב וראש ישיבה

name: ר׳ יעקב חיים סופר
bio: ר׳ יעקב חיים סופר (c. 1870–27 May 1939), generally known as בעל כף החיים, was an Iraqi-born Sephardi halakhist and kabbalist whose encyclopedic commentary became a major guide to practical law and custom. Born in Baghdad to ר׳ יצחק ברוך סופר and Esther, he studied at the Beit Zilkha yeshivah under ר׳ עבדאללה סומך and absorbed the teaching and communal traditions of ר׳ יוסף חיים, the Ben Ish Chai. His formation joined rigorous halakhic learning, Iraqi minhag and Lurianic Kabbalah. In 1904 he travelled to Ottoman Palestine with Iraqi colleagues, visited sacred sites and chose to remain in Jerusalem. He first joined the kabbalistic circle of Beit El in the Old City and also studied among the Rehovot HaNahar kabbalists associated with ר׳ חיים שאול דוויק הכהן. By 1909 he was teaching at Shoshanim LeDavid, the Iraqi synagogue and yeshivah in the Beit Israel–Bukharan area, where he spent the rest of his scholarly career and served the Babylonian community. There he composed כף החיים, arranged according to Shulchan Aruch. Its eight author-published volumes on Orach Chayim appeared from 1910 to 1933, followed by the first Yoreh De'ah volume in 1936. The work gathers an unusually broad range of Rishonim, Acharonim, local customs and kabbalistic rulings, especially those associated with ר׳ יצחק לוריא, while normally identifying its sources. It consequently became particularly influential in Sephardi and Mizrahi halakhic practice. He also wrote קול יעקב on scribal law, יגל יעקב, ישמח ישראל and חיים עד העולם. ר׳ יעקב חיים died in Jerusalem on 9 Sivan 5699 and was buried on the Mount of Olives. A second Yoreh De'ah volume was issued posthumously from his manuscript and completed by ר׳ עובדיה יוסף; it must therefore not be represented as wholly finished by the author himself.
title: בעל כף החיים, פוסק ומקובל

name: ר׳ עמרם קורח
bio: ר׳ עמרם קורח (1871–1952), the last chief rabbi of Yemen’s Jewish community, was a judge, scribe, communal administrator and historian. Born in Sana’a to ר׳ יחיא קורח, he was orphaned at ten and continued his education under family and communal scholars. His Arabic literacy and legal training led to service as secretary of the rabbinical court under ר׳ סלימאן קארה. He administered the communal heqdesh treasury and headed the Al-Kessar synagogue. In 1932 he was appointed an assistant to ר׳ יחיא אל-אביץ׳; after the latter’s death in 1934 he became chief rabbi and head of the court. Severe conflict within Sana’a Jewry over the Zohar and communal authority led him to resign the chief office after roughly two years, though he continued adjudication, shechita supervision and liaison work with the imam’s government. In 1946 he became a principal intermediary with the Jewish Agency. On the eve of Yom Kippur 1950, during Operation On Eagles’ Wings, he immigrated with his family to Israel and settled in Jerusalem. His posthumously published סערת תימן, based partly on Sana’a court records, is a major chronicle of Yemenite Jewish institutions, customs and upheavals. He died in Jerusalem on 3 October 1952 and was buried in Sanhedria Cemetery.
title: הרב הראשי האחרון ליהודי תימן

name: ר׳ יוסף צבי הרץ
bio: ר׳ יוסף צבי הרץ (1872–1946), Joseph Herman Hertz in English, served from 1913 until his death as Chief Rabbi of the United Hebrew Congregations of the British Empire. Born in Rebrény, he emigrated to New York as a child and became the first rabbinical graduate of the Jewish Theological Seminary in 1894. He served congregations in Syracuse, Johannesburg and Manhattan before moving to London. His 1920–1921 Imperial tour linked distant Jewish communities across the British Empire. He defended Orthodox practice, supported Zionism, aided refugees from Nazism and helped found the Council of Christians and Jews. His Pentateuch and Haftorahs, prayer-book commentary and Book of Jewish Thoughts became enduring educational works.
title: הרב הראשי של הקהילות העבריות המאוחדות באימפריה הבריטית

name: ר׳ אלחנן בונם וסרמן
bio: ר׳ אלחנן בונם וסרמן (1874–1941) was a leading Lithuanian rosh yeshiva, Talmudist, Agudath Israel thinker, and close disciple of ר׳ ישראל מאיר הכהן. Born in Biržai, he studied at Telz under ר׳ אליעזר גורדון and ר׳ שמעון יהודה שקופ, then spent two formative years in Brisk with ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק. After marriage to Michla Atlas he taught in Mstislavl, studied in the Kodashim kollel at Radin, and headed a yeshiva in Brest. During the First World War he led the displaced Radin students in Smilavichy. In 1921, at his teacher’s direction, he became rosh yeshiva of Ohel Torah in Baranovichi, building it into an institution of roughly three hundred students. His sharply organized analytical teachings circulated widely and were later collected as קובץ שיעורים, קובץ הערות and related volumes; קובץ מאמרים preserved his forceful religious and political essays. A 1937–1939 fundraising mission took him across the United States, but he returned to his students. War drove him to Vilna. While visiting Kovno in July 1941, he and other rabbis were seized by Lithuanian collaborators and murdered at the Seventh Fort. His final address, calling for repentance and communal solidarity, became an enduring Holocaust testimony.
title: ראש ישיבת אהל תורה בברנוביץ׳; בעל קובץ שיעורים

name: ר׳ ירוחם הלוי ליבוביץ
bio: ר׳ ירוחם הלוי ליבוביץ (c.1875–1936), known as the Mashgiach of Mir, was one of the formative Musar educators of the twentieth-century yeshiva world. Born in Lyuban in present-day Belarus, he studied at Slabodka under ר׳ נתן צבי פינקל and then at Kelm, whose discipline and intellectual Musar became central to his teaching. After marrying Rivka, a relative of ר׳ שמחה זיסל זיו, he spent extended periods studying at Kelm and in the Kodashim kollel at Radin, where he became mashgiach in 1907. Concerned that his prominence might impinge upon ר׳ ישראל מאיר הכהן, he left Radin and joined Mir around 1910–1911. During the First World War he was separated from the yeshiva’s Poltava exile and subsequently helped rebuild several Lithuanian institutions, including Slabodka and Ponevezh. He returned permanently to Mir in 1923–1924, inaugurating what later students remembered as the yeshiva’s spiritual golden age. His exacting talks united Kelm’s analysis of human motives with a sweeping view of human dignity, divine order, and responsibility. Students included ר׳ יחזקאל לוינשטיין, ר׳ חיים שמואלביץ and many later postwar leaders. He died in Mir on 18 Sivan 5696. His family and students edited his talks as דעת תורה, דעת חכמה ומוסר and related collections.
title: המשגיח של ישיבת מיר; בעל דעת תורה

name: ר׳ אליהו לופיאן
bio: ר׳ אליהו לופיאן (1876–21 September 1970), widely called ר׳ אלי׳, was one of the twentieth century's most influential transmitters of the Kelm school of Mussar. Born in Grajewo to Yaakov and Frida Lopian, he remained in Łomża to study when his family emigrated to the United States, then entered the Kelm Talmud Torah and learned under ר׳ שמחה זיסל זיו and ר׳ יצחק בלאזר. He married Sarah Leah, daughter of ר׳ יצחק דוד רוטמן, and became a central teacher and institutional leader in Kelm. During the First World War he remained with students and continued teaching; afterward he traveled through Lithuanian communities encouraging students to return and helped rebuild the yeshiva. In the later 1920s he settled in London and served at Etz Chaim Yeshiva in the East End alongside ר׳ נחמן שלמה גרינשפן, shaping generations of British rabbinic students. He immigrated to Israel in 1950, taught Mussar in Jerusalem, and in 1951 became the spiritual director of Knesses Chizkiyahu, first at Zikhron Ya'akov and from 1955 at Kfar Hasidim. His demanding Kelm discipline was joined to close personal concern for students. His talks were edited posthumously by his student ר׳ שלום מרדכי הכהן שבדרון as לב אליהו, an enduring anthology of Torah interpretation, faith and ethical self-examination. He died in Jerusalem on 20 Elul 5730 and was buried on the Mount of Olives.
title: מבעלי המוסר של קלם ומשגיח ישיבת כנסת חזקיהו

name: ר׳ פינחס דוד הלוי הורוביץ
bio: ר׳ פינחס דוד הלוי הורוביץ (1876–1941) was a Jerusalem-born Hasidic leader and founder of the Boston dynasty, one of the earliest Hasidic courts created in the United States. A descendant of ר׳ שמואל שמלקה הורוביץ מניקלשבורג and raised after his father’s death under his uncle ר׳ דוד בידרמן מלעלוב, he combined rabbinic learning with architectural work in Jerusalem. Sent to Europe in 1914 as a representative of the Jerusalem community, he was stranded by the First World War and reached Boston in 1915. There he gathered Hasidim of varied European backgrounds, promoted kashrut, Sabbath observance and Jewish education, and became known by the American city in the traditional Hasidic manner. He also participated in Agudath Israel of America and the founding milieu of Yeshiva Torah Vodaath. In 1939 he transferred his court to Williamsburg, Brooklyn, where he died in 1941. His sons ר׳ משה הורוביץ and ר׳ לוי יצחק הורוביץ continued the New York and Boston branches. This person must not be confused with ר׳ פינחס הלוי הורוביץ (1731–1805), author of הפלאה.
base_name: Pinchas David Horowitz, First Bostoner Rebbe
title: מייסד חסידות בוסטון

name: ר׳ אברהם ישעיהו קרליץ
bio: ר׳ אברהם ישעיהו קרליץ (1878–1953), affectionately called ר׳ שעיה’לה and universally known as the חזון איש, was a Lithuanian-born posek and the formative Haredi authority of early Bnei Brak. Born in Kosava to ר׳ שמריהו יוסף קרליץ and Rasha Leah Katzenelbogen, he developed largely through private study and family scholarly circles. After marrying Batya Greineman he lived in Kvidan, Stowbtsy, Minsk and Vilna amid the upheavals of the First World War and revolution. He published the first חזון איש anonymously in 1911, eventually producing a wide-ranging series on the Talmud and halakhah. In 1933 he immigrated to Mandatory Palestine and settled in Bnei Brak, deliberately holding no salaried office while becoming a central address for rabbis, physicians, farmers, yeshiva leaders and public representatives. His rulings shaped observance of agricultural commandments, halakhic measurements, electricity, medicine, Sabbath and communal policy. He helped strengthen the Charedi yeshiva world and advised figures including ר׳ יוסף שלמה כהנמן and his brother-in-law ר׳ יעקב ישראל קניבסקי. He died at his Bnei Brak home in 1953 and was buried in the Shomrei Shabbos cemetery.
title: החזון איש; פוסק ומנהיג התורה בבני ברק

name: ר׳ אליעזר יהודה פינקל
bio: ר׳ אליעזר יהודה פינקל (c. 1879–1965), known as Reb Leizer Yudel, led the Mir Yeshiva in Europe and re-established it in Jerusalem. Born in Kelm to ר׳ נתן צבי פינקל, the Alter of Slabodka, and Gittel Wolpert, he grew up in Slabodka and studied at Telz, Brisk under ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק, Slutsk, Radin and Mir. In 1903 he married Malka, daughter of Mir’s rosh yeshiva ר׳ אליהו ברוך קמאי, joined the faculty and became its leader after his father-in-law’s death in 1917. He rebuilt the yeshiva after a 1911 fire and guided it through wartime exile and its interwar expansion into an international academy. Seeking visas for his students, he reached Mandatory Palestine before the Holocaust. The student body escaped separately through Lithuania, Japan and Shanghai under ר׳ חיים שמואלביץ. In 1944 he opened a Jerusalem branch with ten students, first in Meah Shearim and then Beit Yisrael; it became the renewed Mir Yeshiva. He supported other institutions and helped establish the Brisk yeshiva of ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק. His lectures were edited as דברי אליעזר. He died in Jerusalem and was buried on Har HaMenuchot.
title: ראש ישיבת מיר בפולין ובירושלים; בעל דברי אליעזר

name: ר׳ משה סולובייצ׳יק
bio: ר׳ משה הלוי סולובייצ׳יק (1879–1941) was a Lithuanian rabbi and rosh yeshiva who transplanted the Brisker analytical method to Warsaw and the United States. Born in Volozhin to ר׳ חיים סולובייצ׳יק, he studied with his father in Volozhin and Brisk and married Pesya, daughter of ר׳ אליהו פיינשטיין of Pruzhany. He served as rabbi of Raseiniai and Khislavichi before becoming head of Talmud studies at Warsaw’s Tachkemoni seminary. In 1929 he moved to New York to lead advanced Talmud study at RIETS, where his teaching decisively shaped American Orthodox scholarship. His students included his sons ר׳ יוסף דב סולובייצ׳יק and ר׳ אהרן סולובייצ׳יק. Most of his influence was transmitted orally through lectures, students and posthumously edited novellae.
title: ראש ישיבת רבי יצחק אלחנן

name: ר׳ צבי הירש פרבר
bio: ר׳ צבי הירש פרבר (approximately 1878/79–1966) was a Lithuanian-born British rabbi, halakhist, preacher and exceptionally prolific Hebrew author. Born in Slabodka, adjoining Kovno, to ר׳ שמעון יהודה ליב פרבר and חנה דבורה, he was formed in the Lithuanian mussar and yeshiva world. Sources associate his education with the Slabodka yeshiva and with ר׳ יצחק אלחנן ספקטור, ר׳ יצחק בלאזר and ר׳ נפתלי אמסטרדם. He migrated to England in 1910 or 1911. In Manchester he taught Talmud and helped establish or lead a yeshiva before moving to London. In July 1913 he became rabbi of the West End Talmud Torah Synagogue in Soho, later commonly called the West End Great Synagogue, and served the congregation for more than forty years, retiring in 1954 or 1955. The congregation and its affiliated burial arrangements gave him an unusual degree of independence from Britain's central religious establishment. He became known as an eloquent Lithuanian-style maggid and a leading representative of immigrant Orthodoxy. He established or helped organize the Committee of Orthodox Rabbis, served in leadership of the London Vaad Harabonim and the Hisachdus Harabonim, supported yeshiva education, and worked on shechita, burial and other communal questions. During ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק's First World War residence in London the two rabbis formed a close friendship, documented by surviving correspondence. ר׳ צבי הירש was also a persistent scholar: accounts place him regularly in the British Museum's Oriental Reading Room, and surviving autograph notebooks confirm sustained work on Torah, Talmud, halakhah and homiletics. His principal publication was כרם הצבי, a multi-volume halakhic and aggadic commentary on the Torah issued between 1920 and 1938; he later published a Passover Haggadah under the same title. His many other books and pamphlets addressed festivals, prayer, Pirkei Avot, King David, Jewish thought and practical legal controversies. He died in London in November 1966. Because celebratory rabbinic accounts sometimes differ over exact dates and offices, this record gives priority to Encyclopaedia Judaica, institutional catalogues, archival evidence and surviving manuscripts, while marking unresolved variants explicitly.
title: רב, דרשן, פוסק ומחבר בלונדון

name: ר׳ יוסף יצחק שניאורסון
bio: ר׳ יוסף יצחק שניאורסון (1880–1950), known as הריי״צ and the Frierdiker Rebbe, was the sixth rebbe of Chabad-Lubavitch. Born in Lyubavichi to ר׳ שלום דובער שניאורסון, he directed Tomchei Temimim and succeeded his father in 1920. He organized clandestine Jewish education under Soviet rule, survived a 1927 death sentence after international intervention, and led Chabad from Riga and Poland. Rescued from German-occupied Warsaw, he reached New York in 1940 and rebuilt Chabad education, publishing and relief institutions from 770 Eastern Parkway.
title: הריי״צ; האדמו״ר השישי מליובאוויטש

name: ר׳ יחיאל יעקב ויינברג
bio: ר׳ יחיאל יעקב ויינברג (1884–1966), author of שו״ת שרידי אש, connected Lithuanian yeshiva learning with German Neo-Orthodoxy and academic scholarship. Born in Ciechanowiec, he studied at Mir and Slabodka under ר׳ נתן צבי פינקל, then served as rabbi of Pilviškiai. In Germany he earned a doctorate and became the last rector of the Hildesheimer Rabbinical Seminary. Trapped in Warsaw in 1939, he was transferred as a Soviet citizen from the Warsaw Ghetto to Wülzburg detention camp in 1941 and remained imprisoned until 1945. His student ר׳ שאול ויינגורט later brought him to Montreux, where he wrote influential postwar responsa addressing communal reconstruction, education and modern Jewish life.
title: בעל שרידי אש; ראש בית המדרש לרבנים בברלין

name: ר׳ אריה לוין
bio: ר׳ אריה לוין (22 March 1885–28 March 1969) was a Jerusalem educator and pastoral rabbi remembered as רב האסירים, 'the Rabbi/Father of the Prisoners,' and הצדיק הירושלמי. He was born in Orla near Białystok, then in the Russian Empire and now in Poland, to Binyamin Beinush, a forester, and Ethel. His youth was shaped by poverty and persistent travel in search of Torah education. He studied in Slutsk, Slonim, Brest and Pinsk and, after initially being refused admission to Volozhin because of his age, learned in Hlyusk under ר׳ ברוך דב ליבוביץ. He was later accepted at the Volozhin yeshivah and studied under ר׳ רפאל שפירא. These stages formed his Lithuanian yeshivah background, although the precise year of every move is not firmly documented. In 1905 he immigrated alone to Ottoman Palestine, landed at Jaffa and shortly afterward moved to Jerusalem. In Jaffa he met ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק, then rabbi of Jaffa and the surrounding settlements, beginning a close lifelong relationship. In Jerusalem he studied at Yeshivat Torat Chaim and married Tzipora Chana, daughter of ר׳ דוד שפירא. He received rabbinic ordination in 1909 from ר׳ חיים ברלין, ר׳ שמואל סלנט and ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק. During the deprivation of the First World War, the family endured severe hunger and lost two daughters. From 1917 until the end of his life, ר׳ אריה served as mashgiaḥ and spiritual educator at the Etz Chaim Talmud Torah in Jerusalem. He lived simply, worked closely with children from poor families and resisted attempts to improve his own material circumstances. After ר׳ שלמה אלישיב, author of לשם שבו ואחלמה, immigrated to Jerusalem, ר׳ אריה became his student. His public reputation, however, grew chiefly from sustained acts of pastoral care rather than formal publication or high office. He regularly visited Jerusalem hospitals and deliberately entered institutions whose patients were otherwise socially isolated, including the leprosy hospitals in Talbiya and Bethlehem. He began visiting Jewish criminal prisoners during the British Mandate and continued for roughly twenty-five years. Every Sabbath and festival he walked to the Central Prison in Jerusalem's Russian Compound, prayed with inmates, listened to them, wrote letters and carried messages between prisoners and their families. As underground activists from the Haganah, Irgun and Lehi were imprisoned, he became their trusted spiritual advocate, without limiting his compassion to a single political camp or to political prisoners. His care for condemned underground fighters and other inmates earned the titles רב האסירים and אבי האסירים. Ministry of Defense museum displays preserve this role as part of the history of the Mandate prison. After the 1948 war, he continued visiting prisoners under the new state. In 1949, when the remains of the thirty-five members of the Lamed-Heh convoy were brought for burial and twelve could not be conventionally distinguished, Jerusalem's chief rabbi ר׳ צבי פסח פרנק asked him to conduct the traditional גורל הגר״א procedure. The resulting identifications were accepted by the families and state institutions. This episode belongs to Israeli religious memory; it should be described as a ritual identification accepted at the time, not as a modern forensic method. After independence he established Yeshivat Beit Aryeh in the courtyard of his modest home and appointed his son-in-law ר׳ אליעזר פלצינסקי as its head. He continued work at Etz Chaim, prison and hospital visits, private mediation and support for the poor. Shortly before his death he received the Fighters of the State decoration for assistance rendered during the underground period. He died at Hadassah Medical Center on Friday, 28 March 1969, immediately before Shabbat HaGadol, and was buried that afternoon in Sanhedria Cemetery. The timing fulfilled his request that no eulogies be delivered. His gravestone asks visitors to affirm belief in the resurrection of the dead. Much of the popular memory of ר׳ אריה comes through stories collected by his associate Simcha Raz in איש צדיק היה and צדיק יסוד עולם. These works preserve testimony and shaped his public image, but individual anecdotes require source criticism and should not all be treated as independently verified transcripts. His durable historical significance lies in an unusually inclusive model of rabbinic care that joined Lithuanian learning, Jerusalem education and practical solidarity with prisoners, patients, bereaved families and the poor across religious and political divisions.
title: רב האסירים והצדיק הירושלמי

name: ר׳ איסר יהודה אונטרמן
bio: ר׳ איסר יהודה אונטרמן (1886–1976) was a Lithuanian-trained halakhist, Religious Zionist leader and Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of Israel. Born in Brest-Litovsk, he studied at Maltsh, Mir and Volozhin, becoming a disciple of ר׳ שמעון שקופ and receiving semikhah from ר׳ רפאל שפירא and ר׳ שמחה זליג ריגר. After founding a yeshiva in Vishneva, he served several communities and became rabbi of Grodno. In 1924 he was appointed rabbi of Liverpool, where he united communal institutions, strengthened Jewish education, founded an academy for Torah study and led British Mizrachi. He testified before the Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry in support of Jewish settlement in Palestine. In 1946 he became Ashkenazi chief rabbi of Tel Aviv–Jaffa, established the Shevet MiYehuda kollel and, with ר׳ יעקב משה טולידאנו, created a special court for wartime agunot. Elected Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of Israel in 1964, he served until 1972 and addressed conversion, medical ethics, marriage, statehood and public halakhah. His principal responsa and studies appeared as שבט מיהודה. He died in Jerusalem and was buried on the Mount of Olives.
title: הרב הראשי האשכנזי לישראל; בעל שבט מיהודה

name: ר׳ יחזקאל אברמסקי
bio: ר׳ יחזקאל אברמסקי (1886–1976) was a leading twentieth-century Talmudist, communal rabbi and halakhic judge. Born at Dashkovichy in the Grodno region, he studied in the Lithuanian yeshiva world, notably at Telz, Slabodka and Brisk under ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק, and was closely associated with ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי. After rabbinates in Smolyan and Smalyavichy, he became rabbi of Slutsk in 1923. He resisted the Soviet destruction of Jewish religious life, helped publish the Torah journal Yagdil Torah, and was arrested and sent to forced labour before international intervention secured his release in 1931. In London he served Machzike Hadath and then, from 1934 to 1951, as senior dayan and head of the London Beth Din, greatly strengthening its standing. He settled in Jerusalem in 1951, taught and supported the yeshiva world, and received the 1956 Israel Prize for rabbinic literature. His multi-volume חזון יחזקאל combines textual comparison, explanation and novellae on the Tosefta.
title: אב בית דין לונדון ומחבר חזון יחזקאל

name: ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק
bio: ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק (19 October 1886–11 October 1959), known as the Griz or Brisker Rav, was the last rabbi of prewar Brisk and a central transmitter of the Brisker analytical method. He was born in Volozhin while his father ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק taught there; his mother Lifsha was a daughter of ר׳ רפאל שפירא. After the family moved to Brisk, his father became his principal teacher. He married Alte Hendel Auerbach and succeeded ר׳ חיים as rabbi of Brisk after the latter's death in 1918. His learning emphasized exact textual formulation, conceptual distinctions within halakhic categories and especially close analysis of Rambam's משנה תורה. He also supervised the difficult publication of his father's חידושי רבנו חיים הלוי in 1936. The German invasion of Poland found him away from Brisk at Krynica. He reached Warsaw and then Vilna, escaping to Mandatory Palestine with several children in 1941; his wife and children who remained behind were murdered in the Holocaust. In Jerusalem he declined formal state or chief-rabbinic office and taught a small selected circle in his home, from which the later Jerusalem Brisk yeshivot developed under his sons. He became an influential leader of anti-Zionist Lithuanian Haredi society, opposing participation in state institutions and policies he believed threatened religious autonomy. His own writings were published principally after his death as חידושי מרן רי״ז הלוי on Rambam, Torah and Talmudic tractates; student notebooks form a related but textually distinct literature. He died in Jerusalem in 1959 and was buried at Har HaMenuchot.

title: הגרי״ז — הרב מבריסק

name: ר׳ יוסף שלמה כהנמן
bio: ר׳ יוסף שלמה כהנמן (1886–1969), universally known as the Ponevezher Rav, rebuilt one of Lithuanian Jewry’s great Torah institutions in Israel. Born in Kuliai, he studied at Plungė, Telz under ר׳ אליעזר גורדון and ר׳ שמעון שקופ, Novardok, and Radin under ר׳ ישראל מאיר הכהן and ר׳ נפתלי טרופ. After marrying Feige Rubin, he became rabbi of Vidzy and founded a yeshiva there. In 1919 he succeeded ר׳ יצחק יעקב רבינוביץ as rabbi of Panevėžys, where he created a nationally important yeshiva, schools and an orphanage. He represented Jewish interests in the Lithuanian Seimas and helped lead Agudath Israel and the Vaad HaYeshivot. Abroad when war began in 1939, he remained in Mandatory Palestine and attempted to rescue Lithuanian Jews; his family, students and institutions were largely destroyed in the Holocaust. In late 1943–44 he re-established Ponevezh Yeshiva in Bnei Brak, then built a wide educational complex and Batei Avot for refugee children. Tireless international fundraising made the campus a symbol of Torah reconstruction. His Talmudic teachings and addresses were collected posthumously. He died in Bnei Brak in 1969.
title: הרב מפוניבז׳; מייסד ישיבת פוניבז׳ בבני ברק

name: ר׳ יהודה מאיר שפירא
bio: ר׳ יהודה מאיר שפירא (1887–1933) היה רב חסידי, מנהיג אגודת ישראל, חבר הסיים הפולני, מייסד ישיבת חכמי לובלין ויוזם מפעל הדף היומי. הוא נולד בשאץ שבבוקובינה ולמד אצל אביו ר׳ יעקב שמשון שפירא, סבו ר׳ שמואל יצחק שור ור׳ שלום מוסקוביץ. לאחר נישואיו כיהן ברבנות גלינה, סאנוק ופיוטרקוב. כנציג אגודת ישראל בסיים בשנים 1922–1927 עסק בזכויות יהודי פולין ובבניין מוסדות תורה. בכנסייה הגדולה של אגודת ישראל בווינה בשנת 1923 הציע שכל יהודי העולם ילמדו אותו דף תלמוד מדי יום; המחזור הראשון החל בראש השנה תרפ״ד. חזונו המוסדי התגשם בשנת 1930 עם פתיחת ישיבת חכמי לובלין, שנועדה להעניק לתלמידי חכמים תנאי לימוד, מגורים וספרייה ברמה שלא הייתה מקובלת בישיבות פולין. תשובותיו נדפסו באור המאיר, ואמרי דעת שלו שרד רק בחלקו לאחר אבדות מלחמת העולם הראשונה והשואה. הוא נפטר בלובלין בן ארבעים ושש בלבד. בשנת 1958 הועלו עצמותיו לירושלים, אולם שנת המוות נשארת 1933 כדי שהסמן ייעלם בזמן הנכון.
title: מייסד הדף היומי וישיבת חכמי לובלין

name: ר׳ יואל טייטלבוים
bio: ר׳ יואל טייטלבוים (1887–1979) was the founding rebbe of the modern Satmar Hasidic community. Born in Sighet to ר׳ חנניה יום טוב ליפא טייטלבוים, he served as rabbi in Irshava and Carei before assuming the Satu Mare rabbinate in 1934. In 1944 he was confined in the Cluj ghetto and escaped Hungary on the Kastner train, reaching Switzerland after detention in Bergen-Belsen. After a short stay in Jerusalem he settled in Williamsburg in 1946 and rebuilt Satmar as a major network of synagogues, schools and charities. He also led Jerusalem’s Edah HaChareidis. His ויואל משה systematically articulated his opposition to political Zionism, and his leadership shaped a large transatlantic Hasidic community and Kiryas Joel.
title: האדמו״ר מסאטמר; בעל ויואל משה

name: ר׳ יצחק אייזיק הלוי הרצוג
