bio: ר׳ יצחק אייזיק הלוי הרצוג (3 December 1888–25 July 1959) was a Polish-born scholar, Chief Rabbi of Ireland and Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of Mandatory Palestine and Israel. Born in Łomża, he moved with his rabbinic family to Leeds and Paris. Alongside rabbinic ordination, he studied mathematics and classical and Semitic languages; his doctorate investigated the ancient tekhelet dye. He served Belfast from 1916, Dublin from 1919, and became chief rabbi of the Irish Free State, maintaining warm relations with Irish nationalist leaders while defending shechitah and Jewish communal interests. Elected successor to ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק in 1936, he settled in Jerusalem and led the Ashkenazi Chief Rabbinate through the Holocaust, statehood and the first decade of Israel. He travelled internationally seeking rescue for European Jews and in 1946 toured Europe to recover Jewish children placed in Christian institutions. After 1948 he advocated incorporating halakhic principles into Israeli law while recognizing the practical needs of state institutions, and served as president of the Great Rabbinical Court. His scholarship ranges from Jewish jurisprudence to tekhelet and responsa; היכל יצחק was published principally after his death. He received the Israel Prize in Rabbinical Literature in 1958 and was buried in Sanhedria Cemetery.
title: הרב הראשי האשכנזי לארץ ישראל ולמדינת ישראל

name: ר׳ קלונימוס קלמיש שפירא
bio: ר׳ קלונימוס קלמיש שפירא (1889–1943), the Piaseczna Rebbe, was a Polish Hasidic leader, educational theorist and spiritual leader in the Warsaw Ghetto. A son of ר׳ אלימלך שפירא of Grodzisk and student and son-in-law of ר׳ ירחמיאל משה הופשטיין of Kozhnitz, he became rabbi of Piaseczno in 1913 and later lived principally in Warsaw. In 1923 he founded Yeshivat Da’at Moshe, one of Warsaw’s largest Hasidic yeshivot. His educational writings sought to cultivate the inner spiritual life of children and adults rather than relying on coercion. Under German occupation his home at 5 Dzielna Street became a center of prayer, study, refuge and food relief. His wartime sermons, revised as catastrophe deepened and hidden with the Oneg Shabbat archive, were recovered after the war and published in 1960 as אש קודש. Deported to Trawniki, he was murdered during Aktion Erntefest.
title: האדמו״ר מפיאסצנה; בעל אש קודש

name: ר׳ ראובן מרגליות
bio: ר׳ ראובן מרגליות (30 November 1889–28 August 1971), commonly rendered Reuben or Reuven Margolies, was a Galician-born Israeli rabbinic scholar, editor, bibliographer and librarian. Born in Lemberg to Moshe and Miriam Margolies, he studied with ר׳ משה זאב מזוזה and ר׳ דוד טוניס but developed chiefly through intensive independent study. After his father's death he managed the family business and later operated a Hebrew bookshop that became a meeting place for scholars. He received rabbinic ordination in 1914 from ר׳ מאיר אריק and ר׳ משה באב״ד, yet declined a salaried rabbinate. During the First World War he fled to Vienna and hid from Austro-Hungarian conscription while composing נפש חיה. In Galicia he published prolifically and held posts in Mizrachi and Zionist institutions. Following the death of his first wife, Chaya Gendil, he immigrated to Mandatory Palestine in 1934 and settled in Tel Aviv. From then until retirement in 1967 he directed the Rambam Library, developing it from a tiny collection into a major rabbinic research library. His more than fifty books joined traditional erudition with bibliography, textual comparison, biography, halakhah, Talmud and Kabbalah. Especially influential were מרגליות הים on Sanhedrin, יסוד המשנה ועריכתה, editions of ספר חסידים and responsa מן השמים, and his annotated editions of the Zoharic corpus. He disputed גרשם שלום's interpretation of the ר׳ יעקב עמדין–ר׳ יהונתן אייבשיץ controversy. Awarded the Israel Prize for rabbinic literature in 1957, he died at Ichilov Hospital and was buried in Nahalat Yitzhak Cemetery.
title: חוקר תורני, מהדיר וספרן

name: ר׳ ישראל אבוחצירא
bio: ר׳ ישראל אבוחצירא (1889–1984), universally known as the בבא סאלי, was a Moroccan-Israeli rabbi, kabbalist and communal leader of the Abuhatzeira dynasty. Born in Rissani, he studied in the family yeshiva and was deeply affected by the 1920 martyrdom of his brother ר׳ דוד אבוחצירא. He served the communities of southeastern Morocco, especially Boudenib and Erfoud, as teacher, judge and chief rabbinic authority. After an initial immigration to Israel in 1951 and a return to Morocco, he settled permanently in Israel in 1964, living in Yavne and Ashkelon before Netivot. His reputation rests primarily on lived piety, prayer, oral teaching and communal memory rather than on a securely established corpus of authored books. His tomb in Netivot became a major pilgrimage site.
title: הבבא סאלי; רב ומקובל

name: ר׳ אברהם חיים נאה
bio: ר׳ אברהם חיים נאה (3 May 1890–21 July 1954), commonly called הגרא״ח נאה and בעל השיעורים, was a Jerusalem Chabad halakhist whose system of ritual measurements became one of the principal modern standards. Born in Hebron, he studied with his father ר׳ מנחם מנדל נאה, head of Magen Avot, and later at Ohel Moshe and Torat Chaim in Jerusalem. In 1911 he travelled as a Chabad emissary to Bukhara and served the Jewish community in Samarkand. Returning as war began, he was expelled as a Russian subject to Alexandria, where he established Yeshivat Eretz Yisrael for Palestinian exiles and wrote practical halakhic material for Egyptian Jewry. After the war he returned to Jerusalem, became scribe and secretary of the Edah HaChareidis court and worked closely with ר׳ יוסף חיים זוננפלד. He also served the Bukharan Quarter, taught at Musayof and held leadership roles in Kollel Chabad and Agudath Israel’s rabbinical court. קצות השולחן systematically adapts ר׳ שניאור זלמן מלאדי’s rulings for practical use. שיעורי תורה translated traditional quantities into grams and centimetres; his relatively smaller measures later became famous through debate with ר׳ אברהם ישעיהו קרליץ. He died in Jerusalem and was buried at Har HaMenuchot.
title: בעל השיעורים; פוסק ומחבר קצות השולחן

name: ר׳ יעקב קמינצקי
bio: ר׳ יעקב בן בנימין קמינצקי (1891–1986) was a Lithuanian-born North American rosh yeshiva, halakhic adviser and communal leader. Born in Kalushkove in the Minsk region and raised near Dolhinov, he studied in Minsk and for many years at the Slabodka yeshivah under ר׳ משה מרדכי אפשטיין and ר׳ נתן צבי פינקל. After marrying Etta, daughter of ר׳ דב צבי הלר, he continued in the Slabodka kollel and in 1926 became rabbi of Tytuvėnai. He left Europe in 1937, served briefly at Bikur Cholim in Seattle and then became rabbi of Congregation Toras Emes and a yeshivah head in Toronto. In 1946 he joined Mesivta Torah Vodaath in Brooklyn; after ר׳ שרגא פייבל מנדלוביץ’s death he shared its leadership with ר׳ גדליה שור, serving as rosh yeshiva until retirement. From Monsey he became, alongside ר׳ משה פיינשטיין, a widely consulted guide of American Orthodox Jewry and a senior leader of Agudath Israel and Torah Umesorah. He was renowned for lucid judgment, Hebrew grammar and an unusually broad intellectual curiosity. אמת ליעקב, much of it edited from manuscripts and oral teaching, preserves his biblical and Talmudic insights. He died in Baltimore and was buried at Mount Judah Cemetery in Queens.
title: ראש ישיבת תורה ודעת; חכימא דיהודאי

name: ר׳ צבי יהודה הכהן קוק
bio: ר׳ צבי יהודה הכהן קוק (15 Nisan 5651/1891–9 March 1982), known as הרצי״ה, was the son and principal editor of ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק and the formative rosh yeshiva of postwar Religious Zionism. Born in Žeimelis, he moved with his family to Bauska and immigrated to Jaffa in 1904. He studied at Torat Chaim in Jerusalem and chiefly under his father. During the First World War he taught in Halberstadt, was briefly detained as an enemy subject, and joined his parents in Switzerland. After returning in 1920, he travelled through Europe for Degel Yerushalayim and married Chava Leah Hutner in Warsaw. From 1923 he administered Mercaz HaRav and devoted decades to editing and disseminating his father’s manuscripts, including אורות and extensive letters and halakhic writings. Following ר׳ יעקב משה חרל״פ’s death, he became rosh yeshiva in 1952 and transformed Mercaz HaRav into the central academy of Religious Zionism. His Independence Day address immediately before the Six-Day War and his later teaching treated the State of Israel and settlement of the land as stages in redemption. Students became leading rabbis and founders of yeshivot and settlements; this association with Gush Emunim made him highly influential and politically controversial. His own essays were collected as לנתיבות ישראל. He died in Jerusalem and was buried at Har HaZeitim.
title: ראש ישיבת מרכז הרב וממנהיגי הציונות הדתית

name: ר׳ אהרן קוטלר
bio: ר׳ אהרן קוטלר (1892–1962), born Aharon Pines in Svislach, was a Lithuanian-trained rosh yeshiva who became a principal architect of postwar American yeshiva life. Orphaned young, he studied in Krynki and Minsk before entering Yeshivat Knesset Yisrael in Slabodka, where ר׳ נתן צבי פינקל and ר׳ משה מרדכי אפשטיין shaped his learning. After marrying Chana Perel, daughter of ר׳ איסר זלמן מלצר, he taught in Slutsk and from 1917 served as a regular maggid shiur. Communist pressure led him and many students across the border to Kletsk in 1921; there he built a major Polish-Lithuanian yeshiva and helped organize Vaad Hayeshivot. After Germany invaded Poland, the yeshiva regrouped in Vilna and then Jonava. Soviet authorities closed it in early 1941, and ר׳ אהרן escaped through Siberia and Japan to the United States. He immediately joined Vaad Hatzalah's efforts to rescue rabbis and yeshiva students trapped in Europe. In 1943 he founded Beth Medrash Govoha in Lakewood, deliberately locating intensive full-time Torah study away from New York's distractions. From a small opening group it became the institutional model for a large American kollel and yeshiva culture. He also led Agudath Israel of America's Council of Torah Sages, supported Torah Umesorah and helped establish and sustain Chinuch Atzmai in Israel. His surviving teachings—largely edited after his death as משנת רבי אהרן—combine close Talmudic analysis, lectures on Jewish thought, responsa and institutional correspondence. He died at Columbia-Presbyterian Medical Center in New York on 29 November 1962 and was buried on Har HaMenuchot in Jerusalem.
title: ראש ישיבת בית מדרש גבוה וממנהיגי עולם הישיבות בארצות הברית
aliases: רבי אהרן בן שניאור זלמן קוטלר

name: ר׳ אליהו אליעזר דסלר
bio: ר׳ אליהו אליעזר דסלר (1892–1953) was a Belarus-born British and Israeli mussar teacher and religious thinker. Born in Homel to ר׳ ראובן דב דסלר, he was formed in the disciplined Kelm Talmud Torah, where the legacy of ר׳ שמחה זיסל זיו shaped his ethical psychology. After marriage and years of economic instability, he went to England in 1929. He taught in London’s East End and Dalston and helped create institutions for intensive Torah learning. In the early 1940s he became a founder and guiding spirit of the Gateshead Kollel, a decisive institution in the reconstruction of European Torah scholarship in Britain. In 1947 ר׳ יוסף שלמה כהנמן invited him to become mashgiach of the newly rebuilt Ponovezh Yeshiva in Bnei Brak. His talks combined Kelm mussar, kabbalistic themes and a distinctive account of free will, self-interest, giving and spiritual perception. He published little as a conventional author during his lifetime. After his death, students ר׳ אריה כרמל and ר׳ חיים פרידלנדר assembled letters, notes and talks as מכתב מאליהו, which became one of the most influential works of twentieth-century Jewish thought. He died in Bnei Brak on 31 December 1953 and was buried there.
title: בעל מכתב מאליהו; משגיח ישיבת פוניבז׳

name: ר׳ אהרן ראטה
bio: ר׳ אהרן בן ר׳ שמואל יעקב ראטה (1894–1947), known affectionately as ר׳ אהרל׳ה and as the בעל שומר אמונים, was a Hungarian Hasidic rebbe and religious reformer. Born in Ungvár, he studied in the Hasidic world of Galicia and was influenced especially by ר׳ צבי אלימלך שפירא מבלאז׳וב. In 1921 he gathered an ascetic devotional fellowship in Satu Mare, emphasizing intense audible prayer, ritual purity, modesty, communal discipline and simple faith. After periods in Jerusalem and Transcarpathia, he led a community in Berehovo and settled permanently in Jerusalem around 1940, establishing Shomrei Emunim in the neighbourhoods of the Old Yishuv. His books טהרת הקודש, שולחן הטהור, נועם הלבבות and שומר אמונים combine Hasidic ethics, kabbalistic discipline and detailed communal instruction. שומר אמונים, written amid news of the Holocaust and published in 1942, became his best-known work. He died in Jerusalem in 1947. His followers divided between his son ר׳ אברהם חיים ראטה, leader of Shomrei Emunim, and his son-in-law ר׳ אברהם יצחק קאהן, whose group became Toldot Aharon.
title: בעל שומר אמונים ומייסד חבורת שומרי אמונים

name: ר׳ ישראל ברודי
bio: ר׳ ישראל ברודי (1895–1979), later Sir Israel Brodie, was chief rabbi of Great Britain and the Commonwealth from 1948 to 1965. Born in Newcastle upon Tyne to Lithuanian immigrant parents, he studied at University College London and Jews’ College, earning first-class honours in Hebrew, Aramaic and Syriac, and continued at Balliol College, Oxford. His studies were interrupted by service as a British Army Jewish chaplain in France in 1917–1919. After work in London’s East End he became minister of Melbourne Hebrew Congregation and head of the Victorian Beth Din in 1923. He supported Eastern European immigrants, founded and led the Zionist Federation of Australia, and encouraged cooperation among Australia’s dispersed communities. Returning to Britain in 1937, he served again as a military chaplain during the Second World War, was evacuated from Dunkirk, served with the RAF in the Middle East and became senior Jewish chaplain to the British forces in 1944. Appointed principal of Jews’ College in 1946 and chief rabbi in 1948, he helped consolidate postwar British Orthodoxy and European rabbinic cooperation. His refusal to confirm ר׳ לואיס ג׳ייקובס as Jews’ College principal precipitated the Jacobs Affair. He retired in 1965, was knighted in 1969, died in Lambeth and was buried at Willesden Jewish Cemetery.
title: הרב הראשי של בריטניה וחבר העמים, 1948–1965

name: ר׳ משה פיינשטיין
bio: ר׳ משה פיינשטיין (3 March 1895–23 March 1986) was a Belarusian-born American rosh yeshivah and halakhic decisor whose responsa became central to twentieth-century Orthodox practice. Born in Uzda to ר׳ דוד פיינשטיין and Faya Gittel, he learned first from his father and later in Slutsk and Shklov, regarding ר׳ פסח פרוסקין as his principal teacher; ר׳ איסר זלמן מלצר and his uncle ר׳ יעקב קנטרוביץ were also formative influences. He married Shima Kustanovich in 1920. From 1921 until leaving the Soviet Union he served as rabbi of Lyuban, sustaining communal religious life under increasing state pressure. The family reached New York in January 1937 and settled on the Lower East Side. At Mesivtha Tifereth Jerusalem he developed its advanced beit midrash and semikhah programme and, after 1938, served as rosh yeshivah. Rabbis and individuals worldwide submitted practical questions to him concerning ritual, family law, commerce, medicine, technology and American communal life. His method combined close Talmudic analysis with direct attention to facts and human circumstances, though particular rulings sometimes drew disagreement from other Orthodox authorities. Seven volumes of אגרות משה appeared during his lifetime and additional material was edited posthumously. His תלמוד commentary דברות משה and Torah discourses דרש משה represent other parts of his scholarship. He chaired Agudath Israel of America's Moetzes Gedolei HaTorah, led the Union of Orthodox Rabbis and advised Torah Umesorah and Chinuch Atzmai. He died in New York and was buried at Har HaMenuchot in Jerusalem.
title: פוסק וראש מתיבתא תפארת ירושלים

name: ר׳ אלעזר מנחם מן שך
bio: ר׳ אלעזר מנחם מן שך (1899–2001) was a Lithuanian-born Israeli Talmudist, rosh yeshiva and central leader of non-Hasidic Haredi Judaism. Born in Vabalninkas, he entered the Panevėžys yeshivah as a child and continued in Slabodka, Slutsk and Kletsk amid war, revolution and institutional displacement. His principal teachers included ר׳ איסר זלמן מלצר and ר׳ אהרן קוטלר. He immigrated to Mandatory Palestine in 1940, taught in Jerusalem, Petah Tikva and Rehovot, and joined the senior faculty of Ponovezh Yeshiva in Bnei Brak in the early 1950s. There his analytical lectures and personal authority shaped generations of Lithuanian yeshivah students. His אבי עזרי offers novellae on ר׳ משה בן מימון’s משנה תורה, while later collections preserve letters, public addresses and mussar thought. From the 1970s he became an influential communal and political leader, helping sponsor Shas in 1984 and founding Degel HaTorah in 1988 after conflict within Agudath Israel. His positions on Zionism, secular culture, military service and party politics were often forceful and controversial. He died in Tel Aviv in 2001 and was buried in Bnei Brak after an exceptionally large funeral.
title: בעל אבי עזרי; ראש ישיבת פוניבז׳

name: ר׳ יעקב ישראל קניבסקי
bio: ר׳ יעקב ישראל קניבסקי (17 June 1899–10 August 1985), commonly called the Steipler and בעל קהלות יעקב, was a Novardok-trained Talmudist, yeshiva teacher, author, and influential leader of Lithuanian Haredi Judaism in Israel. He was born in Tashan, Ukraine, to ר׳ חיים פרץ קניבסקי and Bracha; after his father’s death the family returned to Hornostaypil, the town from which his enduring sobriquet was derived. He entered the Novardok yeshiva network as a boy, followed it east to Homel during the First World War, endured conscription into the Red Army, and later crossed into Poland to join its Białystok centre. In 1927 he married Pesha Miriam Karelitz, sister of ר׳ אברהם ישעיהו קרליץ, and served as a senior lecturer at Beit Yosef–Novardok in Pinsk. In 1934 he immigrated to Mandatory Palestine and became head of the movement’s Beit Yosef yeshiva in Bnei Brak. His analytical studies, first issued in separate volumes and later reorganized as קהלות יעקב on the Talmud, became his principal scholarly legacy. He also wrote on biblical interpretation, faith, ethics, Torah study, and halakhic measurements; his correspondence was collected posthumously. Although increasingly consulted for counsel and communal guidance, he devoted most of his time to study, writing, teaching, and receiving petitioners. He died in Bnei Brak and was buried beside ר׳ אברהם ישעיהו קרליץ in the Shomrei Shabbos cemetery.
title: הסטייפלר; בעל קהלות יעקב

name: ר׳ חיים לייב הלוי שמואלביץ
bio: ר׳ חיים לייב הלוי שמואלביץ (1902–1979) was a leading Lithuanian Talmudist, mussar teacher and rosh yeshiva of Mir. Born in Kovno and raised partly in Stutchin, he studied at Shaarei Torah in Grodno under ר׳ שמעון יהודה שקופ before joining Mir about 1924–25. He married Chana Miriam, daughter of ר׳ אליעזר יהודה פינקל, and began giving regular shiurim in 1936. During the Second World War he helped lead Mir's extraordinary flight from Soviet-occupied Lithuania through Vladivostok and Kobe to Shanghai. With ר׳ יחזקאל לוינשטיין he sustained the refugee yeshiva's learning and communal life there until 1947. After six months with the transplanted yeshiva in the United States, he joined Mir in Jerusalem, becoming its rosh yeshiva after his father-in-law's death in 1965. His analytical Talmud lectures reflected the influence of ר׳ שמעון יהודה שקופ, while his intensely delivered ethical discourses drew large audiences. שיחות מוסר, based on talks delivered in 1971–73, became an influential mussar classic; extensive Talmudic manuscripts were published posthumously as שערי חיים. He died in Jerusalem on 3 Tevet 5739 and was buried at Har HaMenuchot.
title: ראש ישיבת מיר בליטא, בשנחאי ובירושלים

name: ר׳ מנחם מענדל שניאורסון
bio: ר׳ מנחם מענדל שניאורסון (18 April 1902–12 June 1994), the seventh Lubavitcher Rebbe, transformed Chabad-Lubavitch from a displaced Hasidic court into an international network of religious education, outreach and social institutions. Born in Nikolaev, he grew up in Yekaterinoslav, where his father ר׳ לוי יצחק שניאורסון served as rabbi and kabbalist under the Russian Empire and Soviet rule. He married Chaya Mushka, daughter of ר׳ יוסף יצחק שניאורסון, in Warsaw in 1928. The couple lived in Berlin and Paris; he studied university subjects in Berlin and earned an engineering diploma in Paris in 1937, while continuing Torah study and work for his father-in-law. They escaped occupied France and reached New York in 1941. He directed Merkos L’Inyonei Chinuch, Machne Israel and Kehot before accepting Chabad leadership in 1951. From 770 Eastern Parkway he expanded shlichut, sending couples to build enduring Jewish institutions, and promoted public mitzvah campaigns, Torah publication, women’s education and use of modern communications for religious purposes. His talks and letters address halakhah, Hasidic thought, biblical interpretation, science, education and public affairs. In his final years, messianic expectation intensified among followers; after his death without a successor, interpretations of those expectations remained contested within Chabad. His institutional system nevertheless continued expanding globally.
title: הרבי מליובאוויטש השביעי

name: ר׳ יהושע דוד פוברסקי
bio: ר׳ יהושע דוד פוברסקי (1902–1999), generally called ר׳ דוד פוברסקי, was a Lithuanian-style Talmudist, mussar teacher and rosh yeshiva who shaped more than five decades of learning at the rebuilt Ponovezh Yeshiva in Bnei Brak. Born David Kustonowitz in Lyuban to ר׳ שלום, he studied as a boy in Slutsk with ר׳ איסר זלמן מלצר. During the First World War he crossed wartime borders using papers bearing the name Yehoshua Povarsky; he retained that surname and added Yehoshua to his own name. His formative education passed through the displaced Slabodka and Mir yeshivot, the Kelm Talmud Torah and the prewar Ponovezh world. ר׳ ירוחם ליבוביץ profoundly influenced his mussar outlook. After marrying Tzipporah, daughter of ר׳ דוד דב קרייזר, he studied in the Baranovich circle of ר׳ אלחנן וסרמן and also delivered shiurim. He escaped Europe with his family in 1941 and initially headed the Tomchei Temimim yeshiva in Tel Aviv. In 1944 ר׳ יוסף שלמה כהנמן recruited him to lead the newly re-established Ponovezh Yeshiva beside ר׳ שמואל רוזובסקי; ר׳ אלעזר מנחם מן שך later joined its senior leadership. His teaching combined exact textual analysis, conceptual clarity, the disciplined ethical inheritance of Kelm and close personal responsibility for students. He avoided political prominence and centered his public life on daily learning and transmission. His Talmudic novellae and lectures were published in the multi-volume ישועת דוד and שיעורי ר׳ דוד, while ישמרו דעת and משכיל לדוד preserve his mussar discourses.
title: ראש ישיבת פוניבז׳ ובעל ישועת דוד

name: ר׳ יצחק יעקב וייס
bio: ר׳ יצחק יעקב וייס (15 February 1902–14 June 1989), known from his responsa as the מנחת יצחק, was a Galician-born halakhic decisor and rabbinical judge. Born in Dolyna, he moved with his family during the First World War to Munkács, where he studied under his father ר׳ יוסף יהודה וייס and received ordination from ר׳ חיים אלעזר שפירא; ר׳ מאיר אריק and ר׳ שמעון גרינפלד further shaped his practical-halakhic method. After marrying the daughter of ר׳ פנחס צימטבוים, he became a dayan in Grosswardein (Oradea) in 1929. He survived the Holocaust through hiding and a perilous escape into Romania, but his first wife died in Bucharest. Returning to Oradea, he helped rebuild communal life and adjudicated difficult agunah cases. Manchester appointed him senior dayan in December 1948; for two decades he led its beth din, strengthened kashrut supervision and helped establish a rabbinic kollel. In 1970 he joined the Edah HaChareidis court in Jerusalem, became presiding raavad in 1972 and gaavad in 1979. His ten-volume שו״ת מנחת יצחק applied classical halakhah to postwar, medical, technological, commercial and ritual questions. He died in Jerusalem and was buried on the Mount of Olives.
title: בעל מנחת יצחק וגאב״ד העדה החרדית

name: ר׳ יוסף דוב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק
bio: ר׳ יוסף דוב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק (27 February 1903–9 April 1993), commonly called Joseph B. Soloveitchik, “the Rav,” or הגרי״ד, was a Talmudist, halakhic authority, religious philosopher and formative leader of American Modern Orthodoxy. Born in Pruzhany in the Russian Empire, he was taught the Brisker method by his father ר׳ משה סולובייצ׳יק and descended from ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק and the בית הלוי. After study in Warsaw and Berlin, he completed a doctorate on Hermann Cohen and married Tonya Lewit. In 1932 they settled in Boston, where he led the Orthodox Vaad HaIr, opened a yeshivah and co-founded Maimonides School. From 1941 he succeeded his father at Yeshiva University’s Rabbi Isaac Elchanan Theological Seminary, commuting from Boston and ordaining close to two thousand rabbis. He led the Rabbinical Council of America’s Halakhah Commission and became an influential Religious Zionist voice. His writings joined rigorous halakhic categories with modern philosophy and existential reflection. איש ההלכה, ובקשתם משם, קול דודי דופק, “The Lonely Man of Faith,” “Confrontation” and The Halakhic Mind address religious personality, covenant, suffering, Zionism, interfaith boundaries and the relation between revelation and modern thought. He retired from regular teaching as illness advanced in the mid-1980s, died in Boston and was buried in West Roxbury.
title: הגרי״ד, ראש ישיבת רבנו יצחק אלחנן וממנהיגי האורתודוקסיה המודרנית

name: ר׳ יצחק הוטנר
bio: ר׳ יצחק הוטנר (1906–1980) was a Polish-born American rosh yeshiva and religious thinker whose teachings joined Lithuanian Talmudic learning, mussar, Hasidic motifs and the thought of ר׳ יהודה ליוואי and ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק. Born in Warsaw, he studied at the Slabodka yeshiva under ר׳ נתן צבי פינקל and accompanied its new branch to Hebron in 1925. He survived the 1929 Hebron massacre because he was away that weekend. He later studied philosophy at the University of Berlin while maintaining an intensive rabbinic intellectual life. After travels in Mandatory Palestine and Europe, he settled in the United States in the 1930s and became the dominant teacher and, from the early 1940s, rosh yeshiva of Yeshiva Rabbi Chaim Berlin in Brooklyn. His festival discourses were edited as the multi-volume פחד יצחק, a distinctive synthesis of conceptual analysis and spiritual teaching. In September 1970 he, his wife, daughter and son-in-law ר׳ יהונתן דוד were among the passengers held in Jordan after the hijacking of TWA Flight 741; they were released later that month. In his final years he established Yeshiva Pachad Yitzchok in Jerusalem. He died there in 1980 and was buried on the Mount of Olives.
title: ראש ישיבת רבנו חיים ברלין ובעל פחד יצחק

name: ר׳ פנחס קהתי
bio: ר׳ פנחס קהתי (1910–1976), born Pinchas Gechtman near Rivne in Volhynia, was a Religious Zionist educator whose משניות מבוארות transformed modern Mishnah study. He studied in yeshivot and at Warsaw's Tachkemoni religious teachers' seminary, became active in Hashomer HaDati and HeHalutz HaMizrahi, and immigrated to Mandatory Palestine in 1935. In Jerusalem he began university studies but financial pressure led him into teaching, movement work and eventually long employment at Bank Mizrahi. He remained deeply involved in HaPoel HaMizrahi and Bnei Akiva. Seeking a commentary accessible to young people and readers without advanced Talmudic training, he began issuing a weekly study pamphlet in 1955: fourteen explained mishnayot for the Mishnah Yomit cycle, together with halakhah and Bible study. By 1964 he had covered all six orders. Revised as a book series, the commentary combined clear modern Hebrew with traditional commentators, relevant Talmudic discussion and halakhic conclusions. It received the Rav Kook Prize in 1967 and became known simply as “Kehati.” He also composed melodies, winning the first Hasidic Song Festival in 1969 with צמאה נפשי. He died in Jerusalem in 1976 and was buried on the Mount of Olives.
title: מחבר משניות מבוארות — משניות קהתי

name: ר׳ שלמה זלמן אויערבך
bio: ר׳ שלמה זלמן אויערבך (1910–1995) was a Jerusalem posek and rosh yeshiva renowned for applying halakhah to electricity, medicine and modern technology. Born and raised in Shaarei Chesed, he was the son of ר׳ חיים יהודה לייב אויערבך, founder of the Shaar HaShamayim kabbalists’ yeshiva. He studied at Etz Chaim under ר׳ איסר זלמן מלצר and, after marriage, at the Bnei Zion kollel led by ר׳ צבי פסח פרנק, where he specialized in agricultural commandments dependent on the Land of Israel. His 1935 מאורי אש was the first sustained monograph devoted to electricity in halakhah. In 1949 he became rosh yeshiva of Kol Torah in Bayit Vegan and held that post until his death, while continuing to live simply in Shaarei Chesed and travel by public bus. His responsa מנחת שלמה became a central source for modern halakhic questions, and his rulings strongly shaped שמירת שבת כהלכתה by his student ר׳ יהושע ישעיה נויבירט. Although consulted worldwide, he declined prestigious official posts and was known for personal warmth and avoidance of factional politics. He died in Jerusalem in 1995 and was buried at Har HaMenuchot.
title: ראש ישיבת קול תורה ופוסק הלכה

name: ר׳ יוסף שלום אלישיב
bio: ר׳ יוסף שלום אלישיב (1910–2012) was a Jerusalem halakhic decisor and one of the most influential leaders of late twentieth- and early twenty-first-century Lithuanian Haredi Judaism. Born in Šiauliai, he was the only child of ר׳ אברהם לוינסון and Chaya Musha, daughter of the kabbalist ר׳ שלמה אלישיב, whose surname the family adopted. They immigrated to Mandatory Palestine in 1924 with assistance from ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק and settled in Mea Shearim. In 1930 he married Sheina Chaya, daughter of ר׳ אריה לוין. He was appointed to Jerusalem’s regional rabbinical court in 1950 and to the Great Rabbinical Court in 1955, serving until his resignation in 1974. Thereafter his daily learning and rulings centred on the modest Tiferet Bachurim synagogue in Mea Shearim. His influence grew through oral rulings transmitted by students, especially on family law, ritual practice, medicine and technology; edited responsa and lectures appeared as קובץ תשובות and הערות. After the deaths of ר׳ אלעזר מנחם מן שך and ר׳ אלעזר מנחם שך’s successors, he became the pre-eminent halakhic address of much of the non-Hasidic Haredi world. He died at Shaare Zedek Medical Center aged 102 and was buried at Har HaMenuchot.
title: פוסק הלכה ודיין בבית הדין הרבני הגדול

name: ר׳ שמואל הלוי ואזנר
bio: ר׳ שמואל הלוי ואזנר (4 September 1913–3 April 2015), widely known as the שבט הלוי, was a Vienna-born rabbinic judge, yeshiva head and influential halakhic decisor. The son of Yosef Zvi and Rachel Wosner, he studied in Vienna and then at Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin under ר׳ מאיר שפירא and ר׳ שמעון מזליחוב. After marrying Rivka Gelber and spending time in Pressburg, he immigrated to Mandatory Palestine in 1939. In Jerusalem he studied at Yeshivat Dushinsky, served as a religious judge and taught in the Geula neighbourhood. At the encouragement of ר׳ אברהם ישעיהו קרליץ and other senior rabbis, he moved to Bnei Brak around 1947. There he became rabbi and av beth din of the Zikhron Meir neighbourhood and re-established Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin, which he led for more than six decades. He later created a beth hora'ah and a network of communities associated with his rulings. His eleven-volume שו״ת שבט הלוי treats all divisions of the Shulchan Arukh and applies halakhah to medicine, electricity, electronic sensors, transport, kashrut and changing domestic technology. Students also published his Talmudic lectures, discourses and practical rulings. He died in Bnei Brak on the first night of Passover 2015.
title: בעל שבט הלוי ורב זכרון מאיר

name: ר׳ אהרן יהודה לייב שטיינמן
bio: ר׳ אהרן יהודה לייב שטיינמן (1914–2017) was a Lithuanian-trained Israeli rosh yeshiva and a central leader of Haredi Judaism. Born in Kamyenyets and raised in nearby Brisk, he studied at Toras Chessed under ר׳ משה סוקולובסקי and heard ר׳ יצחק זאב סולובייצ׳יק; he later studied in Kobrin and Kletsk under ר׳ פסח פרוסקין and ר׳ אהרן קוטלר. Threatened by Polish conscription, he left in 1937 for Yeshivat Etz Chaim in Montreux, Switzerland, where he taught alongside ר׳ משה סולובייצ׳יק. During the Second World War he was interned in a Swiss labour camp. He married the refugee Tamar Kornfeld and immigrated to Mandatory Palestine in 1945. After teaching at Yeshivat Chafetz Chaim in Kfar Saba, he settled in Bnei Brak, led Ponevezh’s junior yeshiva and later Yeshivot Gaon Yaakov and Orחות תורה. His multi-volume אילת השחר offers analytic studies of Torah and Talmud. From the late 1990s, and especially after 2012, he exercised exceptional influence over Lithuanian Haredi education and public affairs while maintaining an austere home at 5 Chazon Ish Street. He died in Bnei Brak aged 103 and was buried in the Ponevezh cemetery.
title: ראש ישיבה וממנהיגי הציבור החרדי־ליטאי

name: ר׳ שלמה וולבה
bio: ר׳ שלמה וולבה (1914–2005) was a German-born Israeli mussar teacher whose educational method shaped the postwar yeshivah world. Born in Berlin as August Wilhelm Wolbe, he studied briefly at the University of Berlin and at the Hildesheimer Rabbinical Seminary before seeking intensive yeshivah study in Frankfurt and Montreux. He then entered the Mir Yeshiva in the town of Mir, now Belarus, where ר׳ ירוחם ליבוביץ became his decisive teacher. As a German citizen he could not accompany the Mir students eastward during the war; he remained in neutral Sweden, worked with Jewish refugees and wrote for Swedish Jews. He immigrated to Mandatory Palestine in 1946 and became a central spiritual educator at Yeshivat Be’er Yaakov, serving there for more than three decades. In later years he taught in Jerusalem and developed small-group frameworks for advanced mussar study. His two-volume עלי שור joined disciplined self-observation, classical mussar and close attention to normal psychological development; זריעה ובנין בחינוך distilled his approach to parenting and education. He opposed both shallow emotionalism and coercive religious growth, stressing gradual acquisition, human dignity and sustained personal work. He died in Jerusalem and was buried at Har HaMenuchot.
title: בעל עלי שור; משגיח ומחנך מוסרי

name: ר׳ אליעזר יהודה ולדנברג
bio: ר׳ אליעזר יהודה ולדנברג (10 December 1915–21 November 2006), universally known from his responsa as the ציץ אליעזר, was a Jerusalem halakhic decisor and rabbinical judge. Born in Jerusalem to ר׳ יעקב גדליה ולדנברג, he studied at Etz Chaim under ר׳ איסר זלמן מלצר and displayed unusual literary productivity while still young, publishing דבר אליעזר in 1934. He helped establish Yeshivat Shaar Zion and served a community near the old Shaare Zedek Hospital, where sustained contact with physicians helped shape his command of medical halakhah. From 1957 he presided over the Jerusalem district rabbinical court and later served on Israel’s Great Rabbinical Court. His multi-volume ציץ אליעזר addresses the full range of practical halakhah and became especially influential in questions of hospitals, surgery, fertility, pregnancy, transplantation and end-of-life care. He also wrote הלכות מדינה on public law in a Jewish state. The Israel Prize in Rabbinical Literature was awarded to him in 1976. He remained rooted in Jerusalem throughout his life, died there aged ninety, and was buried at Har HaMenuchot.
title: בעל ציץ אליעזר; דיין בבית הדין הרבני הגדול

name: ר׳ שלמה גורן
bio: ר׳ שלמה גורן (1917–1994), born Shlomo Goronchik, was a Polish-born Israeli rabbi, scholar and institution-builder. His family immigrated in 1925 and helped found Kfar Hasidim. A prodigy at Etz Chaim and Hebron yeshivot, he published Nezer HaKodesh while still a teenager and also studied at the Hebrew University. He joined the Haganah in 1936. During the War of Independence he organized religious services, formulated military halakhah and personally worked to recover fallen soldiers for burial. He founded and led the IDF Military Rabbinate, remaining its chief until 1971, and famously sounded the shofar at the Western Wall in June 1967. He then served as Chief Rabbi of Tel Aviv-Jaffa and as Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of Israel from 1972 to 1983. His extensive writings address the Jerusalem Talmud, Temple law, Shabbat, festivals, military ethics and the halakhah of the Jewish state.
title: Founder of the IDF Military Rabbinate and Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of Israel

name: ר׳ עובדיה יוסף
bio: ר׳ עובדיה יוסף (1920–2013) was an Iraqi-born Israeli halakhic authority, Rishon LeZion and spiritual leader of Shas. His family moved from Baghdad to Jerusalem when he was four. He studied at Porat Yosef under ר׳ עזרא עטייה. From 1947 to 1950 he served in Cairo as deputy chief rabbi and head of the rabbinical court. Back in Israel he served on rabbinical courts in Petah Tikva and Jerusalem, became a Supreme Rabbinical Court judge, Chief Rabbi of Tel Aviv-Jaffa, and Sephardi Chief Rabbi of Israel from 1973 to 1983. His responsa sought to restore a unified Sephardi practice centered on the rulings of ר׳ יוסף קארו while addressing modern state, medical and technological questions. His major works include Yabia Omer, Yechaveh Da'at and Chazon Ovadia. He received the Israel Prize in 1970.
title: Rishon LeZion, Sephardi Chief Rabbi of Israel and author of Yabia Omer

name: ר׳ עמנואל יעקובוביץ
bio: ר׳ עמנואל יעקובוביץ (1921–1999) was a German-born British Orthodox rabbi, pioneering scholar of Jewish medical ethics and Chief Rabbi of the United Hebrew Congregations of the Commonwealth from 1967 to 1991. Born in Königsberg and raised partly in Berlin, he reached Britain as a teenage refugee from Nazism. After rabbinic and university study in London, he served the Brondesbury Synagogue, became Chief Rabbi of Ireland, and then led New York’s Fifth Avenue Synagogue. His 1959 book Jewish Medical Ethics helped establish Jewish bioethics as a modern field. As Chief Rabbi he emphasized Jewish education and represented traditional Judaism in British public life. Knighted in 1981 and made a life peer in 1988, he was the first British chief rabbi to enter the House of Lords. He died in London in 1999.
title: Baron Jakobovits; Chief Rabbi of the United Hebrew Congregations of the Commonwealth

name: ר׳ מרדכי ברויאר
bio: ר׳ מרדכי ברויאר (14 May 1921–24 February 2007; Marcus Breuer) was a German-born Israeli rabbi, Bible teacher and scholar of the Masoretic text. Born in Karlsruhe to ר׳ שמשון ברויאר and Leah Frankel, he was a great-grandson of ר׳ שמשון רפאל הירש. His family immigrated to Mandatory Palestine when he was twelve. He studied in Jerusalem at Horev, Yeshivat Kol Torah and Yeshivat Hebron, then taught Tanakh from 1947 in religious-Zionist schools and yeshivot, including Yeshivat Kfar HaRoeh, Yeshivat HaDarom, Jerusalem College for Women and Yeshivat Har Etzion. His textual work sought the authoritative Tiberian Masoretic text by comparing manuscripts, Masorah and early printed editions. When he gained access to the Aleppo Codex, its readings closely confirmed the text he had independently reconstructed. His editions entered the Da'at Mikra series, the Horev Tanakh and, with graphic design inspired by the Aleppo Codex, כתר ירושלים—the Hebrew University's official Bible edition and the edition used for ceremonial presentations by the Knesset. Breuer also developed שיטת הבחינות, accepting many literary divisions identified by documentary criticism while interpreting the Torah's contrasting voices as intentionally revealed divine perspectives whose combination expresses a fuller truth. The method generated lasting debate within religious Bible study. His books include פיסוק טעמים שבמקרא, כתר ארם צובה והנוסח המקובל של המקרא, פרקי מועדות and פרקי בראשית. He received the Bialik Prize in 1984, the Israel Prize for original rabbinic literature in 1999, and an honorary doctorate from the Hebrew University.
title: חוקר נוסח המקרא ומפתח שיטת הבחינות
image_credit: Photograph by Yossi; uploaded by Wikimedia user Hanay.

name: ר׳ חיים פרידלנדר
bio: ר׳ חיים בן משה פרידלנדר (23 June 1923–4 August 1986), known through the posthumous שפתי חיים series, was a German-born Israeli mussar teacher, educator and editor. Born in Breslau, he immigrated with his parents משה and צפורה to Mandatory Palestine shortly before the Second World War. After living at Kibbutz Hafetz Haim, he studied at the Lomza yeshivah in Petah Tikva and became one of the first seven students of the newly established Ponovezh Yeshiva in Bnei Brak. There he studied closely with ר׳ שמואל רוזובסקי and became a principal disciple of the mashgiach ר׳ אליהו אליעזר דסלר. Together with ר׳ אריה כרמל he helped edit מכתב מאליהו from ר׳ דסלר's writings. He founded and directed the Torat Emet school in Bnei Brak, served as mashgiach at Yeshivat HaNegev in Netivot, and returned in 1981 as mashgiach of Ponovezh. He also prepared annotated editions of writings by ר׳ משה חיים לוצאטו. After his death, his family edited his lectures and notes as שפתי חיים and מסילות חיים בחינוך.
title: השפתי חיים

name: ר׳ ירחמיאל גרשון אדלשטיין
bio: ר׳ ירחמיאל גרשון אדלשטיין (1923–2023) was a Soviet-born Israeli rosh yeshiva and a foremost leader of the Lithuanian-Haredi community. Born in Shumyachi, he studied Torah clandestinely under Soviet rule before his family immigrated to Mandatory Palestine in 1934. His father, ר׳ צבי יהודה אדלשטיין, became rabbi of Ramat HaSharon. After Lomza Yeshiva in Petah Tikva, he joined Ponevezh Yeshiva in Bnei Brak in 1943 as one of its earliest students, soon joined its faculty, and eventually became rosh yeshiva. In later life he led major Lithuanian-Haredi educational and communal bodies. He died in Bnei Brak at age one hundred.
title: Rosh Yeshiva of Ponevezh and Lithuanian-Haredi communal leader

name: ר׳ יהודה עמיטל
bio: ר׳ יהודה עמיטל (1924–2010), born Yehuda Klein in Oradea, was a Holocaust survivor, Israeli soldier, educator and founding rosh yeshiva of Yeshivat Har Etzion. Deported to forced labor in 1944 while his parents and siblings were murdered at Auschwitz, he reached Mandatory Palestine late that year, studied at Yeshivat Hevron under ר׳ איסר זלמן מלצר and ר׳ יעקב משה חרל״פ, joined the Haganah and fought in the War of Independence. At Yeshivat HaDarom he helped formulate the hesder model combining Torah study with military service. He founded Yeshivat Har Etzion after the Six-Day War and invited ר׳ אהרן ליכטנשטיין to join its leadership. His religious thought emphasized human responsibility, moral seriousness, state-building without messianic certainty, and intellectual humility. He later founded Meimad and briefly served as an Israeli minister without portfolio.
title: מייסד וראש ישיבת הר עציון

name: ר׳ משה שטרנבוך
bio: ר׳ משה שטרנבוך (born 1926) is a London-born halakhic authority, Raavad of the Edah HaChareidis, and rabbi of the Gra Synagogue in Jerusalem’s Har Nof neighbourhood. Raised in a home that hosted visiting scholars, he was examined as a child by ר׳ יחזקאל אברמסקי and met ר׳ אלחנן בונם וסרמן. From 1940 he studied for a decade at Toras Emes in Stamford Hill under ר׳ משה שניידר. After the war he immigrated to Mandatory Palestine, entered Hebron Yeshiva, and formed close relationships with ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק, ר׳ אברהם ישעיהו קרליץ and ר׳ דב בריש וידנפלד. After marrying in 1954 he led Yeshivat Hamasmidim in Jerusalem. He lived in Bnei Brak from 1960, established a kollel and educational initiatives in Rosh HaAyin, and in 1980 moved to Johannesburg, where he served the Orthodox community and taught widely. He later returned to Jerusalem and settled in Har Nof. From 2003 he served as Raavad of the Edah HaChareidis; a 2023 attempt to proclaim him Gaavad remained institutionally disputed, so this record avoids presenting that title as uncontested. His extensive responsa תשובות והנהגות, calendrical work מועדים וזמנים, and Torah commentary טעם ודעת are widely studied. He remained publicly active through 2026, his centenary year.
title: ראב״ד העדה החרדית; רב בית הכנסת הגר״א בהר נוף

name: ר׳ שמריהו יוסף חיים קניבסקי
bio: ר׳ שמריהו יוסף חיים קניבסקי (1928–2022), generally called ר׳ חיים קניבסקי, was a Lithuanian-Haredi Talmudist, prolific halakhic author and communal leader. Born in Pinsk to ר׳ יעקב ישראל קניבסקי, the Steipler, and Pesha Miriam, sister of ר׳ אברהם ישעיהו קרליץ, he immigrated with his family to Mandatory Palestine in 1934 and grew up in Bnei Brak. He studied at Tiferet Zion and the Lomza Yeshiva in Petah Tikva and was deeply shaped by his father and maternal uncle. In 1951/52 he married Batsheva Esther, daughter of ר׳ יוסף שלום אלישיב, and spent decades learning in Kollel Chazon Ish. His exacting annual study cycle encompassed the Babylonian and Jerusalem Talmuds, midrash and numerous minor tractates. His ספרים cover neglected areas of halakhah and rabbinic literature: דרך אמונה systematizes agricultural law in Maimonides’ code, דרך חכמה addresses Temple law, and שונה הלכות arranges practical rulings from משנה ברורה. Although he held no conventional rabbinic office, thousands sought concise answers, advice and blessings at his Rashbam Street home. After the deaths of ר׳ יוסף שלום אלישיב and ר׳ אהרן יהודה ליב שטינמן, he became one of the most authoritative public figures in Lithuanian Haredi society. He died at home in Bnei Brak on 18 March 2022 and was buried in the city’s Zikhron Meir cemetery.
title: בעל דרך אמונה; פוסק ומנהיג הציבור הליטאי

name: ר׳ נחום אליעזר רבינוביץ
bio: ר׳ נחום אליעזר רבינוביץ (1928–2020), born Norman Louis Rabinovitch in Montreal, was a Canadian-British-Israeli halakhist, mathematician and Religious Zionist rosh yeshiva. He studied with ר׳ פנחס הירשפרונג and at Ner Israel in Baltimore under ר׳ יעקב יצחק רודרמן, receiving semikhah while pursuing university mathematics; he later earned a doctorate from the University of Toronto. After congregational rabbinates in Charleston and Toronto, he became principal of Jews’ College in London in 1971. There he trained a generation of British rabbis; ר׳ יונתן זקס described him as a primary role model. In 1982 he moved to Ma’ale Adumim to head Yeshivat Birkat Moshe, which he led until his death. His fourteen-volume יד פשוטה on משנה תורה combines close manuscript work, Talmudic analysis, history and a systematic reading of ר׳ משה בן מימון. His responsa address military service, conversion, technology, medicine and public law in a Jewish state. He supported women’s advanced Torah study and helped establish the independent conversion court גיור כהלכה. Marked by rationalism, intellectual independence and confidence in human freedom, he became a formative decisor of Religious Zionism. He died in Ma’ale Adumim and was buried at Har HaMenuchot.
title: בעל יד פשוטה; ראש ישיבת ברכת משה

name: ר׳ ישראל יעקב פישר
bio: ר׳ ישראל יעקב פישר (1928–2003) was a Jerusalem posek and dayan, rabbi of Zikhron Moshe and, from 1996, Av Beit Din of the Edah HaChareidis. Born to ר׳ אהרן פישר in the Perushim community, he studied at Yeshivat Etz Chaim and became a close student of ר׳ איסר זלמן מלצר. After early service as a neighborhood rav and moreh tzedek, he joined the Edah HaChareidis court and became one of Jerusalem’s most frequently consulted practical halakhic authorities. His nine-volume responsa אבן ישראל treats ritual, family, medical and public questions, alongside volumes of Torah novellae. His rulings were sometimes notably independent, but the record distinguishes documented positions from later anecdotes.
title: ראב״ד העדה החרדית; בעל אבן ישראל

name: ר׳ דוד פיינשטיין
bio: ר׳ דוד פיינשטיין (1929–6 November 2020) was an American rosh yeshivah, halakhic authority, communal leader and author. He was born in Lyuban, then in the Soviet Union and now in Belarus, to ר׳ משה פיינשטיין and Shima Kustanovich Feinstein. His father served as Lyuban's rabbi while maintaining religious life under increasingly hostile Soviet conditions. In January 1937 the family emigrated to New York and settled on Manhattan's Lower East Side, where ר׳ משה became head of Mesivtha Tifereth Jerusalem (MTJ). ר׳ דוד learned at MTJ under his father, later taught advanced classes there and became closely identified with both the yeshivah and the neighborhood in which he lived for the rest of his life. After his father's death in 1986, he succeeded him as rosh yeshivah of MTJ's elementary school, high school and kollel. He also became one of the most frequently consulted Orthodox decisors in the United States. The Orthodox Union sought his rulings on kashrut, youth work and new practical questions; rabbis and individuals approached him on ritual, commercial, medical and communal law. He served for decades on the Moetzes Gedolei HaTorah of Agudath Israel of America, belonged to Torah Umesorah's Vaad Roshei Yeshiva, and was involved with Chinuch Atzmai, Agudas Harabbonim and other institutions. His leadership was notable for reserve, accessibility and reluctance to cultivate public ceremony. His published Torah teaching appeared chiefly under the title קול דודי. English volumes adapted from his lectures cover the Torah, Haftarot, Esther and Ruth; other books address the Passover Seder and the structure and laws of the Jewish calendar. He also wrote the explanations of the Masoretic notes printed at the end of each weekly portion in ArtScroll's Stone Chumash. The publications often relied on compilers and adapters, so their bibliographic descriptions distinguish his authorship and lectures from editorial work by others. ר׳ דוד died in New York on 6 November 2020. After a funeral outside MTJ at 145 East Broadway, his coffin was flown to Israel; a second funeral left Jerusalem's Shamgar Funeral Home, and he was buried on Har HaMenuchot near ר׳ משה פיינשטיין. His significance lies in the combination of institutional continuity, practical halakhic judgment, wide communal responsibility and a deliberately understated personal manner.
title: ראש ישיבת מתיבתא תפארת ירושלים ופוסק הלכה

name: ר׳ אברהם יהושע העשיל טברסקי
bio: ר׳ אברהם יהושע העשיל טברסקי (6 October 1930–31 January 2021), commonly known as Rabbi Dr. Abraham J. Twerski, was an American Hasidic rabbi, psychiatrist, addiction specialist and prolific author. Born in Milwaukee, he was a son of ר׳ יעקב ישראל טברסקי of Hornosteipel and Devorah Leah Halberstam, linking the Chernobyl and Bobov dynasties. He graduated from Hebrew Theological College and received semikhah in 1951, then served beside his father at Congregation Beth Jehudah. Concluding that effective pastoral counseling required professional training, he entered Marquette University and completed medical school in 1960. He moved to Pittsburgh, where he became clinical director of psychiatry at St. Francis Hospital and an associate professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine. In 1972 he opened Gateway Rehabilitation Center in Beaver County, developing a treatment model that joined medicine, Twelve-Step recovery, spirituality and restoration of self-worth. He later helped establish Shaar Hatikvah for released prisoners in Israel. Across more than sixty books—clinical, self-help, Jewish ethical, autobiographical and Torah works—he repeatedly addressed addiction, shame, self-esteem, family relationships, domestic abuse and spiritual growth. He moved to Jerusalem in 2015 and died there from complications of COVID-19. His work made addiction treatment and previously hidden family problems subjects of sustained discussion within Orthodox Jewish communities.
title: רב חסידי, פסיכיאטר ומחלוצי הטיפול בהתמכרויות

name: ר׳ אפרים דב לנדו
bio: ר׳ אפרים דב לנדו (born 5 April 1930), generally known as ר׳ דב לנדו or Rav Dov Lando, is an Israeli rosh yeshiva and leader of the Lithuanian-Haredi community. He was born in Zgierz near Łódź, Poland, to ר׳ טוביה יוסף לנדוי and Devorah, in a family descended from the Strikov Hasidic dynasty. The family immigrated to Mandatory Palestine in 1935 and settled in Rehovot. After studying at Yeshivat HaYishuv HeHadash, he entered Ponovezh Yeshiva, where his principal teachers included ר׳ דוד פוברסקי and ר׳ שמואל רוזובסקי; he also learned for a period with ר׳ אליהו אליעזר דסלר. He subsequently spent about a year at Hebron Yeshiva and regarded ר׳ אברהם ישעיהו קרליץ as his formative halakhic and intellectual authority. He married Adina, a descendant of the Slabodka leadership, and joined Slabodka Yeshiva in Bnei Brak as a teacher. In the early 1980s he became one of its roshei yeshiva, eventually serving alongside ר׳ משה הלל הירש. His published scholarship includes זכר טוב, זכר דבר, מנחת דבר, חידושי רבי דב לנדו, גליונות רבי דב לנדו and the correspondence שיח דבר. Since 2023 he has held a central public-leadership role and serves as president of Vaad HaYeshivot.
title: ראש ישיבת סלבודקה ונשיא ועד הישיבות

name: ר׳ זלמן נחמיה גולדברג
bio: ר׳ זלמן נחמיה גולדברג (1931–2020), widely called הגרז״ן, was a Jerusalem posek, dayan and teacher. Born in Minsk to ר׳ אברהם and Freidel Goldberg, he reached Mandatory Palestine with his family in 1935. He studied at Yeshivat Etz Chaim, Hebron Yeshiva and Ponevezh Yeshiva, and married Rachel, daughter of ר׳ שלמה זלמן אויערבאך. Goldberg served for decades in Israel's rabbinical-court system and became av bet din of the Rabbinical High Court. His decisions addressed marriage and divorce, conversion, monetary law, medicine, technology and the legal status of the Land of Israel. He headed the Sadigura kollel and taught at Jerusalem College of Technology, Yeshivat Torat Emet and other institutions, while examining thousands of candidates for rabbinic ordination. In 2008 he became editor-in-chief of the Talmudic Encyclopedia. His lectures and rulings were gathered in several volumes, notably לב המשפט and בנין אריאל. He died at Hadassah Ein Kerem in Jerusalem and was buried on the Mount of Olives.
title: פוסק, דיין ואב בית הדין הרבני הגדול

name: ר׳ חנוך הכהן ארנטרוי
bio: ר׳ חנוך הכהן ארנטרוי (1932–2022) was a German-born British dayan who shaped Orthodox religious courts in Britain and continental Europe. Born in Frankfurt to ר׳ ישראל ארנטרוי and Bertha Jung, he escaped Nazi Germany with his family in 1938. After British schooling he studied at Gateshead Yeshiva. In 1960 he founded Sunderland Kollel and led it until 1979, when he became communal rabbi and head of the Manchester Beth Din. Chief Rabbi ר׳ עמנואל יעקובוביץ appointed him Rosh Beth Din of London in 1984. During more than two decades he strengthened professional standards in conversion, gittin, kashrut and financial adjudication and supported the North-West London eruv. After retiring in 2007 he continued European work as head of the European Beth Din, supervised conversion systems for the Conference of European Rabbis and helped establish the renewed Hildesheimer Rabbinical Seminary in Berlin. He maintained close consultation with ר׳ יוסף שלום אלישיב and ר׳ שלמה זלמן אויערבך. He died in London on 24 November 2022. His legacy lies chiefly in judicial leadership and institution-building rather than a published authored sefer.
title: ראש בית הדין של לונדון וראב״ד אירופה

name: ר׳ נתן גשטטנר
bio: ר׳ נתן גשטטנר (1932–2010), known from his responsa as בעל להורות נתן, was a Hungarian-born Israeli posek, dayan and rosh yeshiva. Born in Győr to ר׳ עמרם גשטטנר and Malka Schreiber, he descended from the families of ר׳ מאיר איזנשטט and ר׳ משה סופר. The family moved to Újpest in 1933. As a boy he studied with ר׳ בנימין ברגר; after the Holocaust he continued for two formative years in Antwerp under ר׳ יוסף גרינוולד, later the Pupa rebbe. In Israel he became close to ר׳ דב בריש ויידנפלד. In 1965 he was appointed rabbi of Kiryat Agudat Israel in Bnei Brak, where he established the פנים מאירות institutions and served as a dayan and halakhic teacher for the rest of his life. His principal achievement, שו״ת להורות נתן, grew to many volumes and addresses every division of practical Jewish law. Other writings include נתן פריו on Talmudic tractates and studies connected with תקפו כהן and calendrical law. He died in Bnei Brak in 2010.
title: בעל להורות נתן; רב קריית אגודת ישראל וראש ישיבת פנים מאירות

name: ר׳ אהרן ליכטנשטיין
bio: ר׳ אהרן ליכטנשטיין (1933–2015) was a leading Modern Orthodox Talmudist, educator and religious thinker. Born in Paris to ר׳ יחיאל and Bluma Lichtenstein, he escaped occupied France with his family and reached the United States in 1941. He studied at Yeshiva Rabbi Chaim Berlin under ר׳ יצחק הוטנר, then at Yeshiva University, where ר׳ יוסף דב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק became his principal teacher and later father-in-law. Alongside rabbinic ordination, he earned a doctorate in English literature at Harvard. After teaching and heading the kollel at Yeshiva University, he made aliyah in 1971 to lead Yeshivat Har Etzion in Alon Shvut with ר׳ יהודה עמיטל. Over four decades he shaped its rigorous analytical learning, educational culture and synthesis of Torah commitment with moral responsibility and engagement with general culture. His essays addressed halakhah, faith, religious Zionism, ethics, feminism and the value of secular learning, while his Talmudic lectures were published in multi-volume series. Awarded the Israel Prize for Torah Literature in 2014, he died in 2015 and was buried at Har HaMenuchot.
title: ראש ישיבת הר עציון; חתן פרס ישראל

name: ר׳ אריה משה אליהו קפלן
bio: ר׳ אריה משה אליהו קפלן (1934–1983), born Leonard Martin Kaplan in the Bronx, was an American Orthodox rabbi, physicist, translator and exceptionally prolific popularizer of Judaism. After a largely secular childhood he entered Torah Vodaath, then studied at the Mir Yeshiva in Jerusalem and received ordination from ר׳ אליעזר יהודה פינקל. Returning to the United States, he earned degrees in physics at the University of Louisville and University of Maryland and conducted magnetohydrodynamics research at the National Bureau of Standards. He subsequently served congregations in Iowa, Tennessee and New York before devoting himself increasingly to writing, editing and youth education. Working with the Orthodox Union and NCSY, he produced lucid introductions to Jewish belief and practice that became influential in the baal-teshuvah movement. His annotated The Living Torah combined translation with archaeological, linguistic and rabbinic material. He also translated and interpreted ספר יצירה, ספר הבהיר, דרך ה׳ and other classics, and restored meditation to serious discussion within Orthodox Jewish spirituality. He died suddenly in Brooklyn at forty-eight and was buried on the Mount of Olives. Several major works appeared posthumously from completed manuscripts and edited lectures.
title: מחבר, מתרגם ומבאר מחשבת ישראל וקבלה

name: ר׳ יצחק זילברשטיין
bio: ר׳ יצחק זילברשטיין (born 1934) is an Israeli halakhic authority, dayan and the long-serving rabbi of the Ramat Elchanan neighbourhood in Bnei Brak. Born in Będzin, Poland, to ר׳ דוד יוסף זילברשטיין, he immigrated with his family to Mandatory Palestine as a child. He studied at Etz Chaim in Jerusalem and at Slabodka Yeshiva in Bnei Brak. He married Aliza Shoshana, daughter of ר׳ יוסף שלום אלישיב; through this marriage he was also brother-in-law to ר׳ חיים קניבסקי. He taught for several years at the Lucerne yeshiva in Switzerland and later headed the Beit David institutions in Holon before becoming rabbi of Ramat Elchanan. His rulings are especially influential in medical ethics, emergency care and the application of halakhah to unusual practical cases. His numerous publications include תורת היולדת, חשוקי חמד and the עלינו לשבח series, often presenting complex legal questions through memorable real-life situations. He serves as av beit din and is widely consulted by physicians, hospitals and rabbinic authorities. As of 2026 he remains alive and active; therefore this corrected record uses a null death year and carries his map presence through the project’s current final year.
title: רב שכונת רמת אלחנן ופוסק הלכה

name: ר׳ אביגדור נבנצל
bio: ר׳ אביגדור נבנצל (born 1935) is a Jerusalem posek, teacher and former rabbi of the Old City. Born to Yitzhak Ernst Nebenzahl, later Israel’s state comptroller, he was educated in Jerusalem and became a close student of ר׳ שלמה זלמן אויערבאך. After the Six-Day War he joined the renewed Torah community of the Jewish Quarter, taught at Yeshivat HaKotel and served for decades as rabbi of the Old City before transferring that office to his son ר׳ חזקיהו נבנצל. He is senior rosh yeshiva at Yeshivat Netiv Aryeh, teaches at Yeshivat HaKotel, and is associated with the Ramban Synagogue and Kollel Kotel, which he founded. His published rulings and lectures address the festivals, prayer, Shabbat, Tanakh, ethics and the sanctity of Jerusalem.
title: רבהּ לשעבר של העיר העתיקה; ראש ישיבה בישיבת נתיב אריה

name: ר׳ חיים אבישלום כהן פרחיה
bio: ר׳ חיים אבישלום כהן פרחיה (1935–2019), widely known as ‘החלבן’ (the milkman), was a Tel Aviv–Givatayim kabbalist and teacher whose public profile combined ordinary manual work with intensive study of Kabbalah. Born in Jaffa to Blanca and ר׳ עזרא כהן פרחיה, from a Turkish Jewish family, he attended Alliance schools in Tel Aviv and worked for decades in the family dairy founded in 1930, later called Mahlevat Deshen. From about 1965 he studied esoteric Torah with a Tel Aviv circle headed by ר׳ משה יעקב רביקוב, ‘the Shoemaker.’ He married Doba Edith and had four children. Although he did not cultivate conventional rabbinic dress, his private counsel and weekly lessons eventually drew broad audiences. He taught Talmud and Kabbalah at Kollel Givat HaShalom in Givatayim and at the Ramat HaSharon hesder yeshiva led by ר׳ ראובן ששון. From 2010, ר׳ ראובן edited his recorded teachings into the sixteen-volume טללי חיים series. After a prolonged illness he died at Sheba Medical Center on 13 August 2019 and was buried in Jerusalem’s Sanhedria Cemetery. This record corrects an earlier false identification with ר׳ יעקב משה הלל.
title: המקובל המכונה החלבן

name: ר׳ משה שפירא
bio: ר׳ משה שפירא (28 May 1935–7 January 2017), commonly rendered Rav Moshe Shapira or Shapiro, was an Israeli rosh yeshiva and one of the most influential contemporary teachers of Jewish thought and aggadah. Born in Petah Tikva to ר׳ יצחק מאיר שפירא and Rachel, he inherited the Kelm mussar tradition through his father’s family. He studied at Ohr Yisrael, Ponevezh, Knesset Yisrael–Hebron and Beit Yehuda, absorbing the approaches of ר׳ יעקב ניימן, ר׳ יוסף רוזובסקי, ר׳ יחיאל מיכל פיינשטיין and ר׳ יצחק הוטנר. He helped establish Yeshivat Tushiya at Tifrach and Yeshivat Beit HaTalmud, later led Beis Binyomin in Stamford, and taught generations of students in Jerusalem, especially at Ohr Somayach and the Wolfson kollelim. His teaching united close Talmudic analysis with Maharal, the Vilna Gaon and his school, Kabbalah, Hasidic thought and mussar. Much of his influence was oral: students recorded and edited extensive lecture series, including רעה אמונה, אפיקי מים, ממעמקים and שיעורי הגר״מ שפירא. He also guided outreach and adult-education organizations and founded institutions for advanced study. His densely structured lectures shaped a broad network of yeshiva educators and ba’alei teshuvah teachers in Israel and abroad.
title: ראש ישיבה, בעל מחשבה ומורה לאגדה

name: ר׳ סיריל קיצ׳נר האריס
bio: ר׳ סיריל קיצ׳נר האריס (1936–2005) was a Scottish-born British rabbi who served as chief rabbi of the Union of Orthodox Synagogues of South Africa from 1987 to 2004. Educated and ordained at Jews’ College in London, he served British congregations and as senior Jewish chaplain to the British Armed Forces before leading St John’s Wood Synagogue. In South Africa he guided an anxious Jewish community through apartheid’s final years and the transition to multiracial democracy. He publicly supported full democracy, worked with Nelson Mandela, offered a prayer at Mandela’s 1994 presidential inauguration and blessed Mandela’s 1998 marriage to Graça Machel. He and his wife Ann helped establish African Jewish humanitarian initiatives, including what became Afrika Tikkun. His leadership joined Orthodox communal consolidation with public advocacy for reconciliation, social responsibility and Israel. After retiring in 2004, he died the following year in Hermanus and was buried in Jerusalem.
title: הרב הראשי של דרום אפריקה

name: ר׳ משה הלל הירש
bio: ר׳ משה הלל הירש (born 1936) is an American-born Israeli rosh yeshiva and a senior leader of Lithuanian Haredi Jewry. Born Milton Hirsch in Brooklyn to Romanian immigrants David and Malvina Hirsch, he studied at Rabbi Jacob Joseph School and then at Beth Medrash Govoha in Lakewood, where ר׳ אהרן קוטלר became his formative teacher. In 1963 he married Avigail, daughter of Slabodka rosh yeshiva ר׳ מרדכי שולמן, and settled permanently in Israel. He joined the teaching staff of the Slabodka Yeshiva in Bnei Brak and, after his father-in-law’s death in 1982, became one of its roshei yeshiva. His lectures emphasize sustained analytical Talmud study, disciplined character and the transmission of the Lakewood-Slabodka tradition. He serves on Degel HaTorah’s מועצת גדולי התורה and, following the death of ר׳ ירחמיאל גרשון אדלשטיין in 2023, emerged together with ר׳ דב לנדו as one of the principal spiritual leaders of the Lithuanian-Haredi public. His teachings circulate in recorded lectures, the weekly משנת רמ״ה sheets and the edited 2024 volume משנת רבי משה הלל on Bava Kamma. He remains active at Slabodka in Bnei Brak in 2026.
title: ראש ישיבת סלבודקה וממנהיגי הציבור הליטאי

name: ר׳ ישראל מאיר לאו
bio: ר׳ ישראל מאיר לאו (born 1937) is a Holocaust survivor, author, communal rabbi, former Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of Israel and chairman of the Yad Vashem Council. Born in Piotrków Trybunalski to ר׳ משה חיים לאו and Chaya, he was known as Lulek. His father and much of the community were murdered at Treblinka. In 1944 his mother saved him during a selection by directing him toward his older brother Naphtali; she was murdered at Ravensbrück. The brothers endured the Częstochowa labor camp and Buchenwald, where American forces liberated the eight-year-old child in April 1945. They reached Mandatory Palestine that summer. Raised initially by his uncle ר׳ מרדכי פוגלמן in Kiryat Motzkin, he later studied at Kol Torah with ר׳ שלמה זלמן אויערבאך and at Knesset Hezekiah and Ponovezh. Ordained in 1960, he advanced through synagogue and neighborhood rabbinates in Tel Aviv, became chief rabbi of Netanya in 1979, chief rabbi of Tel Aviv–Jaffa in 1988, and Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of Israel from 1993 to 2003. He returned to the Tel Aviv post from 2005 until retiring in 2018. His rabbinate emphasized public communication, Holocaust memory, interreligious dialogue and engagement across religious and secular Israeli society. Awarded the Israel Prize for lifetime achievement in 2005, he has chaired the Yad Vashem Council since 2008. His autobiography אל תשלח ידך אל הנער connects the child survivor’s memory to his later religious leadership.
title: הרב הראשי לישראל לשעבר ויו״ר מועצת יד ושם

name: ר׳ זלמן ברוך מלמד
bio: ר׳ זלמן ברוך מלמד (born 1937) is a leading Religious Zionist rosh yeshiva, founder of Yeshivat Beit El and a prominent disciple of ר׳ צבי יהודה הכהן קוק. Born in Tel Aviv, he studied at Kfar HaRoeh, Knesset Hezekiah and Kerem B’Yavneh before transferring to Mercaz HaRav in 1954. ר׳ צבי יהודה הכהן קוק appointed him to teach there in 1965 and later charged him with founding a new yeshiva. In 1977–78 he led a group of students to Beit El, where he established Yeshivat Beit El and became the community's rabbi. He subsequently helped build a wide institutional network, founded Arutz Sheva and organized the Vaad Rabanei Yesha. He left the municipal rabbinate in 2013 but has continued as rosh yeshiva, teaching Talmud, halakhah and the Religious Zionist thought of ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק and ר׳ צבי יהודה הכהן קוק. His recorded lectures and books, including נתיבי אמונה, have extended that teaching to a large public audience.
title: מייסד וראש ישיבת בית אל

name: ר׳ גרשון לופיאן
bio: ר׳ גרשון לופיאן (approximately 1938–30 January 2014) was a British dayan, communal rabbi and widely consulted halakhic authority. He was the eldest son of ר׳ אריה לייב לופיאן, later rosh yeshiva in Gateshead, and Tzipa, and a grandson of the mussar teacher ר׳ אליהו לופיאן. His education linked the British and Israeli yeshiva worlds: he learned at Gateshead Yeshiva, under his grandfather at Kfar Hasidim, at Hebron Yeshiva in Jerusalem, and under ר׳ חנוך העניך אהרנטרוי at Sunderland Kollel. Sources report that he received semikhah from ר׳ שלמה זלמן אויערבך, ר׳ חנוך העניך פאדווא and ר׳ משה פיינשטיין. From 1976 until retiring in 2006 he led Yeshurun Federation Synagogue in Edgware, afterward remaining its emeritus rabbi. As a dayan of the Federation of Synagogues he became especially known for practical rulings concerning family law, niddah and marital difficulties. Memorial accounts consistently emphasize that he answered questions at all hours, considered the circumstances of the individual rather than treating halakhah mechanically, and trained younger rabbis through practical shimush and semikhah. After retirement he continued making himself available by telephone for questions from Britain and abroad. He died in London on 30 January 2014 and was buried the next day at Edmonton Federation Cemetery. The Federation’s later ShailaText service was dedicated to his memory as an extension of his accessible, confidential model of pastoral halakhic guidance.
title: דיין, פוסק ורב קהילת ישורון באדג׳וור

name: ר׳ יעקב אריה אלתר
bio: ר׳ יעקב אריה אלתר (born 18 May 1939) is the eighth Gerrer Rebbe and a senior leader of Agudath Israel's rabbinic council. He was born in Łódź to ר׳ שמחה בונים אלתר, later the sixth Gerrer Rebbe and author of לב שמחה, and Yuta Hena, a daughter of ר׳ נחמיה אלתר. He was named for ר׳ יעקב אריה גוטרמן of Radzymin. In 1940, amid the destruction of Polish Jewish life, he left Europe with his father and grandfather ר׳ אברהם מרדכי אלתר and reached Mandatory Palestine. He grew up in Jerusalem, studied at the Etz Chaim Talmud Torah and was formed within the post-war rebuilding of Ger. He married Shoshana, daughter of ר׳ מנחם מנדל וייץ, a leader of Yeshivat Chiddushei HaRim. For many years he lived and studied in Bnei Brak, particularly at the Rashi Shtiebel. After his father became Rebbe in 1977, ר׳ יעקב אריה increasingly handled institutional and political affairs for Ger and Agudath Israel. His uncle ר׳ פינחס מנחם אלתר led the dynasty from 1992 until March 1996; following his death, ר׳ יעקב אריה succeeded him. His leadership has centred on an extensive network of Gerrer synagogues, yeshivot, kollelim and schools in Israel and diaspora communities, alongside membership in the presidium of מועצת גדולי התורה. He relocated from Bnei Brak to Jerusalem in 2011, and the movement's principal court and large central beit midrash are now based there. Because he is living, reports concerning wealth, politics and internal disputes are treated as contemporary claims requiring careful sourcing rather than settled biography. No independently authored major sefer is securely catalogued under his name; published institutional volumes chiefly preserve addresses, guidance or events held in his presence.
title: האדמו״ר מגור

name: ר׳ צבי שכטר
bio: ר׳ צבי שכטר (born 1941) is an American Orthodox rosh yeshiva, Talmudist and halakhic decisor. Raised in a rabbinic family in Scranton, Pennsylvania, he studied at Yeshiva University and became an assistant to ר׳ יוסף דוב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק at age twenty-two. He received semikhah and an M.A. in Hebrew literature in 1967 and that year joined the RIETS faculty as its youngest rosh yeshiva. Since 1971 he has headed the Marcos and Adina Katz Kollel and holds the Nathan and Vivian Fink Distinguished Professorial Chair in Talmud. As posek for the Orthodox Union’s Kashruth Division, he addresses contemporary questions in kashrut, medicine, public safety, communal governance and technology. His original halakhic works include ארץ הצבי, בעקבי הצאן and גינת אגוז. נפש הרב, מפניני הרב and דברי הרב preserve teachings, practices and recollections of ר׳ יוסף דוב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק. His thousands of lectures and extensive responsa have made him an influential authority within contemporary Modern Orthodoxy.
title: ראש ישיבה ב־RIETS ופוסק של מערך הכשרות של OU

name: ר׳ נתן צבי פינקל
bio: ר׳ נתן צבי פינקל (1943–2011) was an American-born Lithuanian yeshiva leader who transformed the Mir Yeshiva in Jerusalem into one of the world’s largest centres of Torah study. Born in Chicago to Eliyahu Meir and Sara Finkel, he attended Jewish day school and Ida Crown Jewish Academy. During a family visit to Israel in 1957, his great-uncle ר׳ אליעזר יהודה פינקל recognized his aptitude and encouraged him to study at Mir. He returned permanently at seventeen and learned under leading Mir scholars, including ר׳ חיים קמיל. In 1964 he married Leah, daughter of ר׳ בנימין ביינוש פינקל. In February 1990 he succeeded his father-in-law as rosh yeshiva. Despite Parkinson’s disease, he continued teaching, mentoring students and fundraising internationally. Under his leadership Mir expanded from roughly one thousand students to several thousand, added study halls and developed branches including Mir Brachfeld in Modi’in Illit. He served on Degel HaTorah’s Council of Torah Sages and became known for personal attentiveness to students as much as institutional growth. He died suddenly in Jerusalem in 2011 and was buried on Har HaMenuchot. His mussar talks were collected posthumously as שיחות רבי נתן צבי.
title: ראש ישיבת מיר בירושלים

name: ר׳ ישראל הגר
bio: ר׳ ישראל הגר (נולד ב־19 באפריל 1945, ו׳ באייר תש״ה) הוא האדמו״ר מוויז׳ניץ בבני ברק. הוא נולד בתל אביב לר׳ משה יהושע הגר, בעל ישועות משה, וללאה אסתר לבית פנט. לאחר לימודיו במוסדות ויז׳ניץ נשא את שרה חנה חיה, בת ר׳ משולם זושא טברסקי מצ׳רנוביל. אביו מינה אותו לרב קריית ויז׳ניץ בבני ברק, אך משבר פנימי בשושלת הרחיק אותו במשך שנים ממוקדי ההנהגה. בראשית שנות האלפיים חודש הקשר עם אביו, והוא שב בהדרגה למעמד ציבורי. לאחר פטירת ר׳ משה יהושע הגר בשנת 2012 הוכתר ר׳ ישראל כממשיכו וכאחד משני האדמו״רים המרכזיים של ויז׳ניץ בבני ברק, לצד אחיו ר׳ מנחם מנדל הגר המנהיג חצר נפרדת. הוא עומד בראש מערכת בתי מדרש, ישיבות ומוסדות חסד בישראל ובעולם וחבר במועצת גדולי התורה של אגודת ישראל. דברי תורתו והשיחות הנמסרות בטישים נערכים בקובצי החצר, אך אין לייחס לו ספר מודפס בעל תאריך ודאי ללא קטלוג מוסמך. הוא חי ומכהן בבני ברק, ולכן שנת פטירתו נשמרת null; שנת 1954 השגויה ברשומה הישנה תוקנה ל־1945.
title: האדמו״ר מוויז׳ניץ בבני ברק

name: ר׳ מרדכי וויליג
bio: ר׳ מרדכי וויליג (born 1947) is an American Orthodox rosh yeshiva, communal rabbi and halakhic authority. Educated at Yeshiva University, he received a B.A. in mathematics in 1968, an M.S. in Jewish history and RIETS semikhah in 1971. He joined the Mazer School of Talmudic Studies as a rosh yeshiva in 1973 and later became Rosh Kollel of the Bella and Harry Wexner Kollel Elyon and a supervisor of advanced dayanus training. Since 1974 he has served as spiritual leader of the Young Israel of Riverdale in the Bronx. He has been active in the Beth Din of America and in developing standards and agreements addressing Jewish divorce, conversion, marriage and contemporary medical ethics. His principal published series, עם מרדכי, applies close Talmudic analysis to Berakhot, Shabbat, the festivals and practical Shulchan Arukh. He holds Yeshiva University’s Rabbi Dr. Sol Roth Chair in Talmud and Contemporary Halakhah and continues to teach and publish.
title: ראש ישיבה וראש כולל ב־RIETS ורב ישראל הצעיר של ריברדייל

name: ר׳ יונתן זקס
bio: ר׳ יונתן זקס (8 March 1948–7 November 2020), formally ר׳ יעקב צבי בן דוד אריה, was a British Orthodox rabbi, philosopher, educator, broadcaster, and public intellectual. Born in Lambeth and educated in Finchley, Cambridge, Oxford, London, and rabbinical colleges, he credited formative 1968 conversations with ר׳ יוסף דוב סולובייצ׳יק and ר׳ מנחם מנדל שניאורסון with directing him toward the rabbinate. After serving Golders Green and Western Marble Arch synagogues and leading Jews’ College, he became Chief Rabbi of the United Hebrew Congregations of the Commonwealth in 1991 and served until 2013. He promoted Jewish education, communal renewal, interfaith responsibility, and an intellectually confident Judaism able to engage modern democratic society. His writing joined Torah commentary with moral philosophy and public theology, addressing covenant, human dignity, religious violence, science, politics, and social fragmentation. He published more than forty books, delivered the annual Covenant & Conversation commentaries, and taught at institutions including King’s College London, New York University, and Yeshiva University. Knighted in 2005, he entered the House of Lords as the crossbench life peer Baron Sacks of Aldgate in 2009 and received the Templeton Prize in 2016. He died in London after cancer and was buried at Bushey New Cemetery. His speeches, manuscripts, correspondence, and Chief Rabbinate papers are preserved in the National Library of Israel.
title: Chief Rabbi; Baron Sacks of Aldgate

name: ר׳ ישכר דב רוקח
bio: ר׳ ישכר דב רוקח (born 1948) is the fifth Belzer Rebbe and the leader responsible for the postwar consolidation and global expansion of Belz Hasidism. Born in Tel Aviv to ר׳ מרדכי רוקח of Bilgoray and Miriam, he was the nephew of ר׳ אהרן רוקח, the fourth Belzer Rebbe, who became his guardian after his father died in 1949. Following ר׳ אהרן’s death in 1957, the child was recognized as the dynasty’s future leader but did not assume active leadership until 1966. In 1965 he married Sarah, daughter of ר׳ משה יהושע הגר of Vizhnitz, and lived for a period near the Vizhnitz court in Bnei Brak. As rebbe he rebuilt the educational, communal and welfare network of Belz in Israel, Europe and North America. The movement’s institutional centre shifted decisively to Jerusalem, where the immense Belz Great Synagogue was dedicated in 2000 after years of construction. He is a member of Agudat Israel’s Council of Torah Sages. His oral discourses and teachings are preserved in Belz publications including אמרי קודש; they should be distinguished from similarly titled works of earlier Belzer rebbes. He remains the serving Belzer Rebbe, so his death year is correctly null.
title: האדמו״ר מבעלזא

name: ר׳ שמעון גרשון רוזנברג
bio: ר׳ שמעון גרשון רוזנברג (1949–2007), הידוע בראשי התיבות שג״ר, היה ראש ישיבה והוגה דתי־ציוני שחיבר בין לימוד תורה, חסידות, קבלה, אקזיסטנציאליזם ופוסטמודרניזם. הוא נולד בירושלים, למד בישיבת נתיב מאיר ובישיבת כרם ביבנה, הוסמך לרבנות ושירת בחיל השריון. במלחמת יום הכיפורים נפצע קשה בקרבות ברמת הגולן, ושניים מחבריו לצוות נהרגו; החוויה נעשתה יסוד מרכזי בהגותו על אמונה, שבר ושפה דתית. לאחר המלחמה למד במרכז הרב ואצל ר׳ שלמה פישר והחל ללמד בישיבת הכותל. בהמשך היה בין מקימי ישיבת מקור חיים ושימש בבית מורשה. בשנת 1996 ייסד עם ר׳ יאיר דרייפוס את ישיבת שיח יצחק, תחילה בבית שמש ולאחר מכן באפרת. דרכו הציעה נאמנות הלכתית בצד פתיחות לעולם הרוח העכשווי, והעמידה דור של תלמידים וחוקרים. רוב ספריו נערכו משיעורים ומכתבי יד בידי מכון כתבי הרב שג״ר, בחייו ולאחר פטירתו מסרטן בשנת 2007. הוא נקבר בהר הזיתים בירושלים.
title: הרב שג״ר; מייסד ישיבת שיח יצחק

name: ר׳ אשר זליג וייס
bio: ר׳ אשר זליג וייס (born 25 March 1953) is an American-born Israeli posek, dayan and rosh yeshivah, widely known from his מנחת אשר series.
